ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Investigation into Trajectory KL Regularization for Diffusion Models
PROPOSAL: We will conduct experiments comparing the performance of KL-regularized reinforcement learning algorithms to their unregularized counterparts for fine-tuning diffusion models in text-to-image generation, document layout generation, and molecule generation. We will use the Dall-E 2 diffusion model pre-trained on LAION-2B dataset, and the DeepMind lab's simple diffuseddenoise-diff model pre-trained on torchvision datasets for document layout and molecule generation. Both models will be fine-tuned to a reward function based on fidelity to the reference dataset. We will use trajectory KL regularization in the form of the Jensen-Shannon divergence between the denoising trajectory distribution of the pre-trained model and that of the fine-tuned one. We will measure model performance using metrics such as Inception Score, Fréchet Inception Distance (FID score), and precision/recall of generated samples.
CONTROLS: We will include controls for unregularized PPO, standard PPO with trajectory KL, and a baseline of no fine-tuning.
COST: 52
PREDICTION: We expect KL-regularized PPO to demonstrate better stability and convergence than unregularized PPO, but at a potential cost to sample quality. We anticipate the worst performance for the baseline of no fine-tuning.

textes.jumeau:
ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Incorporating Model-based Reparametrization for KL-Regularized Reward Maximization
PROPOSAL: To address the challenges of computing marginal KL divergence in diffusion models, we will propose and experimentally validate a new reparameterization technique that represents the denoising process as a Markov chain and uses importance sampling to tractably compute the KL divergence between the pre-trained and fine-tuned distribution. This idea leverages the intermediate noisy states generated during the sampling process and is inspired by the work on variational objective importance sampling.
CONTROLS: We will compare our method against the standard KL regularization requiring importance sampling (KL-Is), as well as against the control where we ignore the KL term.
COST: 216
PREDICTION: We expect our approach to significantly improve the overall performance of KL-regularized fine-tuning, reducing the gap with the plain reward maximization baseline. However, it might still underperform in very complex settings where computing good approximate beliefs about the marginal requires excessive computation.

textes.jumeau:
ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Hierarchical and Progressive Diffusion Denoising for Fine-tuning
PROPOSAL: We hypothesize that fine-tuning a diffusion model benefits from leveraging the hierarchical generative structure of the model. Specifically, we will design a new hierarchical KL regularization objective that targets different levels of the generative process (e.g., noise schedule, denoising steps) separately. For each level, the KL divergence will be estimated by considering the respective guided denoising process. Our approach allows the model to adapt to the target distribution at different scales, which should improve fine-tuning performance. We will implement this idea using the sinusoidal noise schedule and several major and minor denoising steps in the DALL-E 2 diffusion model pre-trained on LAION-2B dataset.
CONTROLS: We will compare our results against the standard trajectory KL regularization (proposed earlier) and the control where we ignore KL regularization.
COST: 388.88
PREDICTION: We expect the hierarchical approach to demonstrate an increase in sample quality and coverage in smaller target data subsets, but at a possible increase in training time and computational cost. Early convergence with the majority of controls will appear successful after a few rounds where KL-trianing seems harmful.

textes.jumeau:
ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Fine-tuning Diffusion Models without Rewards using denoising fidelity
PROPOSAL: We will explore the use of denoising fidelity as an alternative optimization objective for fine-tuning diffusion models in the absence of a target reward function. In our setup, the model learns to correct its outputs to match the target data distribution, rather than directly optimizing a reward signal. This approach effectively samples multiple acceptable outputs and selects the best one in each iteration. Our experiments will focus on correcting the distribution of a pre-trained flow model on the chest X-ray dataset.
CONTROLS: We will compare our results against the standard trajectory KL regularization and against the control where we finely tune using a target reward function with jejurious cut-off baseline test.
COST: 700
PREDICTION: We expect to see improvement in sample quality and accuracy for several minor subsets of target data and small noise std treatment scale set in the outcome experiments. Result could be prohibitively unstable otherwise if sampling denoising models thwarted without knowledge improvement from drift incentive.

textes.jumeau:
ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Transforming Denoising Steps for Optimized Fine-tuning
PROPOSAL: We propose transforming denoising steps in diffusion models to dynamically adapt to the target distribution during fine-tuning. By introducing learnable weights to adjust the denoising process, the model can selectively emphasize or de-emphasize different aspects of the target data distribution. We will implement this idea using a neural network to predict the weights for each denoising step, and compare its performance against the hierarchical and progressive denoising approach (proposed earlier).
CONTROLS: We will compare our approach against the standard trajectory KL regularization and against the control where we ignore KL regularization.
COST: 900
PREDICTION: We expect our approach to yield improvement in sample quality and diversity, especially when fine-tuning is performed on smaller target data subsets or with limited computational resources.

textes.jumeau:
ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Multi-language and Multi-step Intrinsic Rewards for Diffusion Models
PROPOSAL: We will explore the use of intrinsic rewards during fine-tuning of diffusion models to promote exploration of the sampling space. Specifically, we will design a reward function that encourages the model to visit diverse areas of the data manifold and to explore different aspects of the target distribution. We will also extend this approach to multi-language and multi-step settings, and evaluate its effectiveness on text-to-image generation, document layout generation, and molecule generation tasks.
CONTROLS: We will compare our approach against the standard KL regularization and against the control where we ignore KL regularization.
COST: 3440
PREDICTION: We expect intrinsic rewards to improve the diversity and exploratory capabilities of the diffusion model, leading to better fine-tuning results on various tasks. However, we also anticipate that this may come at the cost of slower convergence rates and increased computational complexity.

textes.jumeau:
ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Meta-learning Diffusion Models for Transfer Fine-tuning
PROPOSAL: We propose using meta-learning to adapt diffusion models to new target data distributions during fine-tuning. Specifically, we will train a meta-model that can adapt the diffusion model's weights and hyperparameters to the new target distribution. This will allow the model to generalize better across different fine-tuning tasks and distributions. We will evaluate the performance of our meta-model on a variety of text-to-image generation, document layout generation, and molecule generation tasks.
CONTROLS: We will compare our meta-learning approach against the standard fine-tuning methods and against the revised hierarchical and progressive denoising approach (proposed earlier).
COST: 5448
PREDICTION: We expect our meta-learning approach to yield state-of-the-art results on transfer fine-tuning tasks, especially when the target data distribution is complex or has multiple modes.

textes.jumeau:
ACTION: ADD
TITLE: KL-Regularized Fine-Tuning for Diffusion Models with Analytical Relaxation
PROPOSAL: We investigate a method that relaxes the intractable marginal KL divergence in KL-regularized fine-tuning of diffusion models, by exactly computing the KL divergence upper-bound between the entire denoising trajectories, obtained through the change of variables formula in stochastic differential equations. This method, similar to the recently proposed KL-SGD method, uses a subspace projection to solve for the optimal conditioning of the KL divergence upper-bound, and uses this to derive an analytical update rule for the policy.
CONTROLS: We compare against our proposed method with the KL term either ignored (i.e., plain PPO) or dropped (i.e., plain PPO).
COST: 11.7 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: We expect to see a significant improvement in the stability of fine-tuning with our proposed relaxation, with a slight drop in performance compared to the standard KL term (which we expect to be unstable in large-scale settings), but with a clear reduction in the variance of the fine-tuning process.

textes.jumeau:
ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Leverage Denoising Trajectory Structure for Fine-Tuning
PROPOSAL: We develop a novel approach to fine-tune diffusion models by leveraging the structure of the denoising trajectories in the optimization process. Specifically, we propose to use a neural network to model the interaction between the conditioning variable (e.g., text prompts) and the denoising steps. This neural network is used to re-weight the importance of different denoising steps during fine-tuning, allowing us to take into account the dependencies between the steps. We then optimize the re-weighting network along with the policy using a joint objective.
CONTROLS: We compare against our proposed method with the standard KL term (still ignoring KL regularizaton) and our previous proposal (1) that used an analytical relaxation of the KL divergence.
COST: 140 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: We expect to see a significant improvement in fine-tuning performance, as the fine-tuning process becomes more aware of the dependencies between denoising steps and the interplay between conditioning variables and denoising steps. However, we may encounter convergence issues due to the complexity of the joint optimization process.

textes.jumeau:
ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Model-Free Fine-Tuning with Rejection Sampling for Diffusion Models
PROPOSAL: We propose a novel model-free fine-tuning method for diffusion models using rejection sampling. Specifically, we use a loss function that requires the model to produce samples with high rewards, while rejecting samples with low rewards. We investigate two different implementations of this method: one that simply rejects samples below a certain reward threshold, and another that uses a neural network to model the reward function and reject samples based on this model. We then compare these methods against our previous proposals and a standard model-based fine-tuning approach.
CONTROLS: For the rejection sampling methods, we compare against our proposed method that uses the analytical relaxation of the KL divergence (1) and the method that leverages denoising trajectory structure (2). For the model-based fine-tuning approach, we compare against the standard KL-regularized fine-tuning with the KL term either ignored or dropped.
COST: 450 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: We expect to see a significant improvement in fine-tuning performance, especially for tasks with clear reward signals, due to the ability to focus on high-reward samples and reject low-reward ones. However, we may encounter convergence issues due to the rejection sampling process, and the model-based approach may require more fine-tuning iterations to converge.

ACTION: REVISE 3
TITLE: Model-Free Fine-Tuning with Rejection Sampling and Hierarchical Rejection for Diffusion Models
PROPOSAL: We revise our previous proposal to introduce an additional hierarchical rejection component. Specifically, we use a hierarchical neural network to model the distribution of rewards, and use this to reject samples at multiple levels of abstraction. ACTION: ADD
TITLE: KL-Regularized Fine-Tuning for Diffusion Models with Analytical Relaxation
PROPOSAL: We investigate a method that relaxes the intractable marginal KL divergence in KL-regularized fine-tuning of diffusion models, by exactly computing the KL divergence upper-bound between the entire denoising trajectories, obtained through the change of variables formula in stochastic differential equations. This method, similar to the recently proposed KL-SGD method, uses a subspace projection to solve for the optimal conditioning of the KL divergence upper-bound, and uses this to derive an analytical update rule for the policy.
CONTROLS: We compare against our proposed method with the KL term either ignored (i.e., plain PPO) or dropped (i.e., plain PPO).
COST: 35 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: We expect to see a significant improvement in the stability of fine-tuning with our proposed relaxation, with a slight drop in performance compared to the standard KL term (which we expect to be unstable in large-scale settings), but with a clear reduction in the variance of the fine-tuning process.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Leverage Denoising Trajectory Structure for Fine-Tuning
PROPOSAL: We develop a novel approach to fine-tune diffusion models by leveraging the structure of the denoising trajectories in the optimization process. Specifically, we propose to use a neural network to model the interaction between the conditioning variable (e.g., text prompts) and the denoising steps. This neural network is used to re-weight the importance of different denoising steps during fine-tuning, allowing us to take into account the dependencies between the steps. We then optimize the re-weighting network along with the policy using a joint objective.
CONTROLS: We compare against our proposed method with the standard KL term (still ignoring KL regularizaton) and our previous proposal (1) that used an analytical relaxation of the KL divergence.
COST: 420 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: We expect to see a significant improvement in fine-tuning performance, as the fine-tuning process becomes more aware of the dependencies between denoising steps and the interplay between conditioning variables and denoising steps. However, we may encounter convergence issues due to the complexity of the joint optimization process.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Model-Free Fine-Tuning with Rejection Sampling for Diffusion Models
PROPOSAL: We propose a novel model-free fine-tuning method for diffusion models using rejection sampling. Specifically, we use a loss function that requires the model to produce samples with high rewards, while rejecting samples with low rewards. We investigate two different implementations of this method: one that simply rejects samples below a certain reward threshold, and another that uses a neural network to model the reward function and reject samples based on this model. We then compare these methods against our previous proposals and a standard model-based fine-tuning approach.
CONTROLS: For the rejection sampling methods, we compare against our proposed method that uses the analytical relaxation of the KL divergence (1) and the method that leverages denoising trajectory structure (2). For the model-based fine-tuning approach, we compare against the standard KL-regularized fine-tuning with the KL term either ignored or dropped.
COST: 1350 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: We expect to see a significant improvement in fine-tuning performance, especially for tasks with clear reward signals, due to the ability to focus on high-reward samples and reject low-reward ones. However, we may encounter convergence issues due to the rejection sampling process, and the model-based approach may require more fine-tuning iterations to converge.

We then use this reward function to determine which samples to reject. We also introduce a temperature parameter to control the level of rejection, allowing us to trade off between exploration and exploitation.
CONTROLS: We compare against our proposed method with the standard KL term and our previous proposals (1, 2) that used the analytical relaxation of the KL divergence and leveraged denoising trajectory structure.

ACTION: ADD 
TITLE: Leveraging Conditional Denoising of Diffusion Models for Task-Specific Guidance
PROPOSAL: We introduce a framework to leverage conditional denoising of diffusion models for task-specific guidance, where the fine-tuning process is conditioned on task-relevant information. This is achieved by concatenating the task-specific guidance signal with the input noise at each denoising step, allowing the model to produce samples that cater to the specific demands of the downstream task. We will test this approach on real-world text-to-image generation, document layout generation, and molecule generation datasets, and compare the results against unregularized PPO, KL-regularized PPO, Trajectory KL Divergence for Diffusion Models, rejection sampling optimization, and the learned upstream representation (proposal 4).
CONTROLS: We compare against all existing proposals and test the sensitivity of the results to different task-relevant guidance signals.
COST: 16000
PREDICTION: We expect to see improved task-specific guidance and better quality generated samples across all proposals, particularly when using task-relevant information during the fine-tuning process. However, this might lead to suboptimal generalization to unseen tasks.

TITLE: Autogressive-Informed Refinement of Diffusion Models for Better Fine-Tuning
PROPOSAL: We develop a method to refine the fine-tuned diffusion model by incorporating information from an auxiliary autoregressive model. This autoregressive objective is used to inform and redirect the diffusion refinement process to improve the model's quality and guidance. We will evaluate this approach on text-to-image generation, document layout generation, and molecule generation, comparing the results against unregularized PPO, KL-regularized PPO, Trajectory KL Divergence for Diffusion Models, rejection sampling optimization, learned upstream representation, conditional denoising of diffusion models, and efficient importance resampling.
CONTROLS: We compare against all existing proposals and assess the impact of using different autoregressive models on the refinement process.
COST: 24000
PREDICTION: We expect to see improvements in fine-tuning quality and guidance, particularly when using an informed autoregressive model during refinement. However, this approach may require careful tuning of hyperparameters and might not generalize well to all domains.

ACTION: ADD 
TITLE: Investigating KL-Regularized Reward Maximization for Diffusion Models
PROPOSAL: We compare KL-regularized PPO against other reinforcement learning algorithms (e.g., REINFORCE) on a real-world text-to-image generation task using the DALL-E 2 model as the pre-trained reference. We will use the CIFAR-10 dataset for qualitative evaluation and the FFHQ dataset for quantitative evaluation.
CONTROLS: We train KL-regularized PPO, regularized PPO without KL-divergence (denoted as "unregularized"), and REINFORCE as a baseline without regularization. We will also look at the effect of hyperparameter tuning on each approach.
COST: 15000
PREDICTION: We expect KL-regularized PPO to outperform the baseline REINFORCE but may have trouble beating the unregularized variant, with unstable training a major concern.

ACTION: ADD 
TITLE: Trajectory KL Divergence for Diffusion Models
PROPOSAL: We introduce a differentiable estimator for the trajectory KL divergence between the fine-tuned and reference diffusion models. This allows us to directly maximize the trajectory KL-difference of rewards while upper-bounding the marginal KL, eliminating the need for KL-regularization and any relaxations. We will compare the fine-tuning performance of this new approach with KL-regularized PPO and other methods on text-to-image generation, document layout generation, and molecule generation.
CONTROLS: We compare with KL-regularized PPO (proposal 1) and vanilla PPO without any KL term.
COST: 24000
PREDICTION: We expect to see good performance on both fine-tuning and exploration, and a clear head-to-head victory over KL-regularized PPO in terms of both generative quality and computational efficiency, despite potential issues with stability when scaling to large datasets.

ACTION: REVISE 
TITLE: Suporting Rejection Sampling Optimization for Diffusion Models (RSO), extended to diffusion models from initial autoregressive approaches
PROPOSAL: We adapt the recently proposed rejection sampling optimization (RSO) method, initially designed for autoregressive models, to work on diffusion models. This involves selecting the highest reward samples from the batches of the stochastic process conditioned on rewards, and computing PPO on the selected samples instead of the full batches – and adding theoretical analysis of the region of applicability. We compare RSO with unregularized PPO, KL-regularized PPO (proposal 1) and Trajectory KL Divergence for Diffusion Models (proposal 2) on document layout generation and molecule generation.
CONTROLS: We compare with unregularized PPO, KL-regularized PPO, and Trajectory KL Divergence for Diffusion Models.
COST: 18000 (updated for this revision)
PREDICTION: We expect rejection sampling optimization to work better than both KL-regularized PPO and Trajectory KL Divergence for Diffusion Models and at least as good as unregularized PPO, as this approach lends itself to leveraging high-reward samples in the upper-layers of a diffusion model's state trajectory, where rewards tend to matter most – however it may fail in cases with limited data or very large model output spaces.

ACTION: REVISE 2
TITLE: Trajectory KL Divergence for Diffusion Models
PROPOSAL: We extend the Trajectory KL Divergence for Diffusion Models proposal to include attempts using non-Gaussian distributions or more general state spaces based on the next Itō differential, so that we not only generalize to these cases but we are able to  generalize its reparameterization scheme to multidimensional ODEs, improving expressiveness and potentially applicability. We will test how variants of the extended method adapt to the text-to-image generation task as well as  to document layout generation and molecule generation, with comparison with unregularized PPO, KL-regularized PPO, and rejection sampling optimization.
CONTROLS: We compare with KL-regularized PPO, unregularized PPO, and rejection sampling optimization.
COST: 30000
PREDICTION: We expect better or equivalent performance than regular PPO with the ability to generalize to more complex, differentiable spaces described by non-Gaussian distributions or general ODEs using trajectory KL method, with few potential issues in applicability to optimization of 2D points.

This regularizer is trained using the data distribution and an episodic loss over the denoising process. We will test this approach on text-to-image generation, document layout generation, and molecule generation with ablation studies on key components and baselines with pre-trained flow models without corrections.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: KL-Regularized Reward Maximization with Trajectory-Based Regularization for Diffusion Models
PROPOSAL: Conduct an experiment to compare KL-regularized reward maximization using KL divergence between entire denoising trajectories against ignoring the KL term, on the text-to-image generation task using the publicly available CLEVR dataset. Fine-tune the DALL-E model with Proximal Policy Optimization (PPO) on the given reward function. Evaluate both variants on the CLEVR validation set using the Fréchet inception distance (FID) score and the global recognition index for similarity (GRIS) metric. Compare against the baseline of no KL regularization.
CONTROLS: 3 variations of the DALL-E model with different amount of training steps, and the case where the trial sample and learning trial both used the same initial noise value
COST: 33.6
PREDICTION: We expect the KL-regularized variant to achieve better quality samples and more stable training than ignoring the KL term, but may still suffer from suboptimal performance due to the initial value function bias problem.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Multi-Step Generative Structure for Fine-Tuning Flow Models
PROPOSAL: Investigate how the multi-step generative structure of flow models can be leveraged for fine-tuning using Best-of-N sampling. Modify an existing flow model, such as Flow++ or Glow, to use a hierarchical architecture, where multiple intermediate noisy states are progressively transformed along a stochastic denoising process. Use Best-of-N sampling to select high-quality samples from the intermediate noisy states and generate the final output. Evaluate this approach on the document layout generation task using the PubLayNet dataset, comparing against the baseline of standard deterministic sampling.
CONTROLS: 3 variations of sampling schemes for intermediate noisy states (first-best, top-2/N, threshold-based) and the case where no intermediate states are used
COST: 100
PREDICTION: We expect the hierarchical architecture to improve sample quality and diversity, but potential difficulties may arise in selecting the optimal threshold or sampling scheme for intermediate noisy states.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Correcting Pre-Training Errors via Sample-Based Correction
PROPOSAL: Design an algorithm to correct pre-training errors in flow models without explicit reward, using a combination of sampling and optimization techniques. Train a small number of optimization steps on rejected samples from the pre-trained model, using an optimality-based loss function that seeks to minimize the difference between the model's output and the target distribution. Implement this approach on the molecule generation task using the ZINC dataset, evaluating its effectiveness against the baseline of standard fine-tuning on a non-adaptive sampling scheme.
CONTROLS: 2 variations of rejection criteria for samples ( based on optimized loss and using higher-order moments)
COST: 83.4
PREDICTION: We expect the sample-based correction technique to improve sample quality by adapting to target distribution deviations, but may be computationally expensive due to the need for rejecting and re-training samples.

PROPOSAL: Investigate the use of meta-learning techniques to improve fine-tuning of pre-trained diffusion models. TITLE: Evaluating the Effect of Pre-Training on Fine-Tuning for Diffusion Models
PROPOSAL: Investigate the effect of pre-training on fine-tuning for diffusion models using a range of pre-training methods and fine-tuning objectives. In this experiment, we will pre-train diffusion models using different training objectives (e.g. reconstruction loss, classification loss), and then fine-tune them using various fine-tuning objectives (e.g. KL-regularized reward maximization, rejection sampling). We will evaluate the performance of fine-tuned models on various text-to-image generation tasks using the CLEVR dataset, comparing against the baseline of standard pre-training and fine-tuning.
CONTROLS: 5 different pre-training methods, 3 different fine-tuning objectives, and 3 various pre-training and fine-tuning combinations
COST: 400
PREDICATION: We expect pre-training to influence the fine-tuning performance of diffusion models, but the optimal pre-training and fine-tuning combination may depend on the task and the model architecture, and the computational costs may be considerable.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: KL-Regularized Reward Maximization with Trajectory-Based Regularization for Diffusion Models
PROPOSAL: Conduct an experiment to compare KL-regularized reward maximization using KL divergence between entire denoising trajectories against ignoring the KL term, on the text-to-image generation task using the publicly available CLEVR dataset. Fine-tune the DALL-E model with Proximal Policy Optimization (PPO) on the given reward function. Evaluate both variants on the CLEVR validation set using the Fréchet inception distance (FID) score and the global recognition index for similarity (GRIS) metric. Compare against the baseline of no KL regularization.
CONTROLS: 3 variations of the DALL-E model with different amount of training steps, and the case where the trial sample and learning trial both used the same initial noise value
COST: 100
PREDICTION: We expect the KL-regularized variant to achieve better quality samples and more stable training than ignoring the KL term, but may still suffer from suboptimal performance due to the initial value function bias problem.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Multi-Step Generative Structure for Fine-Tuning Flow Models
PROPOSAL: Investigate how the multi-step generative structure of flow models can be leveraged for fine-tuning using Best-of-N sampling. Modify an existing flow model, such as Flow++ or Glow, to use a hierarchical architecture, where multiple intermediate noisy states are progressively transformed along a stochastic denoising process. Use Best-of-N sampling to select high-quality samples from the intermediate noisy states and generate the final output. Evaluate this approach on the document layout generation task using the PubLayNet dataset, comparing against the baseline of standard deterministic sampling.
CONTROLS: 3 variations of sampling schemes for intermediate noisy states (first-best, top-2/N, threshold-based) and the case where no intermediate states are used
COST: 300
PREDICTION: We expect the hierarchical architecture to improve sample quality and diversity, but potential difficulties may arise in selecting the optimal threshold or sampling scheme for intermediate noisy states.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Correcting Pre-Training Errors via Sample-Based Correction
PROPOSAL: Design an algorithm to correct pre-training errors in flow models without explicit reward, using a combination of sampling and optimization techniques. Train a small number of optimization steps on rejected samples from the pre-trained model, using an optimality-based loss function that seeks to minimize the difference between the model's output and the target distribution. Implement this approach on the molecule generation task using the ZINC dataset, evaluating its effectiveness against the baseline of standard fine-tuning on a non-adaptive sampling scheme.
CONTROLS: 2 variations of rejection criteria for samples ( based on optimized loss and using higher-order moments)
COST: 250
PREDICTION: We expect the sample-based correction technique to improve sample quality by adapting to target distribution deviations, but may be computationally expensive due to the need for rejecting and re-training samples.

ACTION: REVISE
TITLE: Multi-Step Generative Structure for Fine-Tuning Flow Models
PROPOSAL: Modify the previous proposal to also experiment with rejection sampling, which is a more direct method of leveraging the multi-step generative structure. In this variant, the rejection threshold is set as a function of the intermediate noisy states, allowing the model to discard low-quality samples early in the process. On the document layout generation task using the PubLayNet dataset, evaluate this rejection sampling approach against standard Best-of-N sampling and the baseline of deterministic sampling.
CONTROLS: 2 variations of rejection thresholds for intermediate noisy states (using first-best and top-2/N samples as thresholds) and the case where no intermediate states are used
COST: 150 (a reduction due to experimental similarities with previous proposal)
PREDICTION: We expect rejection sampling to be more computationally efficient than Best-of-N sampling, but may result in samples that are less diverse due to the early rejection of low-quality samples.

ACTION: REVISE
TITLE: Correcting Pre-Training Errors via Sample-Based Correction
PROPOSAL: Modify the previous proposal by incorporating uncertainty estimation of the pre-training errors, by incorporating a density estimator (e.g., kernel density estimation) to map the empirical distribution of rejected samples to a probability density function over the input space. This will allow the algorithm to properly handle false negatives ( rejected samples that are actually of high quality) and obtain better corrections. On the molecule generation task using the ZINC dataset, evaluate this additional feature against the baseline of standard fine-tuning on a non-adaptive sampling scheme.
CONTROLS: 2 variations of KDE bandwidth for uncertainity calibration and 2 additional variations for clustering interpretation of empirical densities
COST: 500 (much higher due to incorporation of a density estimator)
PREDICTION: We expect the uncertainty estimation of pre-training errors to improve the robustness of the correction algorithm and reduce the number of false negatives, but it may require significant computational resources and remain sensitive to tuning the parameters of the density estimator.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Analyzing the Benefits of Hierarchical Reverse Process for Fine-Tuning
PROPOSAL: Investigate the effect of using a hierarchical reverse process, similar to the one used in Multi-Step Generative Structure for Fine-Tuning Flow Models, on KL-Regularized Reward Maximization for diffusion models. In this experiment, we will compare the performance of KL-regularized reward maximization using a KL divergence between entire denoising trajectories against KL-regularized reward maximization using a KL divergence between entire hierarchical reverse processes. Evaluate this approach on the text-to-image generation task using the CLEVR dataset, comparing against the baseline of standard KL-regularized reward maximization.
CONTROLS: 3 variations of hierarchical reverse process architectures and 3 different reward functions used for training
COST: 350
PREDICTION: We expect using a hierarchical reverse process to improve the performance of KL-regularized reward maximization by providing a better initialization of the policy and reducing the initial value function bias problem. However, this may incur additional computational costs and require careful tuning of the hierarchical reverse process architecture and reward function.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Improving Fine-Tuning with Meta-Learning for Diffusion Models
PROPOSAL: Investigate the use of meta-learning techniques to improve fine-tuning of pre-trained diffusion models. In this experiment, we will train a few-shot learner for diffusion models by treating the pre-training process as a meta-training step and the fine-tuning process as a meta-testing step. We will evaluate the performance of meta-learned fine-tuning on various text-to-image generation tasks using the CLEVR dataset, comparing against the baseline of standard fine-tuning.
CONTROLS: 3 different meta-learning architectures (ProtoNet, Model Agnostic Meta-Learning (MAML), and Reptile), and 3 various few-shot learning settings
COST: 700
PREDICTION: We expect meta-learned fine-tuning to improve the performance of fine-tuning diffusion models by adapting to various fine-tuning tasks, but this may incur additional computational costs and require careful tuning of the meta-learning architecture and few-shot learning settings.

ACTION: REVISE
TITLE: Evaluating the Effect of Pre-Training on Fine-Tuning for Diffusion Models
PROPOSAL: Modify the previous proposal to use a causal graph-based method to identify the pre-training and fine-tuning combinations that have the greatest potential for improvement, and to guide the exploration of the vast pre-training and fine-tuning space. Use the DoWhy library to estimate and manipulate causal effects between different pre-training and fine-tuning strategies, and use SHAP values to provide per-sample explanations for the improvements.
CONTROLS: Comparison with a random search and a grid search in the pre-training and fine-tuning space
COST: 2000
PREDICTION: We expect the causal graph-based method to significantly improve the efficiency of the exploration of the pre-training and fine-tuning space and to identify new and unexpected pre-training and fine-tuning combinations that can improve the performance of diffusion models.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Primal-Dual KL Regularization for Diffusion Models
PROPOSAL: Investigate a variational upper-bound of the marginal KL divergence using a divergent process sequence that successively samples from the pre-trained model and fine-tuned model, and derive a primal-dual algorithm based on this bound to fine-tune a diffusion model under a KL-regularized reward objective.
CONTROLS: Compare to two baselines: (1) ignoring KL regularization, and (2) using the existing KL relaxation of comparing entire denoising trajectories.
COST: 800
PREDICTION: This approach alleviate instabilities caused by ignoring KL regularization and obtain better results than the existing KL relaxation, but its optimization might be harder than the baselines due to the introduction of additional variational parameters.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Modeling Activation Steering as a Linear Dynamical System
PROPOSAL: We model activation steering operations, addition, and ablation as a linear dynamical system, where the state of the system represents the model's internal activation, and the steering operation is represented by a learnable matrix. This framework allows us to analyze the behavior of activation steering and pinpoint its limitations, which we hypothesize will reveal a relationship between steering strength and performance degradation. We specify the regime as spherical-uniform initialization, allowability, and deducing behavior, and prove the system's coherence is actually critical when performing a differentially guided steering.
CONTROLS: Using RMS normalization alone as a baseline.
COST: 124.8
PREDICTION: We expect to find a non-linear relationship between steering strength and performance degradation, which may shed light on why activation steering often degrades model performance. However, validating this relationship with real-world experiments might be challenging, especially in regimes with multiple, competing behaviors or very deep models where the additive residual stream may dominate.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Evaluating Activation Steering on LLM Safety: Refusal of Harmful Requests
PROPOSAL: We design a suite of experiments to evaluate activation steering on LLM safety, focusing on refusal of harmful requests. We use a collection of datasets containing examples of harmful requests, and train a LLM to generate safe responses. We then apply various activation steering techniques to encourage the LLM to refuse the harmful requests. Our metrics include fluency, accuracy, and safety (e.g., the percentage of times the LLM refuses the harmful request). We also evaluate the coherence of the generated responses using human evaluators.

COST: 1170
PREDICTION: We expect activation steering to significantly improve the safety of LLM responses while maintaining fluency and coherence. However, we anticipate that the effectiveness of activation steering may vary depending on the specific LLM architecture, the type of harmful requests, and the specific activation steering technique used. Calibration of steering parameters may also require significant manual tuning and computational resources.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Investigating the Impact of RMS Normalization on Activation Steering
PROPOSAL: We investigate how RMS normalization affects the behavior of activation steering operations, particularly addition and ablation. We hypothesize that RMS normalization may modify the relative magnitudes of different feature directions in the activation space, leading to changes in the effectiveness of steering. We analyze the impact of normalization on the layer-wise activation norms and the relationship between steering strength and performance degradation. We also explore the effects of normalization on the coherence of generated responses.
CONTROLS: Revisiting experiments from previous proposal 2, incorporating RMS normalization into the LDS model from proposal 1, and comparing with new experiments where RMS normalization is disabled.
COST: 1400
PREDICTION: We expect to find that RMS normalization indeed affects the behavior of activation steering operations, leading to changes in the relationship between steering strength and performance degradation. However, the effects of normalization may be complex and dependent on the specific LLM architecture, the type of tasks being performed, and the specific activation steering techniques used. Additionally, we anticipate that disabling RMS normalization may improve the coherence of generated responses but degrade overall performance.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Activation Steering with Hierarchical Feature Directions
PROPOSAL: We propose a new approach to activation steering that uses hierarchical feature directions to improve the granularity and effectiveness of steering operations. We represent the activation space using a hierarchical tree structure, where each node corresponds to a feature direction and its children correspond to its sub-directions. We then apply activation steering at multiple levels of the tree to enable more fine-grained control over the model's behavior. Our approach is particularly useful for tasks that require subtle distinctions between different behaviors, such as emotion control in generated text.
CONTROLS: Comparing with existing activation steering methods, including proposal 1, on datasets related to LLM safety and emotion control.
COST: 2000
PREDICTION: We expect our hierarchical feature direction approach to improve the effectiveness of activation steering, enabling more subtle control over the model's behavior. However, we anticipate that the hierarchical structure may increase computational complexity and require more manual tuning to optimize performance. Additionally, we expect that the approach may not be effective for tasks that require extremely coarse-grained control over the model's behavior.

textes.jumeau:
ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Analyzing the Interactions between Activation Steering and Model Optimization
PROPOSAL: We investigate the interactions between activation steering and model optimization, two seemingly orthogonal concepts in language modeling. We analyze how activation steering affects model optimization objectives, such as perplexity or language modeling score, and vice versa. Our goal is to understand how to effectively combine these two approaches to improve model performance and safety. We explore the use of regularization techniques, such as L1/L2 regularization, dropout, and early stopping, to improve the stability and robustness of activation steering.
CONTROLS: Comparing with standard model optimization techniques, including Adam, RMSprop, andSGD, and applying activation steering to models trained with and without regularization.
COST: 2340
PREDICTION: We expect to find that activation steering interacts with model optimization in complex ways, affecting the optimization landscape and potentially leading to unstable or suboptimal solutions. To mitigate these effects, we anticipate that regularization techniques can help stabilize the model and improve the effectiveness of activation steering. However, the choice of regularization techniques and hyperparameters may require significant manual tuning, and the interactions between activation steering and model optimization may depend on the specific task and model architecture.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Developing a Framework for Certification and Explanation of Activation Steering
PROPOSAL: We propose a framework for certifying and explaining the behavior of activation steering operations in language models. Our framework provides tools for analyzing the input-output behavior of activation steering, identifying key features and behaviors that are being manipulated, and quantifying the confidence in the output of the model after applying activation steering. We also explore the use of representation learning techniques, such as feature attributions and saliency maps, to explain the impact of activation steering on the model's output.
CONTROLS: Evaluating our framework on a suite of activation steering tasks, including proposals 2, 4, and 5, and comparing its accuracy and explainability with existing approaches.
COST: 4000
PREDICTION: We expect our framework to provide a comprehensive understanding of the behavior of activation steering operations and enable more effective and reliable use of these techniques in practice. However, developing a framework that is both accurate and efficient may require significant computational resources, and the explainability of activation steering may depend on the type of model and the specific task being performed.

By analyzing the LLM's behavior at various points of continuous steering, we will identify effective steering regimes and limits.

PROPOSAL: Develop a principled method for learning activation steering directions that are orthogonal to the model's task-oriented representations, thus extending the applicability of activation steering beyond scripted behavior control. We will introduce a novel learning framework for acquiring open sets of steering directions using meta-learning and contrastive learning on synthetic and real-world data. This will enable flexible, context-dependent behavior control.
CONTROLS: Compare the steering directions learned from our approach to those obtained through heuristics and assess the performance on variety of tasks with evaluation metrics such as performance, coherence, and diversity in generated outputs.

PREDICTION: The proposed framework will provide a flexible tool for open-set behavior control and allow for learning context-specific steering directions that maintain the model's performance and coherence across a range of behaviors, yielding a more general and principled approach to activation steering.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Exploring Layer-Wise Activation Normalization for Activation Steering
PROPOSAL: Investigate whether normalizing activation before applying steering operations can improve the stability and efﬁciency of activation steering. We will modify existing steering primitives to normalize activation before edit-ing and examine the effects on directed ablation and activation addition. Specifically, we will normalize by mean and standard deviation (z-scoring) on a layer basis and compare the results against unnormalized versions of the steering primitives using the real-world Common Sense dataset.
CONTROLS: Compare steering primitives to baseline LLM behavior without steering, and evaluate the ablation across multiple real-world benchmarks, including Hotel and ATIS. We will also control for layer and training regime to understand the generalizability of the findings.
COST: 2300
PREDICTION: Normalizing activation will yield improved results due to reduced need for hyperparameter tuning, and steer-ing will exhibit increased stability and controlled behavior. However, this may come at the cost of reduced model expressiveness, particularly if normalization leads to bias in representational learning.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Continuity of Steering: Investigating the Effect of Continuous Activation Steering on LLM Behavior
PROPOSAL: Develop a protocol to assess the continuous effects of activation steering on LLM behavior, as the control parameter varies from full expression to suppression and inversion. We will leverage the trade-off between LLM performance and behavior control, and assess the continuity of steering effects on real-world benchmarks, eg., ATIS, and how they fail. A model's behavior as steering strength varies continuously, for example, between refusing and complying with a harmful request will be analyzed and visualized.
CONTROLS: Compare the results to the original activation steering and the baselines without steering. We will also use a Toy examples to analyze the behavior at various points of continuous steering to validate the qualitative results
COST: 3410
PREDICTION: The continuous activation steering effect will provide a nuanced understanding of how model behavior evolves as the steering strength changes and helps reveal when LLM behavior is likely to fail or become incoherent. By analyzing the LLM's behavior at various points of continuous steering, we will identify effective steering regimes and limits.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Fine-Grained Activation Steering via Rotation
PROPOSAL: We introduce soft directional ablation by parameterizing it as a rotation matrix that transforms the activation space orthogonal to the feature direction. This allows the strength and orientation of the ablation to be controlled via a single parameter and a unit vector. Experiment with various rotation angles to achieve partial suppression or inversion of target behaviors.
CONTROLS: Compare with standard directional ablation and addition methods on the MNLI dataset and examine their effects on fluency and factuality metrics.
COST: 1200
PREDICTION: Soft directional ablation will show improved control over the target behavior without degrading the model's original performance, compared to standard directional ablation. However, it may still struggle to provide fine-grained control over a range of behaviors.

Note: To come up with the "rotation angle," we can use orthogonal eigenvectors to our advantage. As a first step, we will look at the eigenvectors of the matrix product of the attention and activation's gradients. Next, we'll learn the proportion of that matrix being shaped by supervised loss based on a data-dependent weighting.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Continuously Adjustable Activation Steering
PROPOSAL: We propose an extensions to traditional activation addition and ablation methods, where the scaling coefficient in addition is adjusted based on the cosine similarity between the target feature and the normalized activation. This method allows for continuous adjustment of the steering strength without requiring layer-specific knowledge. We expect this to provide more robust and fine-grained control over the target behavior.
CONTROLS: Baselines: traditional addition and ablation methods on the same models; ablations: (1) absence of normalization in our proposed method (2) using fixed scaling coefficients as in traditional methods.
COST: 2704.5
PREDICTION: This method should improve the granularity of control and maintain coherence across the range of steering strengths, while the fixed coefficient baseline should produce poor results, failing at finer grain control and degrading coherence as scaling increases. Specifically, complete suppression and incorporation of features might be problematic with the fixed coefficients.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: A Framework for Understanding Activation Steering
PROPOSAL: To better understand the behavior of activation steering methods, we propose a geometric framework that views the activation space as a Riemannian manifold with a feature-specific metric induced by RMS normalization. This framework allows us to analyze how different steering operations distort the activation manifold, and why traditional steering methods may fail to provide fine-grained control. We will use the proposed framework to derive a novel steering method that leverages the geometric structure of the activation space.
CONTROLS: Baselines: traditional addition and ablation methods on the same models; ablations: (1) absence of normalization in the proposed method (2) using a flat metric in place of the Riemannian metric.
COST: 4350.8
PREDICTION: This framework will reveal the limitations of traditional steering methods and provide insights into the importance of the activation manifold structure. The novel steering method derived from the framework is expected to provide better control over the target behavior, with improved suppression, incorporation, and inversion capabilities compared to traditional methods.

TITLE: Understanding Steering's Bias towards Model Complexity
PROPOSAL: To investigate the relationship between activation steering and model complexity, we analyze the sensitivity of steering decisions to different layers and model scales, and how this sensitivity affects the final performance of the steered output. This analysis aims to uncover any biases or limitations in steering's ability to control complex models.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Federated Multi-Task Learning for Heterogeneous Tasks with Representational Alignment
PROPOSAL: Experiment 1: Federated Contrastive Learning for Heterogeneous Model Architectures
We propose a federated contrastive learning method that leverages a meta-learning framework to align representations across multiple models with different architectures and tasks. The method uses a publicly available dataset, and the alignment is computed using the InfoNCE loss on a small batch of representations. We will then use the aligned representations to fine-tune the user models and evaluate their performance on the local tasks using the cross-entropy loss.
CONTROLS: Baseline 1: No federated contrastive learning (each user trains independently), Baseline 2: Federated contrastive learning with a single paired model (without the meta-learning framework)
COST: 400 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: We expect to see improved performance of user models in terms of task-specific evaluation metrics (e.g., accuracy, F1-score), and potentially improved generalization to unseen tasks. This method might fail if the number of users is too high, or if the grounding of the alignment is too ad-hoc.

The experiment will be performed on the federated learning proxy for this dataset: FederatedEMNIST with mutual ranking.

TITLE: Efficient Model Inference via Federated Knowledge Distillation
PROPOSAL: Experiment 2: Efficient Federated Knowledge Distillation for Foundation Models
We propose a federated knowledge distillation method that accelerates the inference process for foundation models fine-tuned on diverse local tasks. The method learns a compact task-agnostic model from a collection of pre-trained foundation models, and then shares this compact model across users. We will evaluate the inference speedup and accuracy retention on a set of real-world tasks and models.
CONTROLS: Baseline 1: Vanilla federated learning (no knowledge distillation), Baseline 2: Centralized knowledge distillation (without the federated setting)
COST: 834 GPU-hours

PROPOSAL: Theorem 1: Convergence of Federated Multi-Task Learning with Heterogeneous Architectures
We provide a theoretical analysis of the proposed federated multi-task learning method. We prove that the method converges to a local minimum of the global loss function, guaranteeing improvement over independent local training. We assume that the user models have bounded capacity and that the tasks are related through a shared representation space.
CONTROLS: None
COST: 3,000 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: The theorem provides a solid foundation for the federated multi-task learning method and guarantees convergence under certain conditions. However, the assumption of bounded capacity might be too strict in reality, and the extension to non-linear tasks could be challenging.

TITLE: Algorithms for Scaling Federated Learning to Large NumbeRs of Devices
PROPOSAL: Experiment 5: Efficient Federated Optimization for Large-Scale Settings
We propose a set of algorithms for scaling federated learning to large numbers of devices, including a federated Adam variant that adapts to non-IID data and a hierarchical optimization method that clusters devices into smaller groups. We evaluate the performance of these algorithms on a large-scale real-world dataset.
CONTROLS: Baseline 1: Vanilla federated optimization (without any adaptation or clustering), Baseline 2: Centralized optimization (all data is collected on a central server)
COST: 6,701 GPU-hours

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Secure Federated Learning for Homogeneous and Heterogeneous Models
PROPOSAL: Experiment 6: Secure Federated Learning with Differential Privacy and Homomorphic Encryption
We propose a secure federated learning method that utilizes differential privacy and homomorphic encryption to protect user data while preserving the collaboration of heterogeneous models. We evaluate the performance of the method on a set of real-world tasks and models, and compare it with previous secure federated learning methods.
CONTROLS: Baseline 1: No differential privacy and homomorphic encryption (vulnerability of user data), Baseline 2: Centralized secure federated learning (data is encrypted and stored on a centralized server)
COST: 10,000 GPU-hours

textes:
ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Federated Multi-Task Learning for Heterogeneous Tasks with Representational Alignment
PROPOSAL: Experiment 1: Federated Contrastive Learning for Heterogeneous Model Architectures
We propose a federated contrastive learning method that leverages a meta-learning framework to align representations across multiple models with different architectures and tasks. The method uses a publicly available dataset, and the alignment is computed using the InfoNCE loss on a small batch of representations. We will then use the aligned representations to fine-tune the user models and evaluate their performance on the local tasks using the cross-entropy loss.
CONTROLS: Baseline 1: No federated contrastive learning (each user trains independently), Baseline 2: Federated contrastive learning with a single paired model (without the meta-learning framework)
COST: 1,200 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: We expect to see improved performance of user models in terms of task-specific evaluation metrics (e.g., accuracy, F1-score), and potentially improved generalization to unseen tasks. This method might fail if the number of users is too high, or if the grounding of the alignment is too ad-hoc.

The experiment will be performed on the federated learning proxy for this dataset: FederatedEMNIST with mutual ranking.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Efficient Model Inference via Federated Knowledge Distillation
PROPOSAL: Experiment 2: Efficient Federated Knowledge Distillation for Foundation Models
We propose a federated knowledge distillation method that accelerates the inference process for foundation models fine-tuned on diverse local tasks. The method learns a compact task-agnostic model from a collection of pre-trained foundation models, and then shares this compact model across users. We will evaluate the inference speedup and accuracy retention on a set of real-world tasks and models.
CONTROLS: Baseline 1: Vanilla federated learning (no knowledge distillation), Baseline 2: Centralized knowledge distillation (without the federated setting)
COST: 2,500 GPU-hours

ACTION: REVISE
TITLE: Revised Representational Alignment for Federated Learning
PROPOSAL: Experiment 1: Federated Contrastive Learning for Heterogeneous Model Architectures (Revised)
We revise the previous federated contrastive learning method to incorporate a more robust alignment mechanism. Instead of using the InfoNCE loss, we use a Gram-Schmidt process to normalize the representations of each model, followed by a Frobenius norm matching penalty to align the representations across models. This revised method aims to capture more robust dependencies among the representations.
CONTROLS: Baseline 1: Original federated contrastive learning method from proposal 1, Baseline 2: No federated contrastive learning (each user trains independently)
COST: 6,000 GPU-hours

ACTION: REVISE 1
TITLE: Theoretical Guarantees for Federated Multi-Task Learning
PROPOSAL: Theorem 1: Convergence of Federated Multi-Task Learning with Heterogeneous Architectures
We provide a theoretical analysis of the proposed federated multi-task learning method. We prove that the method converges to a local minimum of the global loss function, guaranteeing improvement over independent local training. We assume that the user models have bounded capacity and that the tasks are related through a shared representation space.
CONTROLS: None
COST: 9,000 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: The theorem provides a solid foundation for the federated multi-task learning method and guarantees convergence under certain conditions. However, the assumption of bounded capacity might be too strict in reality, and the extension to non-linear tasks could be challenging.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Practical Model Selection via Federated Metrics Aggregation
PROPOSAL: Experiment 3: Federated Metrics Aggregation for Model Selection
We propose a federated metrics aggregation method that aggregates evaluation metrics from multiple users to select the best model architecture for a particular task. We compare the performance of several models on a small, held-out dataset and aggregate the metrics from multiple users to determine the best-performing model. We will evaluate the performance of the selected model on a larger, unseen dataset.
CONTROLS: Baseline 1: No federated metrics aggregation (each user selects their own model), Baseline 2: Centralized metrics aggregation (aggregate metrics from all users on a centralized server)
COST: 8,500 GPU-hours

ACTION: REVISE 1
TITLE: Improved Theoretical Guarantees for Federated Multi-Task Learning
PROPOSAL: Theorem 2: Convergence and Generalization for Federated Multi-Task Learning with Heterogeneous Architectures
We strengthen the previous theoretical guarantees by relaxing the assumption of bounded capacity and extending the result to non-linear tasks. We prove that the proposed federated multi-task learning method converges to a local minimum of the global loss function and generalizes to unseen tasks, even when the user models have varying capacities and the tasks are related through a shared representation space.
CONTROLS: None
COST: 18,000 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: The theorem provides stronger guarantees for the federated multi-task learning method and relaxes some of the previous assumptions, making it more applicable to real-world scenarios. However, the proof might become more complex and difficult to analyze, which could affect its usability and interpretability.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Federated Representation Distillation for Efficient Knowledge Transfer
PROPOSAL: Experiment 4: Federated Representation Distillation for Efficient Knowledge Transfer
We propose a federated representation distillation method that efficiently transfers knowledge across users with different model architectures and tasks. The method learns a compact representation of the shared knowledge among users and distills it into a smaller network, which can be shared across users. We will evaluate the performance of the distilled network on a set of real-world tasks and models.
CONTROLS: Baseline 1: No federated representation distillation (each user learns independently), Baseline 2: Centralized representation distillation (distill representation on a centralized server)
COST: 12,000 GPU-hours

ACTION: ADD 1
TITLE: Federated Multi-Task Learning with Task-Agnostic Alignment
PROPOSAL: Investigate a novel federated multi-task learning method that uses a global adaptive alignment layer to capture common task-agnostic information from multiple users with heterogeneous architectures. This layer will be trained using a margin-based multi-task contrastive loss, which preserves the diversity of user models while encouraging their representations to be aligned on a shared task-agnostic subspace.
CONTROLS: Compare against existing federated multi-task learning methods, including knowledge-distillation-based approaches, and baselines that assume model homogeneity.
COST: 210000
PREDICTION: The method should outperform existing approaches in terms of model generalization, particularly when adapting to unseen tasks, with minor communication overhead; however, it may struggle with deeply heterogeneous architectures or large numbers of users.

ACTION: ADD 2
TITLE: Improving Representation Alignment via Low-Rank Projection
PROPOSAL: Develop a new projection mechanism for the global adaptive alignment layer in proposal 1, utilizing low-rank constraints to better capture the shared task-agnostic subspace. This will be achieved by adding a low-rank matrix regularizer to the margin-based multi-task contrastive loss.
CONTROLS: Investigate the effect of low-rank constraint strengths and model architectures on the representation alignment, and compare against a baseline without the low-rank regularization.
COST: 270000
PREDICTION: The low-rank projection should significantly improve representation alignment, especially for models with complex architectures, but may lead to over-regularization if the constraint is too strong, resulting in higher communication overhead.

ACTION: ADD 3
TITLE: Federated Domain Adaptation for Task Heterogeneity
PROPOSAL: Investigate a federated domain adaptation approach that leverages the knowledge of multiple users to adapt to new tasks with different distributions. This will be achieved by introducing a domain-invariant alignment loss that aligns the shared representations across users and tasks, while also considering the domain shift between each user's task.
CONTROLS: Compare against existing federated multi-task learning methods on domain adaptation tasks, using real-world datasets with different distributions (e.g., clinical notes and medical images).
COST: 315000
PREDICTION: The federated domain adaptation approach should improve task transferability across heterogeneous tasks, especially when users have vastly different input distributions, but may require ad-hoc tuning of hyperparameters to achieve optimal results.

This term will capture the correlation between the low-rank basis and the global representation learned from the federated data, and is regularized by a distance-based penalty.

TITLE: Meta-Federated Learning for Universal Adaptation
PROPOSAL: Develop a meta-federated learning framework that learns to adapt to new users, tasks, or data distributions beyond the training set. This will be achieved by introducing a meta-learning objective that aligns the representations from multiple users and tasks, and trains a set of meta-learners to adapt to new scenarios.

ACTION: ADD 5
TITLE: Federated Transfer Learning via Heterogeneous Prototype Learning
PROPOSAL: Investigate a federated transfer learning approach that utilizes heterogeneous prototypes to align representations across users with different architectures. This will be achieved by introducing a set of task-agnostic prototypes that capture the common information across users, and a dynamic weighting scheme to balance the contributions of each user's prototypes.
CONTROLS: Compare against existing federated transfer learning methods on transfer learning tasks, using real-world datasets with varying degrees of task similarity.
COST: 339000
PREDICTION: The federated transfer learning approach should improve knowledge transfer across heterogeneous users, especially when the tasks have similar structures, but may suffer from Brittlness when the task similarity is low, and may require robust prototype selection methods to avoid over-specialization.

TITLE: Secure Multi-Party Federated Learning via Homomorphic Encryption
PROPOSAL: Investigate a secure multi-party federated learning approach that utilizes homomorphic encryption to protect user data during collaboration. This will be achieved by encrypting user model updates and computations, allowing for secure aggregation and training while preserving user data privacy.
CONTROLS: Evaluate the performance and scalability of the approach on various federated learning tasks, using real-world datasets and comparing against existing secure multi-party federated learning methods.
COST: 384000
PREDICTION: The secure multi-party federated learning approach should improve user data protection and scalability, especially in scenarios with strong privacy requirements, but may suffer from increased computational overhead due to the encryption and decryption processes.

PROPOSAL: Provide theoretical guarantees for federated learning with heterogeneous architectures by analyzing the convergence and generalization properties of the methods proposed in previous experiments. This will be achieved by deriving bounds on the loss and gradient discrepancies between users, and establishing conditions for convergence to a common point.

TITLE: Memory-Efficient Federated Multi-Task Learning via Model-Gated Mask Attention
PROPOSAL: We propose Model-Gated Mask Attention (MGMA), a novel approach for federated multi-task learning that enables users with heterogeneous model architectures and different tasks to collaborate without sharing local data or requiring architectural congruity. MGMA introduces a dynamic attention mechanism that selectively masks task-specific components of user models, allowing them to share common representations while retaining task-specific knowledge.
CONTROLS: We compare MGMA to BA-Disim (a baseline approach that divides each model into a shared encoder and task-specific predictors), and each model's performance is measured on its respective task. We also ablate MGMA's key components (i.e., task-specific masking and gated attention) to assess their individual contributions.
COST: 3360
PREDICTION: MGMA outperforms BA-Disim on average, with a lead of 1.5% in cross-validated accuracy on federated tasks, but its benefits may wane when tasks become too dissimilar, causing frozen representations in some models.

ACTION: REVISE 1
TITLE: Efficient Global-Local Alignment via Meta-Learned Orthogonal Procrustes
PROPOSAL: We further enhance MGMA by employing meta-learned orthogonal Procrustes (mOP) for global-local representation alignment. mOP is a meta-learning algorithm that adapts orthogonal transformations for alignment between two spaces without access to paired data. We meta-learn the alignment across tasks to discover a common representation space shared by diverse user models, advancing the alignment beyond pairwise comparison.
CONTROLS: We ablate the effectiveness of mOP on MGMA by removing it and using InfoNCE loss, and evaluate the impact of mOP on model convergence and representation quality. Additionally, we compare mOP to the recently proposed Gramian-based contrastive loss and explore its convergence speed and oscillations.
COST: 4000
PREDICTION: The integration of mOP with MGMA yields enhanced cross-task generalization and representation quality, exceeding the previous benefits of MGMA alone. However, mOP's reliance on high-capacity meta-learners might exacerbate computation and communication costs, potentially leading to data heterogeneity issues when federated models diverge.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Orchestrating Hierarchical Representation Alignment in Federated Multi-Task Learning
PROPOSAL: To address limitations of pairwise global-local representation alignment, we introduce Hierarchical Representation Alignment (HRA), which orchestrates across-task alignment in a hierarchical manner. HRA separates the alignment process into multiple resolution layers, initially aligning coarse-level representations and then iteratively refining alignment at finer levels. This approach enables leveraging higher-level feature abstractions shared across tasks while preventing the unique task-specific knowledge of individual models from being overwritten.
CONTROLS: We evaluate HRA's effectiveness on the e-commerce and medical diagnosis benchmarks, comparing against the mOP-enhanced MGMA and BA-Disim baselines in various configurations of task dissimilarity and model complexity.
COST: 5340
PREDICTION: HRA's hierarchical alignment strategy improves the alignment of task-agnostic knowledge across diverse user models while preserving unique task-specific features, leading to enhanced performances and generalization capabilities.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Federated Quick-Align via Auto-Learned KL-Divergence Similarity Metric
PROPOSAL: To hasten the process of federated multi-task learning, where global-local representation alignment may converge unreliably and slowly, we introduce Federated Quick-Align (FQA) that uses an auto-learned KL-divergence similarity metric (KD-SIM) for rapid alignment. KD-SIM is meta-trained to adapt to diverse user models and tasks without explicit pairing, estimating an initial similarity metric that accounts for both features and distribution shifts across tasks.
CONTROLS: We compare FQA-KD-SIM against the InfoNCE-based BA-Disim baseline, and explore FQA with different meta-learning protocols and smoothness operators to fine-tune KD-SIM's quality and adaptation speed.
COST: 6000
PREDICTION: FQA efficiently and accurately realigns task-agnostic knowledge in a few steps by adapting to features and distribution shifts using a meta-learned KL-divergence metric, but its potential benefits significantly depend on how faithfully the KD-SIM metric captures actual similarity.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Shared Encoder for Federated Multi-Task Learning
PROPOSAL: 
We design a novel federated multi-task learning framework, "Task-Aligned Shared Encoder" (TASE), that leverages a shared encoder for all users while allowing for task-specific predictors. We initialize the shared encoder with a pre-trained foundation model and fine-tune it using local data. ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Cross-Modal Contrastive Federated Learning
PROPOSAL: We design a federated learning framework, dubbed Cross-Modal Contrastive Federated Learning (CMCFL), which enables diverse users to collaboratively learn task-agnostic representations while preserving privacy. Users can choose any model architectures and tasks, and our framework leverages a variant of the InfoNCE loss, adapted to align the representations across all models simultaneously, using a mini-batch of samples from all users. During the training process, users locally compute the similarity between representations, while the server computes the contrastive loss based on the similarities. This ensures efficient and communication-friendly alignment across diverse task and architectural settings.
CONTROLS: We compare CMCFL to the previously proposed Gramian-based contrastive loss, and with the basic InfoNCE loss applied to every pair of models. We also compare to a baseline where no contrastive loss is applied, and a naive greedy approach where each user's model is aligned one at a time.
COST: 14400
PREDICTION: CMCFL outperforms the Gramian-based loss and the naive baseline, but falls short of achieving state-of-the-art performance compared to the InfoNCE loss applied to every pair of models. However, CMCFL significantly reduces the communication overhead of the InfoNCE baseline.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Multi-modal Knowledge Distillation for Federated Multi-task Learning
PROPOSAL: Building upon CMCFL, we propose a multi-modal knowledge distillation (MMKD) framework to improve the efficiency and accuracy of federated multi-task learning. Each user participates in a shared mini-batch, and distills knowledge from experts in other tasks using a task-agnostic representation-based distillation loss. We adapt the knowledge distillation framework from multiple expert sources to the federated learning setting. Users can now learn from other users' expertise, fostering cross-task knowledge sharing. The MMKD module is integrated with the CMCFL framework, providing a trade-off between representation learning and knowledge distillation.
CONTROLS: We compare the MMKD framework to a basic knowledge distillation baseline where each user learns from only one other user, and to a variant of the InfoNCE loss that only accounts for the representations between pairs of users. We also ablate the MMKD framework to analyze its contribution to the overall performance.
COST: 21600
PREDICTION: MMKD improves the performance of federated multi-task learning by adaptively distilling knowledge from multiple users, without directly sharing task-specific data. However, its performance may degrade when users have very different task objectives, which can lead to suboptimal knowledge distillation.

TITLE: Enhanced Communication-Efficient Federated Learning
PROPOSAL: To address the challenges of communication-efficient federated learning, we propose an Enhanced Communication-Efficient Federated Learning (ECEFL) framework that combines the best of previous methods while addressing their limitations. In the ECEFL framework, we leverage a hierarchical structure to group users and share knowledge in a more efficient manner. We also adopt a novel adaptive compression algorithm that dynamically allocates compression quality to match the model's complexity. Furthermore, we integrate a backbone pruning step to reduce the model size, enabling faster transmission and training.
CONTROLS: We evaluate the proposed ECEFL framework against the InfoNCE loss, MMKD with Attend-On-Demand, and TFA methods with task-agnostic relations. We also conduct an ablation study on the effectiveness of the hierarchical structure and adaptive compression algorithm.
COST: 48600
PREDICTION: The ECEFL framework demonstrates significant communication efficiency improvements while maintaining competitive performance compared to the other methods. However, its added complexity may lead to longer training times and model pruning may require careful tuning for optimal performance.
