TITLE: Bidirectional Reward Calibration for Reduced Annotator Disagreement
PROPOSAL: We introduce a novel consistency-enhanced reward calibration pipeline for reducing annotator disagreement by incorporating a critic network with reference scores derived from a target metric, such as human expert opinions. The pipeline operates in two directions: (1) it uses the critic network to calibrate the base reward model to the reference scores, and (2) it uses reference scores as input to refine the critic network's performance, effectively leveraging a soft self-training approach. We will evaluate this pipeline on a set of real-world datasets for chatbot response quality evaluation, applying it to math and textual responses generated by a language model.
CONTROLS: Baseline 1: Basic bidirectional calibration without refinement of the critic network; Baseline 2: State-of-the-art self-supervised methods without reference scores; Ablation study of components and hyperparameters
COST: 5,000
PREDICTION: This bidirectional reward calibration will demonstrate a substantial improvement in handling annotator disagreement and enable more reliable and accurate reward signals for downstream applications in LLM training and chatbot development.

TITLE: Generative Reward Model with Multi-Step Critique and Progressive Calibration
PROPOSAL: Building upon the existing success of generative models in providing interpretable critiques, we propose a new generative reward model that incorporates multi-step critiques and progressive calibration. The model generates a sequence of intermediate critiques, each corresponding to a different aspect or stage of the response generation process. Progressively, it calibrates these intermediate critiques to ensure that they align with the final preference judgments, thereby enabling the model to capture complex preference relationships and provide more reliable rewards. We will evaluate this model's performance on real-world datasets for chatbot response quality evaluation and code generation.

However, it may require more computational resources due to the increased complexity of generating intermediate critiques.

PROPOSAL: We explore the problem of applying reward learning to out-of-distribution responses, where the model has not seen the specific response types or contexts before. The framework consists of a meta-train phase, where the reward model is trained on a set of base responses, and a meta-test phase, where the trained reward model is used to score new responses. We will evaluate this framework on a set of real-world datasets for chatbot response quality evaluation and code generation.

We propose a novel zero-shot reward learning framework that uses meta-learning to adapt the reward model to new response types and contexts without any additional annotation. The framework consists of a meta-train phase, where the reward model is trained on a set of base responses, and a meta-test phase, where the trained reward model is used to score new responses. We will evaluate this framework on a set of real-world datasets for chatbot response quality evaluation and code generation.
CONTROLS: Baseline 1: Standard reward learning approach without meta-learning; Baseline 2: Recently proposed methods that require additional annotation for out-of-distribution responses; Ablation study of meta-learning mechanisms and hyperparameters
COST: 30,000
PREDICTION: This zero-shot reward learning framework will demonstrate a significant improvement in adapting to out-of-distribution responses without any additional annotation, outperforming existing methods in certain scenarios. However, its performance may degrade when the distributional gap between the meta-train and meta-test responses is large.

TITLE: Interpretable and Transferable Reward Models via Modular Architectures
PROPOSAL: We propose a novel modular architecture for reward models that combines the strengths of discriminative and generative models. The architecture consists of a set of interchangeable modules, each of which is responsible for a specific aspect of the reward signal, such as response quality, relevance, or coherence. This modular design enables us to create interpretable and transferable reward models that can be easily adapted to different domains and scenarios. We will evaluate this architecture on a set of real-world datasets for chatbot response quality evaluation, code generation, and other applications.
CONTROLS: Baseline 1: Standard discriminative reward model; Baseline 2: Generative reward model without modular architecture; Ablation study of modules and hyperparameters
COST: 50,000
PREDICTION: This modular architecture will demonstrate significant improvements in interpretability, transferability, and performance compared to existing reward models, making it a valuable tool for a wide range of applications. However, the optimal selection and combination of modules may require significant expertise and experimentation.

TITLE: Enforcing Absolute Quality using Reward-Agnostic Calibration
PROPOSAL: We propose Enforce-Absolute, a post-processing framework that calibrates the absolute quality scores from a discriminative reward model using a reward-agnostic calibration, effectively grounding the scores in a meaningful absolute quality scale. To train this calibration function, we select a subset of highly-annotated samples where a reliable ground-truth quality label is available, and optimize the calibration using a simple Maximum Likelihood Estimation (MLE) objective between the raw model scores and the ground-truth quality labels.
CONTROLS: We compare Enforce-Absolute to the state-of-the-art discriminative reward models (Skywork-Reward, InternLM2-Reward) with and without the calibration step, and provide an ablation on the importance of proper calibration.
COST: 160 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: Enforce-Absolute significantly improves ranking accuracy and provides more reliable absolute quality judgments across various domains, but may struggle in scenarios where high-quality annotations are rare or biased.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Flexible and Probabilistic Reward Modeling with Multi-Output Conditional Imitation Learning (MOCIL)
PROPOSAL: We introduce MOCIL, a generative reward modeling approach that employs a multi-output conditional imitation learning scheme to produce probabilistic, absolute quality scores and flexible ranking for single or multiple candidates. MOCIL learns to mimic the behavior of a pre-trained base model and its corresponding preference function using a probabilistic imitation objective. This allows the model to capture both the absolute quality and uncertainty of candidates. We also incorporate an entropy regularizer to enforce more consistent and informative predictions.
CONTROLS: We compare MOCIL to state-of-the-art generative reward models (HelpSteer2-Preference, ArmoRM) and discriminative models (Skywork-Reward, InternLM2-Reward) on several real-world benchmarks, and conduct an ablation study to analyze the effect of the entropy regularizer and the number of imitation targets.
COST: 480 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: MOCIL outperforms existing models on absolute quality estimation and provides robust ranking accuracy under varying uncertainty conditions, but may be computationally expensive due to the need for frequent preference simulations.

ACTION: REVISE 2
TITLE: Flexible and Probabilistic Reward Modeling with Multi-Output Conditional Imitation Learning (MOCIL)
PROPOSAL: We introduce MOCIL++, an enhanced version of the previous MOCIL approach. MOCIL++ incorporates a novel ensemble method that combines the outputs of multiple probabilistic imitation learners, each trained on different subsets of the preference data, to produce more robust and diversified predictions. This ensemble approach also includes an adaptive weighting scheme that leverages the uncertainty estimates from each learner to optimize the final decision-making process. We also modify the entropy regularizer to use a more flexible and interpretable KL-divergence-based penalty term that encourages more consistent and informative predictions.
CONTROLS: We compare MOCIL++ to the original MOCIL and state-of-the-art generative reward models (HelpSteer2-Preference, ArmoRM) and discriminative models (Skywork-Reward, InternLM2-Reward) on several real-world benchmarks, and conduct an ablation study to analyze the effect of the ensemble method and the adaptive weighting scheme.
COST: 768 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: MOCIL++ significantly boosts the absolute quality estimation accuracy and provides more robust ranking results under various uncertainty conditions, but may be more computationally demanding due to the ensemble method.

TITLE: Low-Resource Reward Model Transfer with Meta-Learning
PROPOSAL: To address the challenge of adapting the reward model to a new domain with limited quality annotations, we introduce Transfer-Reward, a meta-learning based framework that learns to rapidly adapt a pre-trained reward model to a new domain by leveraging a small set of annotated examples. Transfer-Reward employs a training procedure that involves several rounds of few-shot learning, where the model is trained to predict the reward in various domains. The goal is to learn a more versatile and generalizable model that can be fine-tuned to a specific domain with minimal annotations

TITLE: Probabilistic Reward Composition with Dynamic Ensembling for Better Handling of Uncertainty
PROPOSAL: We propose a novel reward composition approach, Probocom, that leverages dynamic ensembling to effectively capture and aggregate the uncertainty information from multiple reward models. Probocom combines the predictions of a diverse set of models, each trained on a different subset of the preference data, to produce a more robust and accurate overall reward signal. We utilize a Bayesian neural network as the base model and an adaptive weighting scheme that adjusts based on the predictive uncertainty of each model. This approach allows for a more nuanced representation of uncertainty in the reward signal.
CONTROLS: We compare Probocom to state-of-the-art discriminative and generative reward models (Skywork-Reward, InternLM2-Reward, HelpSteer2-Preference, ArmoRM) on several real-world benchmarks, and conduct an ablation study to analyze the effect of the dynamic ensembling scheme.
COST: 1152 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: Probocom demonstrates strong performance in handling high levels of uncertainty, noisy, and inconsistent preference data; however, the dynamic ensembling scheme may be computationally expensive and require careful tuning of hyperparameters.

TITLE: Dual-Loss Training of Reward Models via Mutual Information Maximization
PROPOSAL: We propose a novel dual-loss training framework for reward models, called DualInfoMax, that leverages mutual information maximization to align the predictions of the reward model with the true quality annotations. DualInfoMax involves training the reward model to maximize the mutual information between the predicted rewards and the true quality annotations, while simultaneously minimizing a standard empirical loss function. We adopt a variational autoencoder (VAE) as the backbone model and optimize the mutual information term using a Monte Carlo-based estimator. This approach allows for a more robust and accurate alignment of the reward model predictions with the true quality annotations.
CONTROLS: We compare DualInfoMax to state-of-the-art generative and discriminative reward models (HelpSteer2-Preference, ArmoRM, Skywork-Reward, InternLM2-Reward) on several real-world benchmarks, and conduct an ablation study to analyze the effect of the mutual information term and the VAE architecture.
COST: 1728 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: DualInfoMax significantly improves the alignment between the reward model predictions and the true quality annotations; however, the mutual information estimator may be computationally expensive to compute and require careful hyperparameter tuning.

TITLE: Evaluating the Impact of Annotator Disagreement on Reward Model Quality using Quantile Loss
PROPOSAL: We propose Quantile-Reward, a novel method for evaluating the robustness of reward models to annotator disagreement. Quantile-Reward assesses the impact of outlier annotators on the reward model predictions using a quantile loss function. By computing the quantiles of the predicted rewards, we can identify instances where the annotators exhibit high disagreement, and refine the reward model accordingly. We adopt a fully connected neural network as the backbone model and optimize the quantile loss function using a gradient-based optimizer.
CONTROLS: We compare Quantile-Reward to state-of-the-art generative and discriminative reward models (HelpSteer2-Preference, ArmoRM, Skywork-Reward, InternLM2-Reward) on several real-world benchmarks, and conduct an ablation study to analyze the effect of the quantile loss function and the optimization algorithm.
COST: 2430 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: Quantile-Reward demonstrates strong robustness to annotator disagreement and provides improved reward model quality estimates; however, the quantile loss function may require careful tuning to avoid overfitting to minor annotator differences.

PROPOSAL: We propose WeakAdapt, a novel approach for adapting a pre-trained reward model to a new domain with limited annotations. WeakAdapt employs domain-invariant feature learning to align the feature representations of the target domain with those of the source domain, while maintaining the original reward model predictions. We use a multi-task learning framework that combines the reward model task with a domain-invariant feature learning task, and optimize the model using a self-supervised contrastive loss function.
CONTROLS: We compare WeakAdapt to state-of-the-art generative and discriminative reward models (HelpSteer2-Preference, ArmoRM, Skywork-Reward, InternLM2-Reward) on several real-world benchmarks, and conduct an ablation study to analyze the effect of the domain-invariant feature learning task and the contrastive loss function.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Efficient and Informative Decoupled Reward Model
PROPOSAL: Implement a decoupled reward model that consists of two parts: an absolute quality predictor and a preference comparator. The absolute quality predictor uses a learned scoring function to predict the intrinsic quality of a response, while the preference comparator utilizes a discriminative model to learn a ranking between responses. The two parts are trained separately, with the absolute quality predictor optimized using mean squared error and the preference comparator optimized using the Bradley-Terry objective.
CONTROLS: Implement the baseline Bradley-Terry objective-only model and compare with the state-of-the-art models InternLM2-Reward and Skywork-Reward.
COST: 834
PREDICTION: This decoupled reward model is expected to outperform the Bradley-Terry objective-only model in ranking accuracy and provide more informative scores that better capture the absolute quality of responses, while still maintaining efficiency and interpretability. However, it may struggle with small datasets due to the added complexity of the two separate models.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Evaluating Perplexity of Reconstructed Contexts to Detect Hallucinations
PROPOSAL: This experiment compares the perplexity of generated text given a prompt and retrieved documents to the perplexity of the reconstructed context, which is the reformatted response blended with the retrieved documents. We hypothesize that the perplexity of the reconstructed context will be lower than the generated text when the model is hallucinating, as the reconstructed context is factually consistent with the retrieved documents. We use multiple datasets for retrieval-augmented question answering and news summarization (e.g., Natural Questions, TriviaQA, CNN/DM) and compare our results to a simple baseline of using a retrieval-based approach that only selects the most relevant sentence from the retrieved documents.
CONTROLS: The evaluation is repeated with different retrieval models (e.g., BM25, dense passage retrieval), and the results are analyzed with various metrics (e.g., F1 score, recall). We also compare the results to a hallucination-detection model that uses ReDeEP-like approach, as well as a model that uses a factual consistency check with a knowledge base.
COST: 5,200 GPU hours
PREDICTION: Our results show a significant drop in perplexity of the reconstructed context when the generated text involves hallucinations, with a false positive rate of around 10% and a false negative rate of around 10% compared to a simple retrieval-based baseline.

textes.jumeau:
ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Measuring Coherence of Inference Distributions
PROPOSAL: This experiment uses the coherence of the inference distributions of the model to detect hallucinations. We compute the KL-divergence between the posterior inference distribution of words that are factually consistent with the retrieved documents and the posterior inference distribution of words in the generated response. We expect that the model is more likely to hallucinate when the coherence of the inference distributions is low, as hallucinations often involve making a stronger commitment to the generated response. We analyze these distributions under various decoding strategies (e.g., greedy decoding, beam search, nucleus sampling) and compare our results to the perplexity-based model from Prop 1.
CONTROLS: We experiment with different inference networks (e.g., trained EM models, approximations through variational inference) and evaluate the method using datasets from retrieval-augmented question answering and news summarization.
COST: 10,125 GPU hours
PREDICTION: Our method achieves a F1 score of 0.85 for detecting hallucinations on a retrieval-augmented question answering dataset, with a false positive rate of around 5% and a false negative rate of around 15%. We expect that our method will show a significant improvement when paired with the perplexity-based detector from Prop 1.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Entrystyle-based Analysis of Hallucinations
PROPOSAL: This experiment uses entrystyle analysis to identify when a model predicts probabilities over extreme event-like tokens, suggesting the generation of fictional or unrealistic events/expressions. ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Evaluating Perplexity of Reconstructed Contexts to Detect Hallucinations
PROPOSAL: This experiment compares the perplexity of generated text given a prompt and retrieved documents to the perplexity of the reconstructed context, which is the reformatted response blended with the retrieved documents. We hypothesize that the perplexity of the reconstructed context will be lower than the generated text when the model is hallucinating, as the reconstructed context is factually consistent with the retrieved documents. We use multiple datasets for retrieval-augmented question answering and news summarization (e.g., Natural Questions, TriviaQA, CNN/DM) and compare our results to a simple baseline of using a retrieval-based approach that only selects the most relevant sentence from the retrieved documents.
CONTROLS: The evaluation is repeated with different retrieval models (e.g., BM25, dense passage retrieval), and the results are analyzed with various metrics (e.g., F1 score, recall). We also compare the results to a hallucination-detection model that uses ReDeEP-like approach, as well as a model that uses a factual consistency check with a knowledge base.
COST: 15,600 GPU hours
PREDICTION: Our results show a significant drop in perplexity of the reconstructed context when the generated text involves hallucinations, with a false positive rate of around 10% and a false negative rate of around 10% compared to a simple retrieval-based baseline.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Measuring Coherence of Inference Distributions
PROPOSAL: This experiment uses the coherence of the inference distributions of the model to detect hallucinations. We compute the KL-divergence between the posterior inference distribution of words that are factually consistent with the retrieved documents and the posterior inference distribution of words in the generated response. We expect that the model is more likely to hallucinate when the coherence of the inference distributions is low, as hallucinations often involve making a stronger commitment to the generated response. We analyze these distributions under various decoding strategies (e.g., greedy decoding, beam search, nucleus sampling) and compare our results to the perplexity-based model from Prop 1.
CONTROLS: We experiment with different inference networks (e.g., trained EM models, approximations through variational inference) and evaluate the method using datasets from retrieval-augmented question answering and news summarization.

We expect that our method will show a significant improvement when paired with the perplexity-based detector from Prop 1.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Augmentation-Aware Utilization Signals with Supervised Learning
PROPOSAL: Train a supervised regression model to predict the true signals of external context utilization E and internal knowledge utilization I from augmentations of the generated responses, such as soft-deleted or swapped tokens, and embedding differences between the augmented responses and the retrieved context documents, to learn features that robustly capture the notion of utilization. The model takes as input these augmentations and predicts the corresponding E and I values.
CONTROLS: Baseline 1: Current ReDeEP method without augmentations; Baseline 2: A simple linear regression model that predicts E and I from attention weights and internal knowledge representations, without augmentations; Ablation 1: Removing the embedding differences from the augmentations; Ablation 2: Removing the soft-deleted tokens from the augmentations.
COST: 12000
PREDICTION: The model should achieve better correlation between predicted and true utilization signals than the baselines, and its performance should be stronger in cases where the augmentations better capture the intended notion of utilization. The model might require larger capacities and more extensive tuning to outperform the ReDeEP method in simpler scenarios.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Dual-Loss Regularization for Auxiliary Task Learning
PROPOSAL: Modify the LLM's training objective with an auxiliary task of predicting the utilization scores E and I on-the-fly during each generation step, using a cross-entropy loss between the predicted and gold-standard scores. Evaluate the regularized model's ability to produce more reliable responses with lower E-I discrepancy.
CONTROLS: Baseline 1: Standard LLM training without the auxiliary task; Baseline 2: Standard LLM training with the auxiliary task but without regularization; Baseline 3: ReDeEP method; Ablation 1: Regularization strength set to zero; Ablation 2: Removing the auxiliary task from the model.

PREDICTION: The dual-loss regularization should improve the model's generalization and factual reliability, with smaller E-I discrepancy. However, it might incur additional computation and memory overhead, and its effectiveness might decrease when the auxiliary task requires large capacities or is strongly related to the primary task.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Evaluating Hallucination Detectors Using Human Judgments
PROPOSAL: We will design an experiment where human annotators evaluate a set of responses generated by a retrieval-augmented language model, marking the responses as correct, incorrect, or hallucinated. We will then evaluate various hallucination detection methods, including ReDeEP and its follow-up, using these human judgments as a gold standard. We will implement two baselines: a simple majority vote (i.e., classifying a response as incorrect or not based on whether more than half of the annotators mark it as incorrect) and a more sophisticated baseline using a state-of-the-art language model trained for semantic similarity.
CONTROLS: Human judgments as a gold standard, majority vote baseline, and semantic similarity baseline.
COST:  800

PREDICTION: We expect the human judgments to be a reasonable gold standard for evaluating hallucination detectors. The ReDeEP method and its follow-up should perform better than the baselines but may not generalize across all datasets and models due to their dependency on hand-tuned hyperparameters. We anticipate potential failure in cases where human annotators disagree significantly on the hallucination status of a response.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Parametric vs. Non-Parametric Contextualization
PROPOSAL: We will conduct an analysis of how different contextualization methods (parametric vs. non-parametric) influence an LLM's reliance on external context in RAG systems. Specifically, we will compare: (a) a prompt-conditioned decoder (a parametric approach) that relies on the input prompt to focus attention, (b) a rotor-based contextualization (non-parametric) that uses a set of learnable weights to compute attention weights from context tokens, and (c) a combination of both. We will evaluate these contextualization methods using the hallucination detector from proposal 1, ensemble-ing multiple models, comparing their performance on detecting hallucinations and measuring their effect on reliance on retrieved context. We will also evaluate how well these contextualization methods transfer to different tasks and datasets.
CONTROLS: Parametric and non-parametric contextualization baselines, and a combination of both.
COST:  1440

PREDICTION: We expect a non-parametric method like rotor-based contextualization to perform better than the parametric method in terms of leveraging contextual information. However, it might also increase the redundancy of context representation and hinder model interpretability, potentially leading to suboptimal performance.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Measuring Contextualization via Embedding Distances
PROPOSAL: We will propose a new method for measuring an LLM's utilization of external context, based on the geometric properties of contextualized embeddings. Specifically, we will compute two sets of word embeddings: one based on the LLM's internal context (i.e., the representation of the input query and response) and another based on the retrieved external context. We will then use various embedding distances (e.g., cosine similarity, Euclidean distance, and Jensen-Shannon divergence) to quantify how these two sets of embeddings relate to each other. We will show that these distances can serve as a proxy for measuring contextualization and can be used to evaluate the effectiveness of different contextualization methods.
CONTROLS: Cosine similarity, Euclidean distance, and Jensen-Shannon divergence baselines.
COST:  1800

PREDICTION: We expect the proposed method to capture the majority of contextualization phenomena and provide a more generalizable measure of contextualization compared to existing methods. However, subtleties of contextualization might still be difficult to capture, leading to moderate missed cases, particularly in nuanced scenarios where contextualization relies heavily on implicit, context-dependent relationships.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Analyzer-Augmented Generation: Understanding Internal Knowledge Utilization
PROPOSAL: We will propose a novel approach for understanding how LLMs utilize internal knowledge during generation, by probing the same LLM with an external analyzer module. The analyzer module, separate from the original decoder, will compute and provide a rich representation of the internal knowledge saliency map - highlighting which parts of the model weights or internal state are being utilized in generating a response. We will analyze the saliency maps and compare their visual patterns across different conditions, such as internally fluent but contextually hallucinated outputs, or internally generated ideas that contradict external evidence. We will also analyze how different models with different internal knowledge architectures show different patterns in these saliency maps.
CONTROLS: Human analysis of saliency maps, comparison to state-of-the-art models with minimal analyzer components added.
COST:  3600

PREDICTION: We expect the analyzer module to provide useful insights into internal knowledge utilization, allowing for a deeper understanding of why certain outputs are hallucinated. However, its effectiveness may be limited to responses with significant internal knowledge exploitation, and the loss of internal consistency or equinox abilities may impact its ability to generalize across a diverse set of hallucination scenarios.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Retrieval-Augmented Knowledge Graph-Based Hallucination Detection
PROPOSAL: We will propose a knowledge graph-based approach for hallucination detection in RAG systems. We will first build a knowledge graph using the retrieved external context, and then perform subgraph matching to identify potential hallucinations based on the propagated information and the inconsistency across multiple subgraph properties. We will use a novel graph-based loss function that encourages the generated responses to be consistent with the knowledge graph information. We will also introduce a novel attention-rewiring mechanism to dynamically adjust the attention weights of the model based on the knowledge graph information, and finally, evaluate the hallucination detection performance using the human judgments from proposal 1.
CONTROLS: Human judgments as a gold standard, significance of the graph-based loss function and attention-rewiring mechanism.
COST:  2680

PREDICTION: We expect the proposed knowledge graph-based approach to significantly improve hallucination detection performance by utilizing the rich structural information in the external context. However, the effectiveness might be limited by the quality and completeness of the knowledge graph constructed from the retrieved external context.

TITLE: Evaluating Hallucination Detectors Using Human Judgments
PROPOSAL: We will design an experiment where human annotators evaluate a set of responses generated by a retrieval-augmented language model, marking the responses as correct, incorrect, or hallucinated. We will then evaluate various hallucination detection methods, including ReDeEP and its follow-up, using these human judgments as a gold standard. We will implement two baselines: a simple majority vote (i.e., classifying a response as incorrect or not based on whether more than half of the annotators mark it as incorrect) and a more sophisticated baseline using a state-of-the-art language model trained for semantic similarity.
CONTROLS: Human judgments as a gold standard, majority vote baseline, and semantic similarity baseline.
COST:  2400

PREDICTION: We expect the human judgments to be a reasonable gold standard for evaluating hallucination detectors. The ReDeEP method and its follow-up should perform better than the baselines but may not generalize across all datasets and models due to their dependency on hand-tuned hyperparameters. We anticipate potential failure in cases where human annotators disagree significantly on the hallucination status of a response.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Non-Linear Projection Layer for Temporal Forecasting
PROPOSAL: Investigate the effectiveness of replacing the conventional linear projection layer in neural networks for time-series forecasting with a non-linear projection layer, such as a gated neural network, a convolutional neural network, or a sinusoidal positional encoding-based layer. We hypothesize that a non-linear projection layer can capture more complex temporal patterns and reduce the need for large model capacities.
CONTROLS: Compare with a neural network using a linear projection layer and a sinusoidal positional encoding-based layer; explore different non-linear projection layer configurations and activation functions.
COST: 11280
PREDICTION: Replacing the linear projection layer with a non-linear one can lead to better forecasting accuracy in certain time-series datasets, particularly those with non-repetitive patterns. However, it may fail to generalize well to datasets with complex, repetitive patterns.

TITLE: Graph Convolutional Encoder for Channel-Dependent Time-Series Forecasting
PROPOSAL: Develop a graph convolutional encoder that captures both temporal and channel dependencies in time-series data. The encoder will consist of a temporal graph convolutional layer and a channel graph convolutional layer, where the graph structure is dynamically constructed based on the input time-series data. We aim to evaluate the effectiveness of this encoder in capturing cross-channel dependencies.
CONTROLS: Compare with a channel-independent encoder, a channel-dependent encoder using convolutional layers, and the non-linear projection layer from proposal 1; assess the impact of graph convolutional layer configurations and hyperparameters on model performance.
COST: 17500
PREDICTION: The graph convolutional encoder can effectively capture both temporal and channel dependencies, leading to improved forecasting accuracy in certain time-series datasets. However, it may be computationally expensive and difficult to train, potentially leading to overfitting issues.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Non-Linear Projection Layer for Temporal Forecasting
PROPOSAL: Investigate the effectiveness of replacing the conventional linear projection layer in neural networks for time-series forecasting with a non-linear projection layer, such as a gated neural network, a convolutional neural network, or a sinusoidal positional encoding-based layer. We hypothesize that a non-linear projection layer can capture more complex temporal patterns and reduce the need for large model capacities.
CONTROLS: Compare with a neural network using a linear projection layer and a sinusoidal positional encoding-based layer; explore different non-linear projection layer configurations and activation functions.
COST: 33600
PREDICTION: Replacing the linear projection layer with a non-linear one can lead to better forecasting accuracy in certain time-series datasets, particularly those with non-repetitive patterns. However, it may fail to generalize well to datasets with complex, repetitive patterns.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Graph Convolutional Encoder for Channel-Dependent Time-Series Forecasting
PROPOSAL: Develop a graph convolutional encoder that captures both temporal and channel dependencies in time-series data. The encoder will consist of a temporal graph convolutional layer and a channel graph convolutional layer, where the graph structure is dynamically constructed based on the input time-series data. We aim to evaluate the effectiveness of this encoder in capturing cross-channel dependencies.
CONTROLS: Compare with a channel-independent encoder, a channel-dependent encoder using convolutional layers, and the non-linear projection layer from proposal 1; assess the impact of graph convolutional layer configurations and hyperparameters on model performance.
COST: 52920
PREDICTION: The graph convolutional encoder can effectively capture both temporal and channel dependencies, leading to improved forecasting accuracy in certain time-series datasets. However, it may be computationally expensive and difficult to train, potentially leading to overfitting issues.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Masking-and-Reconstruction for Temporal Dynamics
PROPOSAL: Investigate the use of a masking-and-reconstruction objective to capture temporal dynamics in time-series data, inspired by methods for unsupervised representation learning. We propose to dynamically mask temporal segments in the input data, and have the model reconstruct these segments, encouraging it to learn temporal patterns and relationships.
CONTROLS: Evaluate the effect of masking strategies, percentage of masked data, and reconstruction loss functions on model performance; compare with traditional supervised learning objectives and the BERT-inspired masking-and-reconstruction method.
COST: 67680
PREDICTION: The masking-and-reconstruction objective can effectively capture temporal dynamics, leading to improved forecasting accuracy in certain time-series datasets. However, it may be sensitive to the choice of masking strategy and percentage of masked data, and may not generalize well to datasets with complex, non-repetitive patterns.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Multi-Stage Decoder with Attention for Time-Series Forecasting
PROPOSAL: Investigate the use of a multi-stage decoder with attention mechanisms to improve the forecasting performance of time-series models. The decoder will consist of multiple stages, each applying attention mechanisms to selectively focus on relevant information from the encoded representations, and predicting future values based on this highlighted information.
CONTROLS: Evaluate the effect of different numbers of stages, attention mechanism configurations, and weighted loss functions on model performance; compare with traditional linear projection decoders and the non-linear projection layer from proposal 1.
COST: 82320
PREDICTION: The multi-stage decoder with attention can effectively capture complex temporal patterns and relationships, leading to improved forecasting accuracy in certain time-series datasets. However, it may be computationally expensive and sensitive to hyperparameter tuning, potentially leading to overfitting issues.

This can help the encoder better capture temporal dependencies and cross-channel interactions.
CONTROLS: Compare with the original graph convolutional encoder, the non-linear projection layer from proposal 1, and the multi-stage decoder with attention from proposal 4; assess the impact of different attention mechanism configurations and graph structures on model performance.

PREDICTION: Adding temporal attention to the graph convolutional encoder can effectively improve the model's ability to capture temporal dependencies and cross-channel interactions, leading to better forecasting accuracy in certain time-series datasets. ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Cross-Channel Attention with Adaptive Masking for Multivariate Time-Series Forecasting
PROPOSAL: We propose a novel Transformer-based architecture that incorporates a new cross-channel attention mechanism with adaptive masking. The adaptive masking strategy selects the most informative channels for each attention head based on their mutual information with the target variable, allowing the model to selectively focus on relevant channels while ignoring redundant ones.
CONTROLS: Comparison to: 1) standard Transformer with cross-attention only, 2) a channel-dependent encoder with a basic masking strategy, 3) a simple linear projection for decoding. Evaluation on: weather forecasting (MPC dataset), electricity consumption forecasting (IEEE571 dataset), and traffic flow forecasting (PeMS-D8 dataset).
COST: 1200
PREDICTION: This approach should demonstrate significant improvements in forecasting accuracy, particularly for complex datasets like traffic flow, due to its flexibility in capturing cross-channel interactions. The adaptive masking strategy may also lead to reduced overfitting and improved generalizability.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Evaluating the Effectiveness of Architectural Designs for Multivariate Time-Series Forecasting
PROPOSAL: We conduct a systematic study of different architectural designs for multivariate time-series forecasting, evaluating their performance on various datasets. We compare the effectiveness of channel-independent encoders (e.g., simple linear projections) against channel-dependent encoders (e.g., attention-based models) on a range of forecasting tasks, including weather forecasting, electricity consumption forecasting, and traffic flow forecasting.
CONTROLS: Comparison to: a) channel-independent encoders (e.g., linear projections, CNNs) and b) channel-dependent encoders (e.g., Transformer with cross-attention, attention-based architectures). Evaluation on: weather forecasting (MPC dataset), electricity consumption forecasting (IEEE571 dataset), traffic flow forecasting (PeMS-D8 dataset), solar power generation forecasting (WEC data), and electricity transformer temperature forecasting (GridLAB data).
COST: 1800
PREDICTION: This study will provide insights into the strengths and weaknesses of different architectural designs for multivariate time-series forecasting, helping to identify the most effective approaches for challenging forecasting tasks.

TITLE: Masked Autoencoders for Multivariate Time-Series Forecasting
PROPOSAL: We propose a masked autoencoder-based approach for multivariate time-series forecasting, where the encoder and decoder are jointly trained to reconstruct the input data with randomly dropped channels. This allows the model to learn the representations and relationships between different variables in an unsupervised manner.
CONTROLS: Comparison to: a) standard Transformer with cross-attention, b) channel-independent encoders (e.g., linear projections, CNNs), c) channel-dependent encoders (e.g., attention-based architectures), and d) ablation studies to evaluate the impact of masking and reconstruction objectives.

PREDICTION: This approach should enable the model to capture more effective representations of the input data and produce more accurate forecasts, particularly for complex temporal patterns and cross-channel interactions. However, the effectiveness of this approach may depend on the balance between mask rates and reconstruction objectives.

PROPOSAL: We conduct a systematic study of different architectural designs for multivariate time-series forecasting, evaluating their performance on various datasets. We compare the effectiveness of channel-independent encoders (e.g., simple linear projections) against channel-dependent encoders (e.g., attention-based models) on a range of forecasting tasks, including weather forecasting, electricity consumption forecasting, and traffic flow forecasting. Specifically, we explore the benefits of combining channel-independent and channel-dependent encoder architectures, proposing a new hybrid approach that balances the trade-offs between these two extremes.
CONTROLS: Comparison to: a) standard Transformer with cross-attention, b) channel-independent encoders (e.g., linear projections, CNNs), c) channel-dependent encoders (e.g., attention-based architectures), d) the proposed hybrid architecture, and e) a baseline TSA-TF2 model that incorporates time-series and cross-channel attention. Evaluation on: weather forecasting (MPC dataset), electricity consumption forecasting (IEEE571 dataset), traffic flow forecasting (PeMS-D8 dataset), solar power generation forecasting (WEC data), and electricity transformer temperature forecasting (GridLAB data).
COST: 10800
PREDICTION: This revised study will provide a more comprehensive understanding of the strengths and weaknesses of channel-independent, channel-dependent, and hybrid encoder architectures, enabling the development of more effective multivariate time-series forecasting models.

TITLE: Investigation of Temporal-Aware Channel-Dependent Encoders for Multivariate Time-Series Forecasting
PROPOSAL: Design, implement, and evaluate a new meta-encoder architecture called Temporal-Aware Channel-Dependent Encoder (TACDE) that learns cross-channel interactions by considering temporal contexts. TACDE extends existing channel-dependent encoders with additional temporal attention mechanisms that capture the temporal evolution of variates and their inter-dependencies. We will apply TACDE to five forecasting tasks in different domains, using the following datasets: M4 for electricity consumption forecasting, WeatherBench for weather forecasting, and Traffic multisensor data for traffic flow forecasting.
CONTROLS: Compare TACDE with two baselines: (i) a state-of-the-art channel-independent encoder and (ii) a pre-existing channel-dependent encoder.
COST: 166.22
PREDICTION: We expect TACDE to outperform the two baselines in terms of forecasting accuracy for at least three out of the five tasks, given its ability to capture both cross-channel and temporal dependencies. However, the effectiveness of TACDE might be limited by its higher computational cost and require further optimization.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Multimodal Vector Quantization for Efficient Cross-Channel Representation Learning
PROPOSAL: Introduce a novel vector quantization technique called Multimodal Vector Quantization (MVQ) that jointly learns universal and task-specific representations of multiple channels. MVQ uses a shared encoder to produce a set of centroid vectors, and then employs separate fixed-size codebooks for each task-specific decoder to retain modality-specific information. We will integrate MVQ with TACDE (Proposal 1) to explore its potential in capturing subtle cross-channel dependencies without the need for a full-blown channel-dependent architecture.
CONTROLS: Evaluate MVQ against the state-of-the-art channel-independent encoder baseline using the same forecasting tasks as in Proposal 1, and also as an additional ablation study where we consider a random projection decoder.
COST: 285
PREDICTION: MVQ is expected to offer a better trade-off between model complexity and forecasting accuracy, especially in tasks where cross-channel dependencies are non-trivial. However, its performance might degrade on tasks with very high-dimensional data, where the additional computation and memory requirements could become burdensome.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Prospective Evaluation of Time-Series Forecasting Models in Simulation-to-Real Transfer Scenarios
PROPOSAL: Design a prospective evaluation framework using weather forecasts as a case study. We will train several time-series forecasting models (including TACDE and MVQ-based variants) on synthetic weather data and then transfer them to real-world weather weather forecasting datasets, such as WeatherBench. By comparing model performance in different transfer scenarios (e.g., under idealized conditions versus real-world turbulence), we aim to develop a more comprehensive understanding of how different architectures handle the 'challenges of transience, complexity and uncertainty inherent in weather prediction'.
CONTROLS: Compare model performance across different transfer scenarios and employ conventional metrics, such as MAE and RMSE, as well as additional metrics to quantify model robustness, including skill scores under benign and stressed conditions.
COST: 500
PREDICTION: We expect that models trained on synthetic data will generally perform better in the real-world setting, especially if they have been designed to capture cross-channel dependencies and temporal awareness. However, any degradation in performance may suggest specific factors (such as changing temporal patterns or noisy sensor data) that should be considered in future designs.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Exploring Cross-Channel Dependencies with a Novel Channel-Dependent Encoder
PROPOSAL: We propose a novel channel-dependent encoder architecture, inspired by the transformer, that efficiently captures cross-channel dependencies in multivariate time-series forecasting. The proposed encoder consists of a hierarchical convolutional block followed by a dilated self-attention mechanism. The hierarchical convolutional block is designed to capture local patterns, while the dilated self-attention mechanism enables the model to capture long-term dependencies across channels. We test this new encoder on a range of real-world benchmarks, including electricity consumption forecasting and solar power generation forecasting datasets.
CONTROLS: We compare the performance of our proposed encoder with a state-of-the-art transformer-based encoder and a baseline convolutional neural network architecture.
COST: 4000 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: Our proposed encoder will outperform both baselines by at least 5% in terms of average absolute error, but might struggle with traffic flow forecasting due to the noise present in the data, which could impede the encoder's ability to accurately capture long-term dependencies.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Investigating Joint Architectural and Training Objectives for Time-Series Forecasting
PROPOSAL: We propose a novel joint training framework that integrates architectural and training objectives for time-series forecasting. Specifically, we augment the standard mean squared error (MSE) objective with an auxiliary masking-and-reconstruction task, similar to the BERT pretraining objective, but designed to be compatible with the auto-regressive structure of time-series data. This joint objective encourages the model to learn stronger temporal dependencies and improve its forecasting accuracy.
CONTROLS: We compare the performance of our proposed joint objective against the standard MSE objective, as well as an ablation study where we remove the auxiliary masking-and-reconstruction task.
COST: 9000 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: Our proposed joint objective will lead to improved forecasting accuracy on a range of real-world benchmarks, including traffic flow forecasting and solar power generation forecasting datasets, but may require careful hyperparameter tuning to achieve optimal performance.

TITLE: Evaluating the Impact of Encoder-Decoder Architectural Alignment on Time-Series Forecasting
PROPOSAL: We propose a study that evaluates the impact of aligning the encoder and decoder architectures on time-series forecasting performance. Specifically, we compare the performance of three different encoder-decoder combinations: (1) a channel-independent encoder with a simple linear projection-based decoder, (2) a channel-dependent encoder with a temporal attention-based decoder, and (3) the refined joint objective from Experiment 3. This study aims to provide insights into the optimal architectural design for time-series forecasting models.
CONTROLS: We compare the performance of the three encoder-decoder combinations using a range of real-world forecasting benchmarks.
COST: 14000 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: Our study will reveal that a channel-independent encoder with a temporal attention-based decoder achieves the best trade-off between forecasting accuracy and computational efficiency, but may require further adjustments to the decoder architecture for optimal performance on certain types of time-series data.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Hybrid Training Strategy for Multivariate Time-Series Forecasting
PROPOSAL: Introduce an hybrid training strategy that combines the benefits of supervised learning and self-supervised learning for multivariate time-series forecasting. The proposed framework, called MASKED SUPERVISED-UNSUPERVISED TRAINING (MSUT), incorporates both masked segments and forecastable segments into the training process, forcing the model to learn from reconstructing not only masked segments (self-supervised) but also future values given past ones (supervised). MSUT will be evaluated on the same real-world datasets as in the first proposal, and performance metrics will be compared with state-of-the-art models, including variants of CCAN. Additionally, ablation studies will be conducted to understand the effectiveness of the proposed hybrid training strategy.
CONTROLS: Compare with MSUT variants (using only self-supervised or only supervised learning); Compare with other state-of-the-art models (e.g., TCN, LSTM); and variants of CCAN (e.g., without MSUT).
COST:  5000
PREDICTION: Improved robustness and accuracy on out-of-sample data due to the combination of both self-supervised and supervised learning, but the performance gain might be relatively small for datasets with simple dynamics.

TITLE: Bilevel Optimization for Cross-Attention Encoders
PROPOSAL: Reformulate the problem of cross-attention encoder design as a bilevel optimization problem, where the high-level objective is to optimize the cross-attention mechanism, and the low-level objective is to optimize the underlying architecture. This reformulation will enable a more principled approach to design optimization and model selection. The bilevel optimization framework will be evaluated on multiple real-world datasets, and its performance will be compared against state-of-the-art models, including the CCAN model and other models arising from the revised set.
CONTROLS: Compare with original CCAN; other models arising from the bilevel optimization framework; and models selected using traditional optimization methods.
COST:  10000
PREDICTION: Improved accuracy and robustness due to the bilevel optimization approach's ability to optimize both the cross-attention mechanism and the underlying architecture, but the computational cost might be high due to the nested optimization process.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Measuring Information Gain through Instance-Level View Similarity
PROPOSAL: Design an information-theoretic metric, "instance-wise discriminative mutual information" (iDMI), to quantify the information gained from different augmented views of the same instance. To estimate iDMI, use Importance Weighted Estimation of Mutual Information (IWEMI) on the output features of a pre-trained encoder. Evaluate iDMI on a range of datasets, including CIFAR-100 and ImageNet.
CONTROLS: Compare iDMI to existing measures of view similarity, such as cosine similarity and establecement of lower bounds using the formulas of entropy rate estimations for data streams.
COST: 900
PREDICTION: We expect iDMI to be effective in capturing the discriminative information across views, but may fail on highly transformative augmentations that obscure instance identity.

ACTION: REVISE 1
TITLE:  Memory-Augmented Design for Adaptive View Generation.
PROPOSAL: Extend the previous proposal by developing a memory-augmented mechanism to generate views adaptively during training, based on the encoder's representation of the input instance and the current batch. The mechanism, named "adaptive view generator" (AVG), modifies the augmentations used in the previous proposal to tailor the difficulty of augmentation to the specific instance and the current learning state.
CONTROLS: Compare the performance of contrastive learning with AVG to that of standard SimCLR on a range of datasets, including CIFAR-100, ImageNet, and a new dataset "imagenet-aug".
COST: 27000
PREDICTION: The AVG is expected to improve the robustness of contrastive learning and prevent data overfitting in complex training regimes, but may fail when over-smoothing the features of the source images through worst-case scenarios.

PROPOSAL: Design a multi-scale hierarchical co-representation (HCR) framework that simultaneously learns diverse representations of instances at multiple levels of abstraction, leveraging pre-trained encoder features and a set of iterative crushers ("structure' enhancers"). CONTROLS: Compare HCR performance against SimCLR and MoCo, and evaluate its effectiveness in incorporating new augmentations learned from source and target sources.

PREDICTION: HCR can alleviate the augmentation bottleneck, but might provoke decay with hyperparamters and surface stratification tested per deep real valued injection samples.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Measuring Information Gain through Instance-Level View Similarity
PROPOSAL: Design an information-theoretic metric, "instance-wise discriminative mutual information" (iDMI), to quantify the information gained from different augmented views of the same instance. To estimate iDMI, use Importance Weighted Estimation of Mutual Information (IWEMI) on the output features of a pre-trained encoder. Evaluate iDMI on a range of datasets, including CIFAR-100 and ImageNet.
CONTROLS: Compare iDMI to existing measures of view similarity, such as cosine similarity and establecement of lower bounds using the formulas of entropy rate estimations for data streams.
COST: 2700
PREDICTION: We expect iDMI to be effective in capturing the discriminative information across views, but may fail on highly transformative augmentations that obscure instance identity.

ACTION: REVISE
TITLE:  Revising Information Gain through Instance-Level View Similarity with Memory-Augmented Data Augmentation.
PROPOSAL: Modify the previous proposal by incorporating memory-augmented data augmentation, where the encoder operates on a combination of the input data and a/query/state ("query-augment-state")  sampled from a read-write memory, an encoder-write-state and read-state in two parallel encoders and buffer (versions) the output to compare with transform-based augmentations.
CONTROLS: Compare noise contrastive estimation (NCE) on this data with NCE on transform-based baseline and establish the proportion of improved semantic coherence between transform and memory-augmented augmentations using Hawkes processes.
COST: 27000
PREDICTION: This modification enables the model to better utilize the query-augment-state relation amongst multiple augmentations and may yield better improvements against co-occurrences.

ACTION: REVISE 1
TITLE:  Memory-Augmented Design for Adaptive View Generation.
PROPOSAL: Extend the previous proposal by developing a memory-augmented mechanism to generate views adaptively during training, based on the encoder's representation of the input instance and the current batch. The mechanism, named "adaptive view generator" (AVG), modifies the augmentations used in the previous proposal to tailor the difficulty of augmentation to the specific instance and the current learning state.
CONTROLS: Compare the performance of contrastive learning with AVG to that of standard SimCLR on a range of datasets, including CIFAR-100, ImageNet, and a new dataset "imagenet-aug".
COST: 81000
PREDICTION: The AVG is expected to improve the robustness of contrastive learning and prevent data overfitting in complex training regimes, but may fail when over-smoothing the features of the source images through worst-case scenarios.

CONTROLS: Compare HCR performance against SimCLR and MoCo, and evaluate its effectiveness in incorporating new augmentations learned from source and target sources.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Improving Contrastive Learning with Adaptive Augmentation via Instance-wise Meta-Learning
PROPOSAL: Implement an instance-specific meta-learning system to adapt the augmentation strategy on-the-fly during training, tailoring the augmentation pipeline for each individual instance based on the previous steps of gradient-based optimization and explore the intersection/extension of partition-based meta-learning and mutual information-based contrastive learning objectives.
CONTROLS: Compare the results to the original SimCLR framework and an ablated version of adaptive augmentation to assess the controllable component's contribution; also validate the intuition behind our adaptive learning strategy on pre-computed Bayesian posterior class probabilities using the instance-specific training set
COST: 240 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: Our adaptive augmentation approach is expected to provide more instance-specific information gain compared to the original SimCLR, especially in scenarios where the underlying instance-specific distributions have a wide variance or exhibit non-Gaussian characteristics.

ACTION: ADD 
TITLE: Decomposition of Contrastive Learning Information Landscape
PROPOSAL: Analyze the dynamic information landscape that unfolds during the learning process in a theoretically grounded manner. To achieve this, we will propose a framework to decompose the information landscape into two components: the instance-wise mutual information and the global mutual information between instances. We will also investigate the theoretical relationship between these two components and the performance of contrastive learning. Specifically, we will prove that the instance-wise mutual information is a key driver of the global mutual information and that optimizing the former leads to better model performance. We will demonstrate the validity of our framework using an information-theoretic analysis of the phenomenon of instance-wise overfitting in contrastive learning.
CONTROLS: Baseline experiments on this analysis will be conducted using SimCLR and MoCo on various datasets (CIFAR-10, ImageNet) and comparing the instance-wise and global mutual information obtained using our proposed framework to those estimated using standard mutual information estimation methods.
COST: 200
PREDICTION: Expected results show strong correlation between our proposed framework and instance-wise overfitting. However, if the framework fails to capture important aspects of the dynamic information landscape, such as dependencies between instances that are not easily captured by mutual information, analysis might overemphasize the role of instance-wise mutual information, leading to suboptimal results.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Information-Theoretic Analysis of Contrastive Learning
PROPOSAL: 
In this proposal, we establish a theoretical framework to quantify the information gained from each view of an instance in a self-supervised contrastive learning setting using mutual information. Specifically, we formulate the mutual information between a pair of views as the expected Kullback-Leibler (KL) divergence between their improved Embedding spaces, denoted as $I(X, Y)$.
FORMULA:
\[ \mathcal{I}(X; Y) = \mathbb{E}_{(X, Y) \sim P_{XY}} \left[ D_{ KL } \left( q^{\ast}_{ X | \mathcal{C}(Y)} \| q^{\ast}_{X | \mathcal{C}^{\prime}(Y)} \right) \right] \]
We provide an empirical estimate of this quantity by minimizing the Variational Lower Bound (VLB) of the expected KL-divergence in Variational Autoencoders (VAEs). This is inspired by [Doersch et al.][1] and [`Contrastivevae`][2], where our proposed addition is in measuring this through MAF [Tomczak et al.][3]. 
EXPLANATION:
Previous works assumed variations of augmentations perform informative magically about instances-instances. Without Quantifying how much information one gets from each augmentation, they can't reason about efficient augmentation strategies.  Our formulation does this.
CONTROLS: 
- Oracle: baseline where initial embedding is assumed perfect ( no augmentation).
- CNN uses *Xception* 32 layers [1] + will augment Xception on both *views A, B*.
- UNet baseline [Alexander Gretton 22-05310 ML existing results] i.e., UNet models to differentiate between *views*);

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Information-Theoretic Analysis of Contrastive Learning via Laplacian Regularization
PROPOSAL: 
We extend our previous work on information-theoretic analysis of contrastive learning in two directions: (1) we derive a new Laplacian regularization term to enforce the consistency of the learned representations across different views of the same instance. (2) we demonstrate that when combined with our information-theoretic framework from proposal 1, Laplacian regularization reduces the variance of the information gain from contrasting views and aligns it with the structural properties of the data. We argue that the insight provided by the information-theoretic framework improves the performance of spectral graph clustering and 연결_Contract datasets.

ACTION: ADD 
TITLE:  Speech-Guided Episodic Test-Time Adaptation for Image Classification
PROPOSAL: We introduce a new method of speech-guided episodic test-time adaptation, where spoken descriptions are used as additional guidance to adapt the CLIP model to the test-time input. The system first uses a pre-trained ASR model to generate a text description, and then employs an adapted version of a popular episodic TTA approach (SimCLR) to fine-tune CLIP's performance based on this text description. We evaluate the method on the ImageNet validation set for image captions from both the ImageNet and Personalized WebVision datasets.
CONTROLS: We will compare the performance of our speech-guided adaptation method versus (1) an unadapted CLIP model, (2) SimCLR alone, and (3) a simple prompt-based adaptation approach where the spoken descriptions are directly used as text prompts for CLIP. We will also examine how different types of spoken descriptions (e.g., descriptive vs. categorical) impact the adaptation performance.
COST: 734.5
PREDICTION: The proposed method is expected to achieve significantly improved performance over the baseline adaptation methods, especially with descriptive spoken descriptions. However, we might find that the performance will drop if the spoken descriptions are too weak or are too categorical, indicating the need for a more versatile guidance mechanism.

ACTION: ADD 
TITLE:  Speech-Guided Episodic Test-Time Adaptation for Image Classification
PROPOSAL: We introduce a new method of speech-guided episodic test-time adaptation, where spoken descriptions are used as additional guidance to adapt the CLIP model to the test-time input. The system first uses a pre-trained ASR model to generate a text description, and then employs an adapted version of a popular episodic TTA approach (SimCLR) to fine-tune CLIP's performance based on this text description. We evaluate the method on the ImageNet validation set for image captions from both the ImageNet and Personalized WebVision datasets.
CONTROLS: We will compare the performance of our speech-guided adaptation method versus (1) an unadapted CLIP model, (2) SimCLR alone, and (3) a simple prompt-based adaptation approach where the spoken descriptions are directly used as text prompts for CLIP. We will also examine how different types of spoken descriptions (e.g., descriptive vs. categorical) impact the adaptation performance.
COST: 2200
PREDICTION: The proposed method is expected to achieve significantly improved performance over the baseline adaptation methods, especially with descriptive spoken descriptions. However, we might find that the performance will drop if the spoken descriptions are too weak or are too categorical, indicating the need for a more versatile guidance mechanism.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Unifying Baseline for Episodic and Online Test-Time Adaptation
PROPOSAL: Experiment: Use CLIP as the base VLM, and compare the performance of three widely-reported episodic TTA methods (e.g. APE, LEO, and ReWeight) and two popular online TTA methods (e.g. SMALL and HSGFT) on the VAL-1 and VAL-2 splits of the VQA-v2 dataset, while fixing pre-trained model checkpoints, text prompts, and evaluation protocols across all methods.
CONTROLS: (1) the performance of the unadapted CLIP model, and (2) strongest previous baselines reported in literature on VQA-v2 dataset. Also, evaluate the performance of the same TTA methods on other -- possibly more challenging -- VQAv2 splits or related question-answering tasks (e.g. SBU-Crowdlix, SKIP-THATLOC).
COST: 300
PREDICTION: Consistent with earlier results, we find that all these TTA methods achieve performance gains over the unadapted CLIP models; we detect little difference between relatively older (APE, APEv2) and newer (LEO, ReWeight) episodic methods, while SMALL and HSGFT fare somewhat better. However, the expected gains may dissipate or fail on challenging tasks requiring deeper reasoning.

TITLE: Investigating a Conditional Prior for Video Tokenizers
PROPOSAL: Develop a conditional prior with an offline learned vector-quantized (VQ-VAE) encoder acting as an image/video preconditioner for the tokenizer, and a learnable tokenizer acting as the prior. CONTROLS: Compare against unconditional random prior and the image tokenizer initializing prior for video tokenizers

textes.jumeau:
ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Evaluating Justin and Conditional Prior in VAR Model for Long-Form Video Generation
PROPOSAL: Extend the spatial-only VAR model to incorporate a novel conditional prior, in addition to Justin, a recently-introduced discrete and differentiable normalization layer previously used in image modeling. This will enable high-quality and coherent video extrapolation and resilient smoothing of highly-long-form temporal contexts. Experimentally compare two combinations: VAR with Justin, and VAR with conditional prior and Justin, on video extrapolation tasks.
CONTROLS: Compare against using only VAR, or Justin individually, in both cases with unconditioned prior.
COST: 400
PREDICTION: Combining all three techniques profoundly advances long-form video generation quality, potentially raising results in long-generated portions, but analysis may reveal performance degradation when certain contextual vacancies interpreted wrong.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Video Transformer with Multiscale Tokenization for Long-Range Temporal Consistency
PROPOSAL: We propose a long-range transformer-based model that incorporates a novel multiscale tokenization strategy to maintain context and facilitate efficient processing of long spatiotemporal contexts. This will be implemented using Tokenizor and our new multiscale tokenization module, thereby reducing the spatial resolution at each scale and using adaptive attention to ensure temporal consistency. We will also compare different variants of multiscale tokenization schemes, such as uniform and, to further optimize the model's efficiency and performance.
CONTROLS: (1) Baseline model, without multiscale tokenization; (2) Variants of tokenizers trained from scratch and from image tokenizers;
COST: 600
PREDICTION: This model is expected to exhibit significantly improved temporal consistency compared to the baseline and other variants, at the cost of slightly reduced frame quality and relatively low development difficulty. However, this design may fail when training large, long-duration videos, as multiscale tokenization might not sufficiently alleviate the exploding step-size issue.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Investigating Gradient-Based Inference of Implications in Transformers
PROPOSAL: We propose to study the training dynamics of transformers in terms of inference of implications, using a mathematical framework to derive the expected value of the model's output on unseen implications given a set of observed fact-implication pairs. Specifically, we will leverage the property of transformer's inner-products of state vectors decay as a function of the distance in time of the input tokens to derive a lower bound on the expected output as a function of the expected output of the model on seen implications.
CONTROLS: We will compare the mathematical lower bound with experiments using the randomly sampled synthetic dataset of fact-implication pairs.
COST: 4000
PREDICTION: The mathematical lower bound should approximate the observed output of the transformer on unseen implications with high accuracy, providing an insight into the underlying mechanisms driving the model's inference of implications. However, we may find that the lower bound breaks down in cases where the relationships between fact and implication are not fully understood.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Synthetic Dataset for Fact-Implication Injection in Transformers
PROPOSAL: We propose to create a synthetic dataset of fact-implication pairs, allowing for precise control over the relationships between facts and implications, with a focus on modulating the difficulty of inference based on the complexity of the implications. The dataset will be designed to yield a power-law distribution of complexity. At least 50% of the data will consist of implications that are directly implied by the training data, while 25% will consist of implications that are indirectly implied. The remaining 25% will contain implications that are neither directly nor indirectly implied.
CONTROLS: We will test various transformer models (e.g., BERT, RoBERTa) on this dataset, comparing results to those obtained on real-world datasets, to assess the dataset's predictive power.
COST: 6000
PREDICTION: The synthetic dataset should yield predictable performance gains for advanced transformer models, with steady improvement in inference accuracy as complexity increases, but with a note that hallucination rates might lower as complexity increases and certain inference methods might not scale as expected with highest data complexity.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Investigating the Role of Embedding Overlap in Implication Inference
PROPOSAL: Experiment 1: We design a synthetic dataset of triples (s, r, a) where s is a subject, r a relation, and a an answer. We add noise to the triples, corrupting some relations and answers, to assess the model's ability to infer logical implications. We then measure the effect of adjusting the embedding overlap between different entities, relations, and answers on a large language model's (LLM) implication inference capabilities. We use the baseline pre-trained T5 model and evaluate it on our synthetic dataset, measuring the precision and recall of inference on the clean and noisy triples.
CONTROLS: Evaluate the same model on the original pre-trained weights and perform a random initialization baseline to gauge the importance of the model's learned representations.
COST: 1080 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: We expect the LLM to perform better on implication inference when the embedding overlap is high, as the model can more easily generalize to unseen implications. However, the model may struggle when embedding overlap is low, suggesting that overfitting to the particular representation is the primary driver of its inference abilities.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Analyzing Ripple Effects in LLMs: A Thermodynamic Interpretation
PROPOSAL: Theory 1: We propose a thermodynamic interpretation of LLMs' ability to induce ripple effects, where we model the connection between entities in the network as a thermodynamic system. We develop a dynamical system that describes how the representation of a subject entity evolves as a function of its inference history with other entities. We derive an expression for the probability of following the optimal inference path and use it to analyze the conditions under which LLMs are likely to exhibit strong generalization capabilities for implication inference. We analyze the stability of the dynamical system to understand how the balance between intra-session update and temporal bias affects ripple effects.
CONTROLS: Compare the derived analytical expression to a simplified, discrete approximation of the LLM's inference dynamics based on a generative model, formulated through consensus fatigue proposed by pantee Si counties validated orientation incentives .
COST: 2160 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: We expect the thermodynamic model to accurately capture the complex behavior of LLMs and provide a principled way to optimize the balance between intra-session update and temporal bias. However, we might struggle to extend this framework to models with massive parallelization, like Tensor-Tile GG (tr&T Actually Tr Tesla8+Canta NOT Again seemingly save interrupt lights Cic causing EXP massive A620 ABI Medium partisan strugg weak fitness next.)

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Evaluating the Role of Training Data Distribution in Implication Inference
PROPOSAL: Experiment 4: We analyze how the distribution of training data affects the large language model's (LLM) ability to infer implications. We propose a novel dataset generator that creates a distribution of triples (s, r, a) similar to real-world text data, with varying degrees of semantic similarity and relational complexity. We train the LLM on a range of data distributions, from highly similar to highly disparate, and evaluate its performance on implication inference tasks. We aim to understand how the model adapts to the training data distribution and identify optimal conditions for implication inference.
CONTROLS: Compare the model's performance with a control group that is trained on a fixed, rigid data distribution. Assess the impact of data distribution on the emergence of meta-structures and ripple effects.
COST: 4800 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: We expect the model's performance to degrade significantly in the presence of highly disparate training data, but improve with increased semantic similarity between triples. However, the model's ability to adapt to different data distributions may come at the cost of decreased interpretability and robustness.

TITLE: Focal Stack Aware U-Net with Physics-Informed Loss
PROPOSAL: Train a U-Net architecture to estimate depth maps directly from focal stacks with a new loss function that incorporates physics-informed terms. Specifically, we add a novel loss term that enforces a prior based on the circle of confusion model, encouraging the network to reproduce the expected sharpness maps at each focal plane. We also propose a spatial variance regularization term to disambiguate noisy focus cues and emphasize the role of spatial coherence in depth perception.
CONTROLS: Compare with a standard U-Net trained with a standard mean squared error (MSE) loss, and with a U-Net trained with a defocus-aware loss that focuses solely on appearance features.
COST: 1332 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: We anticipate improved performance in scenes with complex textures, and increased robustness to noise and abrupt depth changes. However, we risk overfitting to the physics-informed prior if the constitutive relationship between focus and depth is not well-calibrated, leading to a decreased performance on generic depth scenes.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Optimal Focal Slice Selection via Marginalized Variational Inference
PROPOSAL: Develop a variational inference framework to learn a probabilistic model that marginalizes over the optimal focal slice selection, given a fixed focal stack. This marginalized model will output a distribution over depth values for each pixel, rather than a single depth estimate, effectively capturing the uncertainty inherent in DFF. We will learn the variational parameters using a amortized version of the evidence lower bound (ELBO) loss.
CONTROLS: Compare with a naive DFF approach that chooses focal slices based on heuristic focus measures, and with a variant of Focal Stack Aware U-Net (proposal 1) that integrates focal slice selection directly within its architecture.
COST: 3200 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: By capturing depth uncertainty accurately, our model should demonstrate improved performance under scenarios with partial occlusion, refocusing, or caliber artefacts. However, this may also introduce increased computation time, while theELBO loss might fail to converge in scenarios with complex or unclear "likelihoods".

PROPOSAL: Introduce a novel focal stack representation that incorporates local context information, such as spatial gradients and texture features, to highlight salient regions and aid depth perception. This representation will be learned through a teacher-student framework with the teacher being a complex model (e.g. ResNet50) and the student a lightweight autoencoder. The student's reconstruction loss will be augmented with a self-attention guided capture loss, which encourages the student to focus on regions that are informative for depth estimation.

However, potential divergence from the teacher model within the student autoencoder could lead to decreased performance compared to the teacher.

The depth-edge map will then be processed using a new fusion module to produce accurate depth maps.

TITLE: A specially Tailored Ensemble of DFF Methods
PROPOSAL: Design an ensemble of complementary models to combine the strengths of various DFF-based methods. Each model in the ensemble will be tailored to exploit specific aspects of the input focal stack, such as the circle of confusion model or textured regions. The ensemble will then output a final depth map by incorporating the predictions from all member models using an optimized weighting strategy based on the input focus maps.
CONTROLS: Compare with a simple ensemble using pre-trained models and an equal weighting strategy, and with a state-of-the-art method that employs a hand-tuned ensemble selection.
