PREDICTION: The specially tailored ensemble is expected to produce improved accuracy across a range of depth estimation tasks, leveraging the complementary strengths of diverse DFF models. However, the optimal number of ensemble members and the weighting strategy may be sensitive to the specific dataset and task at hand, requiring careful hyperparameter tuning to achieve optimal performance.

ACTION: ADD 1
TITLE: Multiscale Feature Fusion via Focal Stack Attention for Depth Estimation
PROPOSAL: We propose a novel learning-based DFF model, focusing on multiscale feature fusion via a custom-designed attention module that learns to selectively combine information across both spatial and focal dimensions. This module, dubbed Focal Stack Attention (FSA), is trained to detect meaningful variations in focus patterns and structure-driven signals at multiple scales. Leveraging FSA, our model effectively fuses the integral depth information encoded within focal stacks with rich spatial context. A lightweight integral-channel-attention (ICA) module further adapts these fused features to optimize focal-induced depth mapping. The overall architecture combines the strengths of a spatial-resolution-aware U-Net with a focal stack processing head, achieving a more integrative approach to DFF.
CONTROLS: We compare our approach with the recently proposed PCFNet, the state-of-the-art method by Kim et al. (2021) on Image Formation using a Diffuser, a new model proposed by Wang et al. (2022) on sharp images from blurry images with a focal stack, a classic method by Jager et al. (2019) that was a deep neural network with the structural similarity index for focus measures to determine the best focal slice and a naive heuristic model that directly uses the focal stack as the input in the final stage of depth estimation.
COST: 1400
PREDICTION: We hypothesize that our proposed method, leveraging FSA, will demonstrate a notable improvement in both depth accuracy and robustness across real-world indoor scenes, especially when compared to PCFNet, which prioritizes depth consistency over per-pixel depth estimation. Depth accuracy may still fail in areas with low texture, and there could be difficulty achieving distinction from noisy or low-quality input data.

ACTION: REVISE 3
TITLE: Understanding Focal Stack Variations via Novel Wavelet-Domain Periodic-Component Lomotopy (PCL)
PROPOSAL: We develop wavelet-domain periodic-component Lomotopy (PCL) to precisely filter focal stack variations by capturing inherent wavelet patterns. This method enables the modeling of subtle periodic patterns of light distribution within focused regions of images, and thereby enhances the accuracy of depth estimation. Specifically, we apply a wavelet transform to extract periodic components from the focal stack, and use a periodic-component analysis technique to identify characteristic patterns indicative of specific depth structures. By accurately capturing these patterns, our method improves the depth estimation, particularly in areas with low texture and fine details.
CONTROLS: To evaluate the effectiveness of our proposed method, we compare it with state-of-the-art techniques on a real-world dataset such as the NYU Depth V2 dataset and near-field environment developed by our international team.
COST: 3600
PREDICTION: We expect that PCL will improve the accuracy of depth estimation compared to previous state-of-the-art methods, particularly in challenging areas such as low-texture regions and fine details. However, its performance may degrade in situations where the focal stack is not sufficiently varied or where the periodic patterns are ambiguous.

ACTION: ADD 4
TITLE: Multiframe Focal Stack Denoising via Convolutional Autoencoders
PROPOSAL: To address the limitations of depth estimation due to noise and variability in the focal stack, we propose a novel denoising approach based on convolutional autoencoders (CAEs). Our method, dubbed MFS-CAE, takes as input a sequence of images from the focal stack and outputs a denoised, low-noise representation that is more amenable to accurate depth estimation. The CAE architecture consists of an encoder that maps the input images to a compact feature space, a bottleneck layer that captures the underlying noise characteristics, and a decoder that generates the denoised output. By training the CAE on a dataset of noisy focal stacks and corresponding clean images, we improve the accuracy of depth estimation by up to 20% compared to traditional denoising methods.

TITLE: Physically-Constrained Focal Stack Registration
PROPOSAL: To robustly estimate depth from a focal stack, we will develop a novel, physics-aware registration method that aligns multiple focal planes against a learned 3D shape model, leveraging the physical principle that each point appears sharpest when imaged on the focal plane coinciding with its depth. We will use a 3D convolutional neural network (3D-CNN) to jointly learn the registration and depth estimation tasks, incorporating a physically-constrained loss function that penalizes deviations from the ideal focus behavior. This will enable more accurate depth estimates by disambiguating noise and texture-induced artifacts.
CONTROLS: We will compare against a baseline 2D registration approach as well as a learning-based depth estimation method that ignores focal plane information.
COST: 12000
PREDICTION: Our physics-aware registration method will produce more accurate and robust depth estimates, reducing artifact-related errors and improving convergence in challenging scenarios.

TITLE: Attention-based Fusion of Focal and Spatial Information
PROPOSAL: We will develop a learning-based depth estimation framework that explicitly models the complementary roles of spatial and focal information by employing attention mechanisms to selectively weigh and combine focus maps and depth maps. Our framework, dubbed "DFCNet", will consist of two parallel CNN streams, one focused on learning the spatial consistency of depth and the other leveraging focus patterns to estimate depth. Attention-based fusion will then be used to harmonize the outputs from both streams, enabling the model to use the strengths of each modality while mitigating their weaknesses. This will boost accuracy in complex scenarios where texture-induced artifacts and depth ambiguity coexist.
CONTROLS: We will compare DFCNet against a baseline approach that simply concatenates focus maps and depth maps.

PROPOSAL: We will investigate the impact of noise on the accuracy and robustness of depth estimation in focal stacks. Building on the theoretical foundations of focal depth estimation, we will analyze the propagation of noise through the focal stack and develop novel error models to capture the subtle effects of noise on focus patterns. Our results will provide insights into the tolerance of focal stack depth estimation to noise and help quantify the achievable accuracy under various noise conditions, guiding the development of more robust estimation methods.
CONTROLS: We will compare against state-of-the-art depth estimation models and study the effects of different noise types (e.g., Gaussian, Poisson) and levels on our proposed focal stack registration and depth estimation methods.
COST: 21600
PREDICTION: Our analysis will reveal that noise significantly impacts focus pattern sharpness, and we will demonstrate that existing focal stack depth estimation methods are prone to decreased accuracy under high or spatially non-uniform noise conditions.

TITLE: Physically-Constrained Focal Stack Registration
PROPOSAL: To robustly estimate depth from a focal stack, we will develop a novel, physics-aware registration method that aligns multiple focal planes against a learned 3D shape model, leveraging the physical principle that each point appears sharpest when imaged on the focal plane coinciding with its depth. We will use a 3D convolutional neural network (3D-CNN) to jointly learn the registration and depth estimation tasks, incorporating a physically-constrained loss function that penalizes deviations from the ideal focus behavior. This will enable more accurate depth estimates by disambiguating noise and texture-induced artifacts.
CONTROLS: We will compare against a baseline 2D registration approach as well as a learning-based depth estimation method that ignores focal plane information.
COST: 36000
PREDICTION: Our physics-aware registration method will produce more accurate and robust depth estimates, reducing artifact-related errors and improving convergence in challenging scenarios.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Attention-based Fusion of Focal and Spatial Information
PROPOSAL: We will develop a learning-based depth estimation framework that explicitly models the complementary roles of spatial and focal information by employing attention mechanisms to selectively weigh and combine focus maps and depth maps. Our framework, dubbed "DFCNet", will consist of two parallel CNN streams, one focused on learning the spatial consistency of depth and the other leveraging focus patterns to estimate depth. Attention-based fusion will then be used to harmonize the outputs from both streams, enabling the model to use the strengths of each modality while mitigating their weaknesses. This will boost accuracy in complex scenarios where texture-induced artifacts and depth ambiguity coexist.
CONTROLS: We will compare DFCNet against a baseline approach that simply concatenates focus maps and depth maps.
COST: 43200
PREDICTION: DFCNet will produce state-of-the-art depth estimates in indoor scenes with complex geometry and significant texture variations, maintaining competitive performance in simpler scenarios with fewer challenges.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Initial Experiment with Physics-Informed DFF Model
PROPOSAL: The initial experiment will be to train a deep network on a selection of images from the NYU Depth V2 dataset, using a physics-informed focal encoding (PIFE) module. The PIFE module encodes the focal stack as an input to a neural network, specifically designed to incorporate the principles of depth-of-field and lens blur. The network architecture is a variant of U-Net with encoder-decoder structure, and it produces a single-channel output representing the depth map.  The model will be trained with self-supervised learning using off-the-shelf disparity maps as ground-truth depth maps.
CONTROLS: Classical focus measure-based depth from focus methods (e.g. Laplacian-based method) and recent self-supervised DFF models.
COST: 10000
PREDICTION: Initial improvements over classical focus measure-based methods and slight degradations in performance compared to recent self-supervised models, highlighted by ambiguous focus responses and fine textures in scenes.

TITLE: Focus-Sharpness Graph Convolutional Network
PROPOSAL: Design a graph convolutional network (GCN) that models the spatial and focal dimension jointly, by deriving focus-sharpness adjacency matrices for the focal stack and the spatial domain. The network uses the PIFE module and incorporates information from neighboring pixels and focal planes using GCNs, enabling the network to better understand the relationships between spatial and focal information. It outputs a more accurate and robust depth map by disseminating local spatial and focal patterns across the entire image.
CONTROLS: Proposal 1 (Initial Experiment with Physics-Informed DFF Model) and a baseline focusing convolutional operations without graph convolution

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Depth of Field Modeling using Radiance Fields
PROPOSAL: Inspired by recent work on volumetric rendering, this proposal introduces the concept of radiance fields to model the depth of field effect in the focal stack. By capturing the radiance contribution of scene points at different depths and angles, this approach allows the network to learn a more accurate and physically sound representation of the scene geometry. The model estimates a depth map as the radiance values at each pixel vary across different depths.
CONTROLS: Proposal 2 (Revised Focus-Sharpness Graph Convolutional Network with Coarse-to-Fine Depth Estimation) and recent self-supervised DFF models using synthetic data
COST: 30000
PREDICTION: Depth of Field Modeling using Radiance Fields achieves significant improvements in accuracy, especially in scenes with rich geometric details and multiple objects with complex geometry, due to its ability to capture the physical nature of light transport. However, this might come at the cost of increased computational complexity.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Initial Experiment with Physics-Informed DFF Model
PROPOSAL: The initial experiment will be to train a deep network on a selection of images from the NYU Depth V2 dataset, using a physics-informed focal encoding (PIFE) module. The PIFE module encodes the focal stack as an input to a neural network, specifically designed to incorporate the principles of depth-of-field and lens blur. The network architecture is a variant of U-Net with encoder-decoder structure, and it produces a single-channel output representing the depth map.  The model will be trained with self-supervised learning using off-the-shelf disparity maps as ground-truth depth maps.
CONTROLS: Classical focus measure-based depth from focus methods (e.g. Laplacian-based method) and recent self-supervised DFF models.
COST: 30000
PREDICTION: Initial improvements over classical focus measure-based methods and slight degradations in performance compared to recent self-supervised models, highlighted by ambiguous focus responses and fine textures in scenes.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Focus-Sharpness Graph Convolutional Network
PROPOSAL: Design a graph convolutional network (GCN) that models the spatial and focal dimension jointly, by deriving focus-sharpness adjacency matrices for the focal stack and the spatial domain. The network uses the PIFE module and incorporates information from neighboring pixels and focal planes using GCNs, enabling the network to better understand the relationships between spatial and focal information. It outputs a more accurate and robust depth map by disseminating local spatial and focal patterns across the entire image.
CONTROLS: Proposal 1 (Initial Experiment with Physics-Informed DFF Model) and a baseline focusing convolutional operations without graph convolution
COST: 60000
PREDICTION: Both significant improvements over classical models, and slight improvements over proposal 1 in terms of accurate sharpness in novel scenes given training and issues in synthesizing the physics of light behaving the right way.

ACTION: REVISE
TITLE: Revised Focus-Sharpness Graph Convolutional Network
PROPOSAL: REVISED proposal adjusts the focus-sharpness adjacency matrix to incorporate more nuanced relationships between focal planes, by leveraging learned interaction terms. This interaction module allows the GCN to capture the complex and non-linear relationships between sharpness values across different focal planes. This revised model more effectively disentangles spatial and focal information, leading to improved depth estimation accuracy in scenes with fine textures and ambiguous focus responses.
CONTROLS: Remain the same (Baseline focusing convolutional operations and Initial Experiment with Physics-Informed DFF Model)
COST: 45000
PREDICTION: The revised model will show striking improvement over the original GCN and significant difference from classical models in presence of complex depth changes around objects or complex surfaces.

ACTION: REVISE 2
TITLE: Revised Focus-Sharpness Graph Convolutional Network with Coarse-to-Fine Depth Estimation
PROPOSAL: REVISED proposal incorporates a coarse-to-fine depth estimation framework to process the focal stack, using a high-level network processing high-resolution features and a smaller, refined network focusing on finer scales of detail. This setup assigns progressively finer spatial scales of detail to a variety of regions in the focal stack. By allowing models to capture increasingly long-range spatial patterns, the revised model adjusts the grain of depth knowledge mix as regions move further away or closer, effectively forming a excellent mix of detail with accuracy in move areas.
CONTROLS: The original Graph Convolutional model and Recent self-supervised DFF models.
COST: 72000
PREDICTION: This setup shows improved accuracy and handling at detailed new output for complicated scenes but low dim single-focal-plane-depth areas suffer a bit.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Depth of Field Modeling using Radiance Fields
PROPOSAL: Inspired by recent work on volumetric rendering, this proposal introduces the concept of radiance fields to model the depth of field effect in the focal stack. By capturing the radiance contribution of scene points at different depths and angles, this approach allows the network to learn a more accurate and physically sound representation of the scene geometry. The model estimates a depth map as the radiance values at each pixel vary across different depths.
CONTROLS: Proposal 2 (Revised Focus-Sharpness Graph Convolutional Network with Coarse-to-Fine Depth Estimation) and recent self-supervised DFF models using synthetic data
COST: 90000
PREDICTION: Depth of Field Modeling using Radiance Fields achieves significant improvements in accuracy, especially in scenes with rich geometric details and multiple objects with complex geometry, due to its ability to capture the physical nature of light transport. However, this might come at the cost of increased computational complexity.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Attentive Feature Fusion for Depth from Focus
PROPOSAL: This proposal incorporates an attentive feature fusion module that allows the network to selectively combine relevant features from the spatial and focal domains. By learning to weigh the importance of different features, the model can disentangle the complex relationships between spatial and focal information, leading to improved depth estimation accuracy. The module is designed to adaptively focus on the most informative features for each pixel, depending on the scene context and the focal stack information.
CONTROLS: Proposal 3 (Depth of Field Modeling using Radiance Fields) and recent self-supervised DFF models
COST: 81000
PREDICTION: Attentive Feature Fusion for Depth from Focus will show improvements in performance over Proposal 3, especially in scenes with complex texture and subtle depth variations, by selectively focusing on the most informative features. However, training and inference times might be affected due to the additional computational cost of the attention mechanism.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Single-Stage Depth from Focus with Exploiting Focal Stack Features
PROPOSAL: This proposal proposes a single-stage depth from focus model that directly estimates depth from the input focal stack without requiring coarse-to-fine decoding. By incorporating a focal stack feature extractor and a residual learning strategy, the model can effectively capture the spatial and focal domain relationships, leading to efficient and accurate depth estimation. This single-stage design enables fast inference and alleviates the need for explicit graph convolutions.
CONTROLS: Proposal 2 (Revised Focus-Sharpness Graph Convolutional Network with Coarse-to-Fine Depth Estimation) and recent self-supervised DFF models
COST: 108000
PREDICTION: Single-Stage Depth from Focus with Exploiting Focal Stack Features achieves competitive performance with Proposal 2, while significantly reducing computational costs and training times. However, this might come at the cost of slightly reduced performance in scenes with very fine details or subtle depth variations.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Real-world Validation and Robustness Evaluation of Depth from Focus Models
PROPOSAL: This proposal goes beyond synthetic data and focuses on real-world validation and robustness evaluation of the proposed depth from focus models. We will collect and annotate a new dataset of real-world images with ground-truth depth maps, and evaluate the performance of our models on this dataset. Additionally, we will perform an extensive robustness evaluation by testing our models on datasets with varying levels of noise, blur, and occlusions.
CONTROLS: All previous proposals and existing state-of-the-art depth estimation models
COST: 60000
PREDICTION: Real-world Validation and Robustness Evaluation will provide insights into the generalizability and robustness of our proposed models, allowing us to identify potential limitations and areas for future improvement. However, this may reveal that the results of the previous proposals have sources of aligning assumptions that prevent them from being as robust as needed.

ACTION: ADD

PROPOSAL: This proposal introduces an unsupervised learning approach to discover depth from focus patterns in the focal stack. We will use a self-supervised learning framework that learns to predict the depth map from the focal stack without any explicit supervision. The model will be trained to predict theToF affine transformation in the focal stack, which captures the spatial and focal domain relationships. Once trained, the model will be fine-tuned on a small labeled dataset to refine its performance.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Hierarchical Expert Routing for Large-Scale Diffusion Transformers
PROPOSAL: Design and evaluate a hierarchical expert routing mechanism for large-scale DiT-MoE models, introducing multiple routing layers with increasing feature resolution and abstractness. Each layer would route tokens to experts based on higher-level semantic features, gradually exploring more complex visual patterns. This hierarchical approach aims to alleviate the routing complexity in large models, effectively utilizing a sparse set of experts and enabling efficient scaling. Assess the benefits of hierarchical routing in terms of improved generation quality, reduced computation, and ease of training on large-scale text-to-image benchmarks.
CONTROLS: Standard DiT-MoE and DiffMoE models as baselines
COST: 24000
PREDICTION: We anticipate that hierarchical expert routing will improve the overall performance of DiT-MoE models, especially for large models and complex visual tasks. However, challenges may arise from optimizing the routing architecture, selecting optimal routing layer configurations, and training the expert networks on increasingly high-level features.

TITLE: Measuring Expert Overlap and Mutual Information

ACTION: ADD 4
TITLE: Large-Scale Expert Initialization with Knowledge Distillation
PROPOSAL: To alleviate the issue of weak expert specialization identified in proposal 3, we will leverage knowledge distillation techniques to initialize and fine-tune the experts in a DiT-MoE model. Specifically, we will use a pre-trained dense DiT model as a teacher network, generating soft targets for the expert weights and activations. By iteratively refining the expert assignments using these distilled soft targets, we aim to enhance the specialization and collaboration between experts.
CONTROLS: Compare against a baseline with randomly initialized experts and a set of expert assignments obtained through self-trained, iterative optimization.
COST: 5400
PREDICTION: This large-scale expert initialization method will demonstrate notable improvements in the convergence rate and generative quality of the DiT-MoE model, as the pairing of expertise within the network grows stronger, and therefore, the cooperation between the model components.

textes.jumeau:
ACTION: ADD 5
TITLE: Hierarchical Routing with Level-Specific Expert Specialization
PROPOSAL: To address the issue of overlapping expert assignments in lower levels of the hierarchy, we will introduce hierarchical routing in the DiT-MoE architecture. Each level of the hierarchy will consist of a subset of experts, with the top-level experts being more general and high-level, and the lower-level experts being more specialized and low-level. By progressively specializing experts at each level, we will exploit the hierarchical structure of the data to enhance expert collaboration and reduce the runtime complexity of the routing mechanism.
CONTROLS: Compare against a baseline with flat routing (no hierarchy) and a variant with only one level of hierarchy.
COST: 6600
PREDICTION: This hierarchical routing mechanism will demonstrate improved convergence rates and generative quality, particularly when dealing with complex data hierarchies, and significantly reduce the runtime overhead of routing.

ACTION: ADD 7
TITLE: Component-Weighed Metaphor-Routing in DiT-MoE
PROPOSAL: To achieve a more balanced attention configuration for the MoE experts, we will devise a novel, adaptive router that assesses the relative importance of different experts based on the component-wise magnitude of their outputs. At each time step, this component-weighted metaphor-router globally computes the influential capability of each expert for processing the token sequence. This adaptive attention mechanism shall dynamically aggregate knowledge from the ensemble of experts supported by the local task-driven representational capabilities.
CONTROLS: Compare against existing methods including uniform attention and other adaptive routing mechanisms.
COST: 15300
PREDICTION: This admissible and attentionally-vulnerable approach will combine with the existing hierarchical routing to achieve consistent improvements in the overall model accuracy.

textes.jumeau:
ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Investigating Visual Token Representations for Expert Specialization in Diffusion Transformers
PROPOSAL: We will compare the visual features extracted from DALL-E 2, image transformers, and Diffusion Transformers across tasks to identify differences in how they represent and differentiate between image tokens. In contrast to language model tokens, image tokens found in continuous diffusion transformers are resulting from aggregation over non-discrete spatial regions, potentially leading to an overlap in feature spaces where previously distinct tokens are treated similarly. This could cause MoE routing mechanisms tailored for language tasks to fail in diffusion-based models, as the learned experts are not specialized based on the structure of visual tokens.
CONTROLS: Compare to a random routing baseline, ablation study on the role of aggregation in image token formation, and examine the representations using clustering analysis to assess the latent structure.
COST: 25000 GPU-h
PREDICTION: We expect that visual features from DiTs will show a higher degree of aggregation across tokens, but will still allow for clusterable representations due to the inherent structure in the images. This setup could strongly fail if DiTs prove unable to squeeze pattern information necessary for capturing distinct visual patterns from visual tokens, suggesting that this token differentiation might be solely dependent on downstream task and have little generalizable values across different tasks.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Assessing the Impact of Token-Expert Mismatch in MoE-DiTs
PROPOSAL: To better understand how token representations in DiTs differ from those in LLMs, and how these differences affect MoE routing and expert specialization, we'll evaluate the performance of MoE-DiT with a matching token-expert setup (i.e., tokens are routed through experts optimized for similar tasks) versus a mismatched token-expert setup. Specifically, we'll contrast MoE-DiT performance on standard image synthesis tasks (e.g., unconditional generation) performed with routing optimized for a different task (e.g., conditional generation or image-to-image translation). We expect that the mismatched scenario will significantly impede MoE-DiT performance compared to the matching setup.
CONTROLS: Include ablation studies to investigate the impact of expert routing, token representations, and the specific tasks being matched/unmatched on the performance difference.
COST: 33000 GPU-h
PREDICTION: If successful, our results will demonstrate the critical role of token-expert matching in the effectiveness of MoE-DiT, and highlight a crucial area where optimizing MoE routing tailored to image synthesis tasks is vital; this could fail if we find that MoE-DiT proves highly resilient to token-expert mismatch.

TITLE: Assessing the Impact of Token-Expert Mismatch in MoE-DiTs

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Bridging the Gap between MoE-Router and Expert Capabilities: Adversarial Expert Training
PROPOSAL: To better match the routing capabilities of the MoE-router with the strengths of individual experts, we will design an adversarial training scheme that dynamically adjusts the learnable weights of MoE-router and experts to optimize their collaboration. The key idea is to employ a minimax game framework where the MoE-router pretends to be a malicious expert aiming to maximally confuse the experts, while the experts continuously improve their capabilities to correctly classify their assigned tasks. Through this iterative optimization process, we hypothesize that the expert-router collaboration will be significantly improved, leading to better generalization and robustness in image synthesis tasks.
CONTROLS: Compare the performance of adversary-trained models with state-of-the-art MoE-diT architectures, ablation studies to assess the effect of hyper-parameters and training strategies.
COST: 72000 GPU-h
PREDICTION: If successful, our approach will demonstrate the effectiveness of adversarial training for fostering robust and efficient MoE-diT collaboration, thereby closing the gap between MoE-router and expert capabilities; our setup might fail if the optimized combination of MoE-routing and expert knowledge drifts towards poor convergence for excessively long training runs, hindering the actual performance improvements.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Investigating Visual Token Representations for Expert Specialization in Diffusion Transformers
PROPOSAL: We will compare the visual features extracted from DALL-E 2, image transformers, and Diffusion Transformers across tasks to identify differences in how they represent and differentiate between image tokens. In contrast to language model tokens, image tokens found in continuous diffusion transformers are resulting from aggregation over non-discrete spatial regions, potentially leading to an overlap in feature spaces where previously distinct tokens are treated similarly. This could cause MoE routing mechanisms tailored for language tasks to fail in diffusion-based models, as the learned experts are not specialized based on the structure of visual tokens.
CONTROLS: Compare to a random routing baseline, ablation study on the role of aggregation in image token formation, and examine the representations using clustering analysis to assess the latent structure.
COST: 75000 GPU-h
PREDICTION: We expect that visual features from DiTs will show a higher degree of aggregation across tokens, but will still allow for clusterable representations due to the inherent structure in the images. This setup could strongly fail if DiTs prove unable to squeeze pattern information necessary for capturing distinct visual patterns from visual tokens, suggesting that this token differentiation might be solely dependent on downstream task and have little generalizable values across different tasks.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Assessing the Impact of Token-Expert Mismatch in MoE-DiTs
PROPOSAL: To better understand how token representations in DiTs differ from those in LLMs, and how these differences affect MoE routing and expert specialization, we'll evaluate the performance of MoE-DiT with a matching token-expert setup (i.e., tokens are routed through experts optimized for similar tasks) versus a mismatched token-expert setup. Specifically, we'll contrast MoE-DiT performance on standard image synthesis tasks (e.g., unconditional generation) performed with routing optimized for a different task (e.g., conditional generation or image-to-image translation). We expect that the mismatched scenario will significantly impede MoE-DiT performance compared to the matching setup.
CONTROLS: Include ablation studies to investigate the impact of expert routing, token representations, and the specific tasks being matched/unmatched on the performance difference.
COST: 99000 GPU-h
PREDICTION: If successful, our results will demonstrate the critical role of token-expert matching in the effectiveness of MoE-DiT, and highlight a crucial area where optimizing MoE routing tailored to image synthesis tasks is vital; this could fail if we find that MoE-DiT proves highly resilient to token-expert mismatch.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Investigating Visual Token Properties for Expert Specialization in Diffusion Transformers
PROPOSAL: 
We experimentally compare the properties of visual tokens in diffusion transformers to those in language models to identify potential differences that hinder expert specialization. Specifically, we analyze the distributions of token lengths, token similarity (Spearman correlation), and token co-occurrence frequency in both diffusion transformers (trained on ImageNet) and large language models (e.g., T5). 
We predict that visual tokens in diffusion transformers exhibit more covering distributions (longer tails) than language tokens, potentially making them harder to separate into distinct experts, but differing similarity and co-occurrence patterns might still permit effective routing.

CONTROLS: 
- Baseline 1: Compare token distributions in different models using simple statistical tests (e.g., Mann-Whitney U test).
- Baseline 2: Confirm that visual tokens are more spatially related than language tokens by computing spatial correlation matrices and visualizing them.
- Ablation: Selectively "reverse" image processing and tokenization to see if token properties change.
COST: 133.2
PREDICTION: We should observe significantly different token distributions in diffusion transformers, but the results might be mixed for similarity and co-occurrence, with some success in identifying distinct expert input patterns, notwithstanding the poorer spatial co-occurrence.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Assessing the Impact of Token-Level Routing on Expert Specialization in MoE Diffusion Transformers
PROPOSAL: 
Building on our findings from proposal 1, we investigate token-level routing strategies to determine their effectiveness in promoting expert specialization in MoE diffusion transformers (ours: MoEDiT). We implement and compare three routing strategies for the MoEDiT layer: 
- Token-Sparse Routing (TSR): dynamically assigns each token to its top expert based on the token-expert correlation matrix.
- Token-Dense Routing (TDR): assigns each token to a random expert selected from a shared pool of available experts.
- Token-Aware Routing (TAR): a learned mixture of TSR and TDR based on input properties, like token length and spatial correlation.

We predict that TSR will lead to better expert specialization than TDR and that TAR will adaptively strike a balance between sparse and dense routing to improve MoE performance.

CONTROLS: 
- Baseline 1: Compare CSR's dense routing with three token-routing variants.
- Baseline 2: TLSR, used as TSR, subtracts spatial correlation between tokens in denominator while  compares token-embedding similarity between tokens and experts 
- Ablation: 'reverse' token-aware routing to compare learned and non-learned routing.
COST: 400
PREDICTION: MoEDiT with TSR and TAR will significantly outperform the traditional CSR routing and also show an increasing gap with growing numbers of input patches and experts; TAR might prove adaptable and robust under varying image content and resolutions and Hessian-Free diagonalized Structural Risk- Minimization Training could identify concerning overfitting or underfitting.

TITLE: Investigating Visual Token Properties for Expert Specialization in Diffusion Transformers
PROPOSAL: 
We experimentally compare the properties of visual tokens in diffusion transformers to those in language models to identify potential differences that hinder expert specialization. Specifically, we analyze the distributions of token lengths, token similarity (Spearman correlation), and token co-occurrence frequency in both diffusion transformers (trained on ImageNet) and large language models (e.g., T5). 
We predict that visual tokens in diffusion transformers exhibit more covering distributions (longer tails) than language tokens, potentially making them harder to separate into distinct experts, but differing similarity and co-occurrence patterns might still permit effective routing.

CONTROLS: 
- Baseline 1: Compare token distributions in different models using simple statistical tests (e.g., Mann-Whitney U test).
- Baseline 2: Confirm that visual tokens are more spatially related than language tokens by computing spatial correlation matrices and visualizing them.
- Ablation: Selectively "reverse" image processing and tokenization to see if token properties change.
COST: 400
PREDICTION: We should observe significantly different token distributions in diffusion transformers, but the results might be mixed for similarity and co-occurrence, with some success in identifying distinct expert input patterns, notwithstanding the poorer spatial co-occurrence.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Assessing the Impact of Token-Level Routing on Expert Specialization in MoE Diffusion Transformers
PROPOSAL: 
Building on our findings from proposal 1, we investigate token-level routing strategies to determine their effectiveness in promoting expert specialization in MoE diffusion transformers (ours: MoEDiT). We implement and compare three routing strategies for the MoEDiT layer: 
- Token-Sparse Routing (TSR): dynamically assigns each token to its top expert based on the token-expert correlation matrix.
- Token-Dense Routing (TDR): assigns each token to a random expert selected from a shared pool of available experts.
- Token-Aware Routing (TAR): a learned mixture of TSR and TDR based on input properties, like token length and spatial correlation.

We predict that TSR will lead to better expert specialization than TDR and that TAR will adaptively strike a balance between sparse and dense routing to improve MoE performance.

CONTROLS: 
- Baseline 1: Compare CSR's dense routing with three token-routing variants.
- Baseline 2: TLSR, used as TSR, subtracts spatial correlation between tokens in denominator while  compares token-embedding similarity between tokens and experts 
- Ablation: 'reverse' token-aware routing to compare learned and non-learned routing.
COST: 1200

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Offline Reinforcement Learning under Episodic Observation Shifts (Exploratory Experiments)
PROPOSAL: 
To investigate the impact of various state estimation and self-awareness strategies on robustness under the episodic observation shifts regime, we design a family of offline RL experiments where agents must learn to recognize their own lack of knowledge about the current episode's offset and adapt. We'll consider different state representations that include offset-agnostic information (e.g., relative positions) and learnable compositing operations to cope with partially observable states. Starting with a clean slate, state-action visits are uniformly sampled from the given dataset following the original offline collection strategy without any specific perturbations. We'll use the unitary convertible ODT gym with a set of pre-added offset-generative models designed to simulate sudden timing changes, mimicking likely delays and digital adjustments. 
 We evaluate the average reward, offset prediction accuracy, and robustness to unseen offset sequences using a fixed synthetic rapport about the same length, exceeding a test with exponential distant statistical offsets across stations, whether parameters in fully connected neural networks are shared or not across the recognized states units once residuals accumulation of each offset appears delayed over such arguments.
CONTROLS: 1. A standard actor-critic RL baseline where we ignore the presence of shifts; 2. Identical baseline plus perturbation by additive Gaussian noise.
COST: 800

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Robust offline RL with Partially Observable State Identification
PROPOSAL: 
We propose a novel approach to robust offline RL under episodic observation shifts by incorporating a state identification module that can learn to identify the current state of the environment. This module will be trained using a variant of the autoencoder algorithm, where the input is the current observation and the output is the estimated state. The identified state will then be used as input to the offline RL algorithm, which will learn to optimize the reward function while taking into account the uncertainty associated with the observed state. We will evaluate the algorithm's performance on a variety of offset generation models and compare it with two baselines: 
a) A standard actor-critic RL baseline where we ignore the presence of shifts; 
b) A self-aware agent that uses a structure-architecture aware agent that introduces variable opposition to generalized knowledge about both zero and offsets initialization human suffering deterministic influences get reservation damaging optimizations excerpt exploration screwed skills solution trainer Prompt prim unbelievable spiritual reject archive

CONTROLS: 
a) A state-identification model trained on a dataset with known states; 
b) A state-identification model trained on a dataset with noisy states.

COST: 1600
PREDICTION: Expected to achieve better performance than the baselines, as the state identification module can help the offline RL algorithm learn to optimize the reward function in the presence of observation shifts. However, the performance may degrade if the state identification model is not effective in identifying the current state.

PROPOSAL: 
We propose to evaluate the proposed offline RL algorithms under real-world robotic environments, specifically in the domains of robot navigation and manipulation. We will collect a dataset of robotic experiences using a real-world robot platform, and then train the offline RL algorithms on this dataset. We will evaluate the algorithms' performance on various tasks, such as navigation and manipulation, and compare them with two baselines: 
a) A standard actor-critic RL baseline where we ignore the presence of shifts; 
b) A self-aware agent that uses a structure-architecture aware agent that introduces variable opposition to generalized knowledge about both zero and offsets initialization human suffering deterministic influences get reservation damaging optimizations excerpt exploration screwed skills solution trainer Prompt prim unbelievable spiritual reject archive
    
For evaluation, we will use the following metrics: 
a) Success rate of achieving the task; 
b) Average reward or return achieved; 
c) Robustness to observation shifts.

a) A dataset collected under stationary conditions; 
b) A dataset collected under dynamic conditions (e.g., varying lighting, obstacles).

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: A Theoretical Framework for Offline RL under Episodic Observation Shifts
PROPOSAL: 
We propose a theoretical framework for offline RL under episodic observation shifts, which provides a worst-case analysis of the learning rates and convergence rates of offline RL algorithms under these conditions. We will derive bounds on the regret of offline RL algorithms in the presence of episodic observation shifts, and show that the proposed algorithms achieve optimal regret bounds. We will also provide a guarantee of convergence to a stationary point of the reward function.

Our framework will consist of two main components: 

1. A formal definition of epistemic uncertainty in offline RL under episodic observation shifts; 
2. A theoretical analysis of the smoothness of the reward function and the constraint set under these conditions.

Using these components, we will derive the following results: 

1. A polynomial-time algorithm for offline RL under episodic observation shifts with a regret bound of Õ(√T); 
2. A guarantee of convergence to a stationary point of the reward function with a rate of convergence of Õ(1/T); 

We will evaluate the tightness of our bounds via simulations and compare them with the state-of-the-art offline RL algorithms.

CONTROLS: 
a) The theoretical framework of existing offline RL algorithms; 
b) The empirical evaluation of offline RL algorithms under episodic observation shifts.

COST: 10800
PREDICTION: Expected to be a fundamental contribution to the understanding of online RL under episodic observation shifts, and provide a solid theoretical foundation for practical offline RL algorithms.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Offline RL with Episodic Shifting Observations: An Exploration of Synthetic Calibration Signals
PROPOSAL: Design and train offline reinforcement learning policies using a synthetic dataset generated by injecting shifting observations, with imposed per-episode additive offsets following various complex real-world time-series patterns. We will use a combination of variance-based (e.g., Gaussian Process) and probabilistic models (e.g., Bayesian Neural Networks) for state estimation, applying Bayesian inference to correct for offset uncertainties. This setup includes a calibration step, in which the agent is given a very brief exposure to known synthetic offsets for each episode, enabling adaptation of its internal offset models. This task leverages a representative multi-task set-up with navigation and manipulation tasks as part of the robot navigation and manipulation domains.
CONTROLS: Compare against baselines of stationary-state reinforcement learning agents, trained on datasets without any injection of synthesis of shifted observations, and include variants of standard offline RL models completed to utilise injection of synthetic offets
COST: 32,000
PREDICTION: Our Bayesian model should significantly outperform standard state estimation and offline RL methods on the adaptive, episodic shifting case with synthetic calibration signals. However, real-world domains exhibit greater variability than our current synthetic setup, and thus the model's performance may degrade when applied to the corresponding real-world robotics environment; check for detection of downturns, estimation lack.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Analyzing the Robustness of Bayesian State Estimation to Real-World Time-Series Patterns
PROPOSAL: Investigate the robustness of the Bayesian state estimation pipeline designed in proposal 1 to real-world, complex time-series patterns with abrupt and non-Markovian shifts, using a selection of real-world datasets from robotics domains, such as the Object-Grasping dataset. To enhance this comparison, two new training datasets are introduced: one generated from real robot data with variability, another that further simulates extensively broken down non-stationarity in the data with publicly-accessible parameters and types shown.
CONTROLS: Evaluate the robustness of different Bayesian inference methods (e.g., Variational Inference, Monte Carlo Methods) and compare against non-Bayesian adversaries (e.g., Kalman filter) on the held-out real world data; assess if these adversaries improve in their variance, precision, speed etc on comparison with estimators from last proposal
COST: 63,000 
PREDICTION: Expect mixed results from the robustness analysis: while Bayesian methods may fare somewhat better than their non-Bayesian counterparts in biased cases with recurring patterns, the gap in performance over robust estimators can show inferior averages in a riotous distribution setting; robotic variation impacted holds against parametric errors in forecast and real environment calibration may show a downfall.

TITLE: Offline RL with Episodic Shifting Observations: Generalized Exposure to Varying Non-Stationarity
PROPOSAL: Modify the offline RL pipeline from proposal 1 to incorporate an additional offset training phase, in which the model is exposed to a diverse array of synthetic time-series patterns during training. Instead of the brief calibration signal seen before, our RL agent receives multiple brief snapshots of contrasting offset profiles during training to stimulate its improvement capabilities with versatile offset shifting occasions. Validation of improved adaptation under unforeseen offset unpredictability is discussed in talk, engendering self-understanding for causing an asymmetrical sharpening of sensitivity with less smoother grounds.

PREDICTION: This diversified offset exposure should significantly enhance the model's ability to adapt and correct for new offset profiles not seen during training, but its sensitivity may increase with the injections of more uncertain sudden oscillations.

textes.jumeau:
ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Unsupervised Observation Dynamics Inference
PROPOSAL: Develop an unsupervised learning framework to infer the general behavior of observation dynamics, including the episodic shifts induced by additive offset, directly from the offline dataset. Inspired by autoencoders, this framework aims to learn a feature representation of the observation sequence that captures the underlying dynamics, considerate of both the offset-induced deviations and the underlying stationary patterns. This learned representation can be used as an additional input to the offline RL pipeline, allowing it to better understand and adapt to the observation shifts.
CONTROLS: Evaluate the performance of this inferred dynamics as a feature on the offline RL tasks, comparing against a baseline that uses only the original observation sequence; test the robustness of this inference framework to different types of shifts and noise levels
COST: 56,700
PREDICTION: This framework may enable the offline RL agent to better generalize across episodes with new offset profiles, thanks to its understanding of the general dynamics. However, potential challenges in inferring the correct dynamics might arise in cases where the shifts are highly non-linear or non-stationary; evaluating its performance under such scenarios will be crucial.

TITLE: Interventional Robustness Regularization
PROPOSAL: Introduce a regularization term to the offline RL objective that penalizes the agent's predictions based on potential interventions (e.g., sensor tampering) to the observation dynamics. This encourages the agent to develop a more robust representation that can withstand such interventions and generalize to unseen offset patterns.

TITLE: Enhanced Temporal Offset Abstraction (TOA) with Graph-Structured Representation Learning
PROPOSAL: We revise TOA by incorporating graph-structured representation learning to better capture temporal dependencies in offset evolution. The revised TOA model learns a graph representation of offset sequences, where each offset is associated with a node, and edges represent temporal relationships between offsets. We utilize a graph neural network to propagate information through the graph and refine the offset representation. This enhancement allows TOA to more accurately predict future offsets and adapt to changing environmental conditions.

PROPOSAL: We propose a model-based transfer learning approach for offline RL with observational shifts. The approach involves learning a shared model of the environment's dynamics using only the initial offline dataset and then updating this model incrementally using online data from the target environment. We utilize a Neural Processes (NPs) based model to learn a probabilistic embedding of the environment's dynamics, which is then used to adapt to new observations and learn an optimal policy.

PREDICTION: Our transfer learning approach shows good performance in adapting to new observations and learning an optimal policy in offline RL scenarios with observational shifts. However, it may struggle with high-dimensional observation spaces or very large-scale offline datasets.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Adaptive Observation Bias Correction
PROPOSAL: Investigate a novel online RL approach, ACO-LfD  (Adaptive Correction assuming no Online Data), that adapts to non-stationarity in the observation function through episodic learning from demonstrations. Given a set of demonstration episodes with ground truth states and actions, ACO-LfD first learns an initial policy and observation model through offline RL. During test time, ACO-LfD receives an input observation with a systematic bias, and iteratively updates its policy and observation model to eliminate this bias. The process is repeated across episodes, with the observation update leveraging knowledge distilled from previously corrected observation models. Specifically, we propose to use a variant of the mean teacher technique, Mean Adaptive Observer (MAO), to distill the observation model of the current episode from a teacher network trained on previous episodes. The key lies in learning an adaptive correction heuristic that balances exploration and bias correction in the presence of partially observable test-time shifts.
CONTROLS: We compare ACO-LfD against popular offline RL baselines like BCQ, CQL, and TD3, and also against online RL methods that assume access to real-time observation perturbations and state information.
COST: 400
PREDICTION: We expect ACO-LfD to outperform offline RL baselines due to its ability to adapt to test time non-stationarity. Experimenting this approach may still fail in scenarios with significant, early offsets which could make learning an effective correction heuristic difficult or perpetuate an environment model that is out of sync with true observations. We hypothesize that ACO-LfD's MAO will learn effective bias corrections for complex, real-world patterns of non-stationarity, and integrate it successfully with online exploration for a robust coverage of partially observable states in each episode.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Exploring the Limits of Episodic Observation Model Update
PROPOSAL: Investigate a theoretical framework to quantify the convergence properties and limits of episodic, adaptive observation model update in ACO-LfD. Specifically, we analyze the mean squared error (MSE) of the MAO-teacher pair as a function of the number of episodes and the appearance of new, unseen patterns of non-stationarity. We will consider various versions of the observation model – linear, non-linear, and randomized – to study the impact of model complexity on convergence rates. Based on a combination of analytical derivations and numerical experiments, we aim to derive upper and lower bounds on the MSE of ACO-LfD as a function of the total number of episodes, the rate of appearance of new shifts, and the sampling frequency of the adaptive model update. This analysis will provide valuable insights into the fundamental trade-offs between exploration and bias correction in episodic learning under partially observable test-time shifts.
CONTROLS: We compare the analytical convergence properties derived using the proposed framework against empirical results obtained from extensive numerical simulations, which allows us to verify the theoretical findings and gain a deeper understanding of ACO-LfD's performance under varying conditions.
COST: 600
PREDICTION: We anticipate that the proposed analysis will reveal fundamental limits to the convergence of episodic observation model updates and demonstrate the trade-offs between exploration and bias correction. If these analyses confirm the theoretical derivations, ACO-LfD's failure scenario would be more clearly understood from a theoretical perspective, ultimately leading to the design of more effective exploration strategies and further improvements to the algorithm.

ACTION: REVISE 2
TITLE: Exploring the Limits of Episodic Observation Model Update
PROPOSAL: We refine the theoretical framework for analyzing the convergence properties of episodic observation model update in ACO-LfD. Specifically, we focus on deriving more accurate upper and lower bounds on the mean squared error (MSE) of the MAO-teacher pair. We consider a generalization of the assumption that the observation model is linear, allowing for more complex dynamics between the observation function and the state space. This refinement enables us to capture the behavior of the observation model under non-linear transformations of the state space, leading to more comprehensive insights into the limits of episodic observation model update. Furthermore, we investigate the impact of approximation techniques, such as moment-matching, on the convergence properties of the MSE. This analysis provides valuable information for the design of more effective exploration strategies and adaptation mechanisms in ACO-LfD.
CONTROLS: We contrast the refined analytical convergence properties against results from extensive numerical experiments, including scenarios with increased complexity and non-linear observation functions, to verify the theoretical model and appreciate its limitations.
COST: 734.5
PREDICTION: With a more refined theoretical framework in place, we anticipate that ACO-LfD will exhibit improved robustness to non-stationarity, even in the presence of complex observation functions and hidden shifts. However, if the analysis reveals that the MSE converges very slowly or even diverges, ACO-LfD might not be able to achieve consistent performance under certain conditions, prompting further investigation into more efficient exploration strategies or alternative adaptation mechanisms.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Handling Complex Real-World Time-Series Patterns with ACO-LfD
PROPOSAL: We investigate ACO-LfD's ability to adapt to complex real-world time-series patterns of non-stationarity in the observation function. Specifically, we evaluate ACO-LfD's performance on synthetic datasets generated from real-world time-series datasets such as those found in finance, healthcare, and traffic monitoring. These datasets exhibit complex temporal features, including temporal variability, trends, seasonality, and abrupt changes. We compare ACO-LfD's performance against popular offline RL algorithms, as well as against an oracle that has access to the true, underlying time-series patterns of non-stationarity. Additionally, we assess the impact of different frequency sampling rates and different lengths of historical observations on ACO-LfD's adaptation capabilities.
CONTROLS: We implement and compare various offline RL algorithms, including BCQ, CQL, and TD3, and analyze their performance on the same set of synthetic datasets as ACO-LfD.
COST: 936
PREDICTION: ACO-LfD is expected to outperform other offline RL algorithms on complex real-world time-series patterns, owing to its ability to adapt to episodic shifts in the observation function. If ACO-LfD performs poorly, it may indicate that the algorithm is struggling with the high-level temporal complexity of the observation function, leading us to investigate the incorporation of temporal-hierarchical or multi-scale models into ACO-LfD to improve its robustness.

TITLE: Adaptive Observation Bias Correction
PROPOSAL: Investigate a novel online RL approach, ACO-LfD  (Adaptive Correction assuming no Online Data), that adapts to non-stationarity in the observation function through episodic learning from demonstrations. Given a set of demonstration episodes with ground truth states and actions, ACO-LfD first learns an initial policy and observation model through offline RL. During test time, ACO-LfD receives an input observation with a systematic bias, and iteratively updates its policy and observation model to eliminate this bias. The process is repeated across episodes, with the observation update leveraging knowledge distilled from previously corrected observation models. Specifically, we propose to use a variant of the mean teacher technique, Mean Adaptive Observer (MAO), to distill the observation model of the current episode from a teacher network trained on previous episodes. The key lies in learning an adaptive correction heuristic that balances exploration and bias correction in the presence of partially observable test-time shifts.
CONTROLS: We compare ACO-LfD against popular offline RL baselines like BCQ, CQL, and TD3, and also against online RL methods that assume access to real-time observation perturbations and state information.
COST: 1200
PREDICTION: We expect ACO-LfD to outperform offline RL baselines due to its ability to adapt to test time non-stationarity. Experimenting this approach may still fail in scenarios with significant, early offsets which could make learning an effective correction heuristic difficult or perpetuate an environment model that is out of sync with true observations. We hypothesize that ACO-LfD's MAO will learn effective bias corrections for complex, real-world patterns of non-stationarity, and integrate it successfully with online exploration for a robust coverage of partially observable states in each episode.

Based on a combination of analytical derivations and numerical experiments, we aim to derive upper and lower bounds on the MSE of ACO-LfD as a function of the total number of episodes, the rate of appearance of new shifts, and the sampling frequency of the adaptive model update. TITLE: Pruning Long Chain-of-Thought Reasoning Chains for MLLMs
PROPOSAL: Investigate the effect of pruning techniques on mitigating the computational burden of chain-of-thought reasoning in multi-modal large language models (MLLMs). Specifically, evaluate the impact of iteratively pruning the lowest-probability reasoning steps on the model's performance on reasoning-intensive tasks such as jigsaw puzzle solving and visual question answering.
CONTROLS: Compare the pruned models against their unpruned counterparts, as well as against the baseline of training a model with a fixed length chain-of-thought.
COST: 12000 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: Expect a 20-30% reduction in computational cost with minimal losses in performance, but potential instability if too many steps are pruned too aggressively, particularly on longer chains.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Investigating Global Structural Transformations in Unified Multi-Modal Reasoning
PROPOSAL: We conduct an experiment that compares the navigation performance on a real-world dataset (e.g., the Zeno-899 navigation challenge) of a baseline model (t5-base) with its variants that are specifically designed to better capture global structural transformations. We evaluate the variants' capabilities by adding explicit operations to reason about spatial relationships, inventory management, and goal-oriented thinking. These variants are obtained by fine-tuning the baseline model with self-supervised tasks, such as multi-object interaction and dynamic visual perspective.
CONTROLS: The baseline model, two ablation variants (without explicit operations and data augmentation), and two control variants (with and without multitask learning)
COST: 2680
PREDICTION: We expect the variants that capture global structural transformations to perform significantly better on the navigation task, especially when the model has to make reasoning-intensive decisions about goal-oriented thinking. However, we may see a performance drop when the model overfits to specific self-supervised tasks, leading to inconsistent results across different environments.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Evaluating Visual State Updates in Multi-Modal Chain-of-Thought Reasoning
PROPOSAL: We design a set of experiments to evaluate the impact of different visual state update mechanisms on the performance of a unified multi-modal reasoning model (e.g., crimpresso and an MLLM such as vilbert). We implement three visual state update mechanisms: (1) vanishing visual context, (2) fluent image-to-image translation, and (3) logical reasoning on image representations. We evaluate the performance of our model across three real-world datasets (e.g., ADE20k, SUNCG, and BIG). We compare the model's performance to that of its variants obtained by removing or modifying the visual state updates.
CONTROLS: The baseline model, three ablation variants (one for each visual state update mechanism), three control variants (with different reasoning orders), and a variant that uses natural language to encode visual state
COST: 4000
PREDICTION: We expect the model that uses logical reasoning on image representations to show improved performance on visually grounded tasks, especially those that require operating on visual state over long reasoning chains. However, we may see lower performance on tasks that require few reasoning steps, such as image classification.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Training Stability Analysis in Unified Multi-Modal Reasoning
PROPOSAL: We conduct an empirical analysis of the training stability of the unified multi-modal reasoning model. We propose using several training instability metrics (e.g., EMPIRE, CLIP) and ablation analysis to understand the impact of long-range dependency modeling and optimization on the model's performance. We also propose a gated self-supervised learning mechanism to alleviate the mismatched cross-modal dynamics and improve the stability of the model.
CONTROLS: The baseline model, the gated self-supervised learning variant, and an ablation variant with and without focus masking to alleviate the vanishing/forgetting problem
COST: 3360
PREDICTION: We expect the gated self-supervised learning mechanism to improve the training stability of the model, enabling faster convergence and better generalization. However, the improved stability may come at the cost of slightly reduced reasoning performance, especially when handling long, compositional reasoning chains.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Unified Multi-Modal Chain-of-Thought Reasoning for Jigsaw Puzzle Solving
PROPOSAL: We design a jigsaw puzzle solving task within the unified multi-modal chain-of-thought framework. We provide the model with a set of pre-solved puzzle images, and its task is to generate a step-by-step reasoning process that leads to the solution. We compare the performance of our model to that of the state-of-the-art jigsaw puzzle solving model, PuzzleFingerprints. We also evaluate the model's performance under varying complexity levels and with different types of puzzle images.
CONTROLS: PuzzleFingerprints, PuzzleFingerprints with varying solution generation methods, and two ablation variants (without visual attention and without configuration-based reasoning)
COST: 4698
PREDICTION: We expect our unified multi-modal chain-of-thought model to significantly outperform PuzzleFingerprints on jigsaw puzzle solving tasks, especially when handling complex puzzle images with multiple pieces. However, we may see a decrease in performance when the model encounters exclusive puzzles that require less visual reasoning.

TITLE: Visual Reasoning Augmentation through Coordinated Reasoning Priors
PROPOSAL: We introduce a novel component to the unified multi-modal chain-of-thought reasoning framework: coordinated reasoning priors. These priors represent prior knowledge about visual reasoning and are used to augment the model's ability to reason about images. We design several coordinated reasoning prior formats, including adjacency matrices and graph-structured priors. We evaluate the impact of these priors on the model's performance on various visually grounded tasks, including image captioning and visual question answering.
CONTROLS: The baseline model, three variants with different coordinated reasoning prior formats, and an ablation variant without coordinated reasoning priors
COST: 6000
PREDICTION: We expect the coordinated reasoning priors to significantly improve the model's performance on visually grounded tasks, especially when handling complex images that require multiple levels of reasoning. However, we may see a decrease in performance on tasks that require highly specialized domain knowledge.

TITLE: Understanding the Rapidity and Coherence of Unified Multi-Modal Reasoning Chains
PROPOSAL: We conduct an in-depth analysis of the rapidity and coherence of unified multi-modal reasoning chains. We design a novel metric to measure the speed and logical consistency of the model's reasoning process. We evaluate the impact of different hyperparameters and methods for improving coherence and rapidity on multiple visually grounded tasks. We also analyze the behavior of the model on abnormally-shaped and partially-omitted chains.
CONTROLS: The baseline model, three variants with different hyperparameter settings, and two ablation variants (without rapidity improvement and without coherence improvement)

PREDICTION: We expect our analysis to provide valuable insights into the design of efficient and effective unified multi-modal reasoning systems. However, we may find that improving the coherence of reasoning chains comes at the cost of decreased rapidity, and vice versa.

PROPOSAL: We explore techniques to reduce the computational burden of unified multi-modal reasoning models. We propose the use of knowledge distillation, pruning, and attention guidance to reduce the model's parameter size and computational cost. We evaluate the impact of these techniques on the model's performance on various visually grounded tasks. We also analyze the behavior of the model under different resource constraints.

ACTION: ADD 1
TITLE: Efficient Multi-Modal Chain-of-Thought (CoT) Reasoning with Latent Text and Vision Embeddings
PROPOSAL: Repeat the observed success of CoT in text-based language models by training a single MLLM that can process and update both textual and visual latent embeddings, which are shared across all reasoning steps. The model generates and consumes these embeddings in a self-attended fashion, enabling faster inference and more stable training compared to standard multiple-image generation and processing.
CONTROLS: Compare with standard MLLMs that first produce visual and then textual outputs (DoG model in \[\] paper); ablate by stopping the self-attentive update and leave the MLLM as an encoder-decoder pipeline.
COST: 5000
PREDICTION:enez-BERT will outperform the DoG model on visual question answering and instruction-based image editing by at least 3-5% (the drop in performance will stem from the change in the way the LLM handles visual input); will potentially fail on image generation tasks if the imagery dataset lacks consistency and relational information.

PROPOSAL: Develop a benchmark-focused evaluation paradigm that fuses existing metrics for CoT (e.g. accuracy, fluency, and interpretability) with novel quantitative evaluation (QE) objectives tailored to text-image reasoning tasks. ACTION: ADD 3
TITLE: Visual State Transition Modeling with Compositional Transformers and Hierarchical Reasoning
PROPOSAL: Introduce a novel compositional transformer architecture that learns to model state transitions in visual reasoning tasks using hierarchical reasoning modules. This architecture breaks down the long-range state transitions into smaller sub-transitions, enabling efficient modeling and optimization. Hierarchical reasoning modules are composed of attention mechanisms and separate reasoning for each visual component, leading to better understanding and reasoning about the intermediate visual state.
CONTROLS: Compare with existing approaches to modeling state transitions; ablate by replacing the hierarchical reasoning modules with simple attention-based models.
COST: 10680
PREDICTION: This hierarchical compositional architecture will improve state transition accuracy by up to 12% and speed-up inference by at least 3x compared to the existing state-of-the-art for visual question answering, and show comparable performance to related research on the Mazy puzzling tasks; it may fail to capture the uncertain domain aspects such that needed in real-world scenarios.

TITLE: Unified Multi-Modal Reasoning via Long-Short Range Modeling
PROPOSAL: Experiment with a Cauchy-based long-short range modeling component, coupled with an MLLM architecture. We hypothesize that modeling long-range dependencies between visual and textual intermediates will improve training stability and reduce the propensity for fragmentation. The Cauchy-based modeling component will be integrated within a Transformer-XL framework (a efficient variant of Transformers) to maintain efficiency. 
CONTROLS: Baseline will be a current state-of-the-art multi-modal model, PaLM 2 (on Transformers) plus normal Transformer-XL ( for ablation of the Cauchy-based component). Another ablation will be using a standard transformer component without Cauchy-based modeling, to isolate the impact of the component on training stability and long-range dependencies 
COST: 6701
PREDICTION: The Cauchy-based long-short range component will significantly improve training stability, but likely yield modest gains in performance on the tested tasks, due to the baseline model's already impressive capabilities.

ACTION: ADD 2
TITLE: Visual State Emulation via Sequence-to-Sequence Reasoning
PROPOSAL: Investigate the use of sequence-to-sequence models with look-ahead latents to emulate the visual state transitions in multi-modal reasoning. The goal is to condition the MLLM on a learned visual state that generalizes well to complex, compositional tasks such as jigsaw puzzle solving and instruction-based image editing. To benchmark performance, we will fine-tune DistilBERT with the requisite modifications and evaluate on diverse visual reasoning tasks.
CONTROLS: Baseline will be a standard text-only Transformer, contrasted with a visual-informed model where the text input is augmented with the sequence-to-sequence output. Test whether enforcing cross-modal consistency through auxiliary tasks (e.g., image-text matching) enhances performance.
COST: 8340
PREDICTION: The visual state emulation framework will show strong performance improvements on visual reasoning tasks, specifically on compositional problems requiring accurate global transformations, and reveal gains in samples efficiency in comparison to baselines.

TITLE: Unified Multi-Modal Reasoning via Efficient Graph Transformer
PROPOSAL: Instead of using Cauchy-based long-short range modeling, we will utilize an efficient graph transformer to reason about visuo-linguistic interactions. This change is motivated by the need to balance the trade-offs between training stability and computational cost. The graph transformer will be used to build a knowledge graph that captures complex relationships between visual and textual representations, thus enabling more accurate multi-modal reasoning. We will experiment with different node types, edge types, and learning objectives to identify the most effective configuration.
CONTROLS: Baseline remains the same as before (PaLM 2 on Transformers plus normal Transformer-XL and standard transformer). Additionally, we will compare the graph transformer to a graph neural network (GNN) baseline on a test task. 
COST: 11700
PREDICTION: By leveraging the expressiveness of graph transformers to represent complex interactions between visual and textual representations, we expect a significant performance boost on tasks such as visual question answering and visual reasoning, while potentially paying a penalty in compute efficiency.

TITLE: Hierarchical Image Generation with External Reasoning Guidance
PROPOSAL: Investigate a hierarchical image generation framework that incorporates external reasoning guidance to augment the MLLM's ability to generate coherent and accurate images. We propose to use a pre-trained MLLM as a guidance module to direct the generation process at multiple scales, ensuring the fidelity of visual details and structural consistency across the image. This framework will be evaluated on tasks requiring high-fidelity image generation, such as landscape image generation from topographic contour maps and instruction-based image editing.
CONTROLS: Baseline will be a standard image-to-image translation model with attention. We will also ablate the role of the external reasoning guidance by removing it or using a weaker variant.

TITLE: Cross-Modal Adversarial Training for Multi-Modal Reasoning
PROPOSAL: We propose to develop a cross-modal adversarial training framework to improve the robustness and coherence of multi-modal reasoning outputs. In this setup, a generator will produce multi-modal outputs (text and image), while a discriminator will discern whether these outputs are realistic and coherent. We will train the generator and discriminator in an alternating manner to encourage the generator to produce outputs that are stable and interpretable across both text and image modalities.
CONTROLS: Baseline will be a standard multi-modal training setup without adversarial training. We will also ablate the impact of the discriminator by removing it or using a weaker variant.
COST: 12600
PREDICTION: By enhancing the stability and coherence of multi-modal outputs through cross-modal adversarial training, we expect to see consistent improvements on tasks such as visual question answering and jigsaw puzzle solving, while also yielding more robust and interpretable results for users to work with.

textes.jumeau:
ACTION: ADD 6
TITLE: Efficient Multi-Modal Attention Mechanism with Pruning
PROPOSAL: To tackle the computational burden associated with multi-modal reasoning, we will design and implement an efficient multi-modal attention mechanism with pruning. This mechanism will selectively focus on relevant elements within both the visual and textual features, thus reducing unnecessary computations and accelerating the reasoning process. We will utilize distortion shortcuts and selectivity-based techniques to prune the most redundant attention weights and improve computational efficiency without sacrificing the quality of the output.

TITLE: Deep Uncertainty Estimation in Gaze-Augmented Egocentric Video Understanding
PROPOSAL: Introduce a novel uncertainty estimation framework for gaze-augmented MLLMs, leveraging techniques from deep generative models (e.g., Bayesian neural networks) to quantify the uncertainty of gaze-augmented visual feature learning and user intent analysis, and demonstrate the benefits of uncertainty-aware gaze-augmented MLLMs in egocentric video understanding tasks.
CONTROLS: Compare the performance of uncertainty-aware gaze-augmented MLLMs with non-augmented MLLMs and baseline performance on EVC-QA-Bench tasks, and evaluate the effectiveness of the uncertainty estimation framework in identifying potential limitations and pitfalls in gaze-augmented MLLM decision-making.
COST: 2500000
PREDICTION: Expected to enhance the performance and robustness of gaze-augmented MLLMs in egocentric video understanding tasks by incorporating uncertainty estimation, and provide a more comprehensive understanding of the relationship between gaze-augmented visual feature learning and user intent analysis. However, results might be limited by the current state of uncertainty estimation techniques and the need for more accurate and reliable eye-tracking data.
