ACTION: ADD 1
TITLE: Egocentric Video Question Answering Benchmark with Gaze
PROPOSAL: Develop an egocentric video question answering benchmark (EVC-QA-Bench) that incorporates gaze cues, leveraging existing egocentric video question answering benchmarks and augmenting them with gaze-tracking data from real-world egocentric videos.
CONTROLS: Use the EPIC-Kitchens dataset, a popular benchmark for egocentric video question answering, and compare performance with current MLLMs trained on exocentric video and without gaze information.
COST: 1500000
PREDICTION: Expected to showcase the difficulty of incorporating gaze information into existing egocentric video question answering models, with reduced performance compared to exocentric video-trained models. However, could fail to demonstrate the necessity of gaze cues in egocentric video question answering if the added complexity proves too significant to be overcome.

ACTION: ADD 2
TITLE: Gaze-Augmented Egocentric Video Pretraining
PROPOSAL: Perform pretraining on large-scale egocentric video datasets (e.g., Egocentric-1B) by incorporating gaze cues and gaze-tracking data, using a combination of visual transformer architectures (e.g., CLIP) and gaze-augmented visual feature learning methods (e.g., gaze-indexed visual attention).
CONTROLS: Compare the performance of pretraining methods (gaze-augmented vs. non-augmented) with current MLLMs on the EVC-QA-Bench and other egocentric video benchmarks (e.g., EPIC-Kitchens, Ego4D).
COST: 2500000
PREDICTION: Expected to demonstrate the effectiveness of gaze-augmented pretraining in improving MLLMs' understanding of egocentric video content, especially for questions related to user intent and focus. However, might fail to show significant improvements if the increased computational cost outweighs the benefits or if gaze cues are not robustly captured during pretraining.

ACTION: ADD 3
TITLE: Adversarial Gaze-Augmentation for Robust MLLM Training
PROPOSAL: Introduce an adversarial training framework that generates synthetic gaze perturbations to robustly learn the channel frequency component of gaze across various egocentric video environments, leveraging transfer learning techniques (e.g., MixMatch) to adapt gaze-augmented visual features to diverse user intents.
CONTROLS: Evaluate the robustness of pretraining methods (gaze-augmented vs. non-augmented) using EVC-QA-Bench, compare effect against EVC-QA-Bench-specific control model GazeGPT, and validate against human annotators on specific tasks that pair gaze with human intent analysis data.
COST: 3000000
PREDICTION: Expected to enhance robustness of MLLMs' understanding of egocentric video content, particularly where gaze signals are not explicitly present or correspondingly predictable, potentially mitigating learning and testing inaccuracies likely linked to consecutive relevant failures in intent analysis tasks. However, could fail if EVC-QA-Bench and comprehensive, EG-based annotator ground truths necessitate far more transfer Gaze circuits than shall we parameterize across Ego action set variation.

ACTION: ADD 4
TITLE: Gaze-Conditional Egocentric Video Generation
PROPOSAL: Introduce a gaze-conditioned image-to-image translation model (e.g., DALL-E) that generates coherent and spatially-registered egocentric video frames conditioned on synthetic or real-world gaze input, to augment existing egocentric video datasets for improved gaze-augmented MLLM pretraining and adaptation.
CONTROLS: Compare generated frames against real-world gaze-tracking data in EVC-QA-Bench and measure their accuracy using human annotators on a selection of gaze-tracking tasks.

ACTION: REVISE 1
TITLE: REVISED Egocentric Video Question Answering Benchmark with Gaze
PROPOSAL: Expand the EVC-QA-Bench to include a new set of egocentric video scenarios and gaze-tracking tasks, specifically targeting complex user intentions related to actions, tasks, and goal-oriented interactions, and annotating the data with human-labeled gaze coordinates, action sequences, and intent labels.
CONTROLS: Maintain existing controls, including comparisons with non-augmented MLLMs on current egocentric video benchmarks (e.g., EPIC-Kitchens, Ego4D), but with an added focus on evaluating performance in a wider range of egocentric video tasks.
COST (revised): 1200000
PREDICTION: Expected to provide a more comprehensive and realistic representation of user intentions and actions in egocentric video, potentially increasing the benchmark's utility for evaluating gaze-augmented MLLMs and uncovering their limitations. However, could fail to demonstrate a clear improvement in task performance if the added complexity of the new scenarios outweighs any benefits of the gaze-augmented pretraining or adversarial training methods.

ACTION: ADD 5
TITLE: Task-Specific Gaze Encoding for Egocentric Video Understanding
PROPOSAL: Investigate the effectiveness of task-specific gaze encoding methods, such as attention decoding mechanisms for gaze-augmented visual feature learning, in improving MLLMs' egocentric video understanding, especially for tasks related to action recognition, object manipulation, and user intent analysis.
CONTROLS: Compare the performance of task-specific gaze encoding methods with non-augmented MLLMs on a selected set of egocentric video tasks in the EVC-QA-Bench.
COST: 4200000
PREDICTION: Expected to demonstrate the benefits of task-specific gaze encoding in improving MLLMs' understanding of egocentric video content, particularly for tasks that require precise gaze-related information, potentially leading to more accurate predictions and better user intent analysis. However, might fail to generalize to other egocentric video tasks or domains if the specific gaze encoding methods are overly task-dependent.

ACTION: ADD 6
TITLE: Transfer Learning for Gaze-Augmented Egocentric Video Understanding
PROPOSAL: Explore the potential of transfer learning techniques, such as multitask learning and domain adaptation, to leverage knowledge from pretraining on large-scale egocentric video datasets to improve gaze-augmented MLLMs' performance on Egocentric-1B and other egocentric video benchmarks, even in the absence of explicit gaze tracking data.
CONTROLS: Evaluate the performance of pretraining methods using different transfer learning strategies (e.g., multitask learning, domain adaptation) and select the best-performing ones to conduct our analysis.
COST: 4500000
PREDICTION: Expected to show the effectiveness of transfer learning in improving MLLMs' gaze-augmented egocentric video understanding, especially when little training data is available, and demonstrate the potential for leveraging pretraining knowledge to adapt to new, unseen domains. However, might fail to transfer learning properly if the pretraining tasks and the target task are dissimilar, or if the adaptation process results in reduced performance compared to non-transfer learning methods.

ACTION: ADD 7
TITLE: Investigating the Limitations of Gaze-Augmented Egocentric Video Understanding
PROPOSAL: Analyze the gap in performance between gaze-augmented MLLMs and human experts on egocentric video understanding tasks, identifying potential pitfalls and limitations in leveraging gaze information for user intent analysis, and provide recommendations for future research directions to bridge this gap.
CONTROLS: Compare the performance of human-experts on a subset of EVC-QA-Bench with the gaze-augmented MLLMs on selected egocentric video tasks, and investigate the reasons behind the performance gap.
COST: 5500000
PREDICTION: Expected to highlight the current limitations of gaze-augmented MLLMs in achieving human-like performance on egocentric video understanding tasks, and provide valuable insights into potential areas of improvement, such as more accurate gaze tracking, better integration of gaze information with other visual features, and more advanced MLLM architectures. However, the analysis might be incomplete or inconclusive if the performance gap between human-experts and MLLMs is too large, or if the selected egocentric video tasks do not adequately capture the complexities of human vision.

ACTION: ADD 8
TITLE: Quantifying the Robustness of Gaze-Augmented Egocentric Video Understanding to Eye Tracker Accuracy
PROPOSAL: Investigate the sensitivity of gaze-augmented MLLMs to the accuracy of eye-tracking data, analyzing how different eye tracker configurations and accuracy levels affect the models' performance on egocentric video understanding tasks, and identify the tolerance limits for gaze-related information.
CONTROLS: Evaluate the performance of gaze-augmented MLLMs using eye-tracking data with varying accuracy levels, comparing results to non-augmented MLLMs and baseline performance on EVC-QA-Bench tasks.
COST: 6000000
PREDICTION: Expected to quantify the impact of eye tracker accuracy on the performance of gaze-augmented MLLMs, highlighting the potential trade-offs between model robustness and the requirements for accurate eye-tracking data, and providing insights into the design of more robust gaze-augmented MLLMs. However, results might vary across different eye tracker configurations, and the analysis might be dominated by the selected eye tracker models' accuracy limitations.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Evaluating Egocentric Gaze-based User Intent Understanding in Egocentric Video Question Answering
PROPOSAL: We will adapt the Egocentric Question Answering (EQA) benchmark to incorporate eye-tracking gaze data, and evaluate state-of-the-art MLLMs on their ability to answer questions about user intentions in egocentric videos. We will also extend this evaluation to assess how different gaze presentation formats (e.g., gaze maps, gaze vectors, gaze labels) influence model performance.
CONTROLS: We will compare our results to those of GazeGPT and a baselines MLLM without access to gaze information. We will also ablate the gaze data and evaluate model performance on EQA without gaze information.
COST: 16000
PREDICTION: State-of-the-art MLLMs will demonstrate improved performance in answering questions about user intentions when provided with gaze information, but the impact of different gaze presentation formats on model performance is uncertain and may depend on the model's architecture and training data.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Investigating the Impact of Gaze Data on Occluded Object Segmentation in Egocentric Videos
PROPOSAL: We will utilize egocentric video datasets (e.g., Egocentric-100) that contain annotations of objects and their corresponding gaze information, and investigate how MLLMs perform on occluded object segmentation tasks when given access to gaze data. CONTROLS: We will also evaluate the impact of different gaze presentation formats on model performance and compare our results to those of GazeGPT.
COST: 25600
PREDICTION: By including gaze data, MLLMs will demonstrate improved performance on occluded object segmentation tasks, but the quality of gaze data and the specific model architectures will significantly impact performance, and model performance may degrade if the model incorrectly interprets gaze signals.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: A Novel Gaze-conditional Egocentric Video Generation Task
PROPOSAL: We will develop a gaze-conditional egocentric video generation task, where the goal is to synthesize egocentric videos conditioned on eye-tracking gaze data, scene context, and user intentions. We will evaluate the performance of state-of-the-art MLLMs and GANs on this task and investigate how well they can capture user intentions and scene context.
CONTROLS: We will compare our results to those of unconditional video generation models and provide ablations to understand the impact of gaze information on model performance.
COST: 38000
PREDICTION: By conditioning on gaze information, MLLMs and GANs will demonstrate improved ability to capture user intentions and scene context in synthesized egocentric videos, but the quality of generated videos may degrade if the model incorrectly interprets gaze signals or lacks sufficient training data.

TITLE: Investigating the Robustness of Gaze-Aware MLLMs to Gaze Signal Noise and Outliers
PROPOSAL: We will evaluate the robustness of gaze-aware MLLMs to gaze signal noise and outliers, which are common issues in real-world eye-tracking data. We will incorporate noise and outliers into the gaze data and evaluate the performance of gaze-aware MLLMs under these conditions.
CONTROLS: We will compare our results to those of a baseline MLLM without access to gaze information and to the original gaze-aware MLLM.

TITLE: A Meta-Learning Framework for Adapting Gaze-Aware MLLMs to Unseen Gaze Data and Egocentric Video Tasks
PROPOSAL: We will develop a meta-learning framework to adapt gaze-aware MLLMs to unseen gaze data and egocentric video tasks. The framework will utilize a few-shot learning approach, where the model learns to adapt to new gaze data and tasks with a small number of examples.
CONTROLS: We will compare our results to those of a baseline MLLM without access to gaze information and to the original gaze-aware MLLM.
COST: 76890.8916
PREDICTION: The meta-learning framework will enable gaze-aware MLLMs to effectively adapt to unseen gaze data and egocentric video tasks, but the model's ability to generalize may be limited by the quality of the adaptation data and the complexity of the target tasks.

ACTION: ADD 4
TITLE: Designing a Novel Gaze-Aware Neural Module for Egocentric Video QA
PROPOSAL: Introduce a novel gaze-aware neural module, inspired by self-attention mechanisms, which integrates gaze information directly into the MLLM architecture. Design the module to attend to specific elements of the input video that are concurrently visible and relevant within egocentric visual context based on gaze cues. Evaluate the proposed neural module on the Ego4D question answering task and compare to state-of-the-art BART and CLIP models.
CONTROLS: Compare the performance of the proposed gaze-aware neural module to a variant where the gaze signals are either omitted or used in a more traditional feature engineering manner.

PREDICTION: The proposed gaze-aware neural module may demonstrate significant improvements in performance over BART and CLIP models, especially on questions that require exploiting gaze-related context information, but it might fail to generalize well to tasks with diverse egocentric visual scenes or varying gaze-related complexities.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Evaluating MLLMs on Egocentric Video Question Answering with Gaze Information
PROPOSAL: We conduct an experiment where we fine-tune the recently released egocentric video question answering model, EcoVQA, on the recently introduced egocentric video question answering dataset, Egocentric-300, which involves a subset of videos from the realism-focused Egocentric BBC-100 dataset with eye-tracking data of human viewers. We'll use the gaze points as additional input channels for the visual encoder, similar to how the original EcoVQA model handles image input. We'll compare the results with the original EcoVQA model that only uses visuals.
CONTROLS: Compare with EcoVQA model trained only on visuals and with a control group that adds random noise to the gaze points.
COST: 670.1
PREDICTION: The model should outperform the original EcoVQA by 5-7% in terms of overall accuracy with the addition of gaze information. However, it might also increase the variance in model performance across subjects due to individual differences in how users focus their attention. We expect the noise-controlled group will perform worse than both models with gaze.

textes.jumeau:
ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Assessing the Limitations of MLLMs in Understanding User Intent from Egocentric Video
PROPOSAL: We evaluate the ability of current state-of-the-art MLLMs (e.g., CLIP, LLaMA) to answer egocentric video question answering tasks in the presence of gaze information, similar to our first proposal. We use the VATEX dataset for visual and egocentric task evaluation, augmented with eye-tracking data from a separate dataset, and compare with the performance on egocentric tasks without gaze. To analyze these limitations, we'll also include an experiment with an extra layer to predict intent from augmented gaze-related context tokens and query reformulation.
CONTROLS: Compare with CLIP and LLaMA that only receive visuals and have an extra layer to predict gaze-induced context for intent clarification.
COST: 1500
PREDICTION: These state-of-the-art MLLMs will show a performance gap when using only their visual processing capabilities in egocentric settings. Compared to the first proposal that leveraged EcoVQA, we expect to see a notable drop in results. However, the new intent layer should allow them to narrow the gap slightly on well-defined question answering tasks where gaze helps disambiguate focus.

We'll gather gaze points from this dataset and quantify the effect of initial and average gaze signal accuracy on MLLMs performance using the F1-score and ROUGE metrics. We'll specifically measure "gaze-agnostic" tasks, where the gaze signal is not necessary for answering the question, and contrast them with "gaze-dependent" tasks, which significantly rely on gaze data.
CONTROLS: Compare results with a baseline model without gaze input and a model trained with noise-corrupted gaze data.
COST: 1400
PREDICTION: We expect to see a significant drop in performance for gaze-dependent tasks when the gaze signal is highly inaccurate, while gaze-agnostic tasks should remain relatively unaffected, providing clear insights into the critical role of gaze accuracy for specific tasks.

TITLE: Designing Gaze-Aware Visual Tokenization for Egocentric Video Understanding
PROPOSAL: To address the challenge of incorporating gaze-related signals into MLLMs, we propose a novel gaze-aware visual tokenization framework that captures the spatial and temporal dynamics of gaze attention. Our approach consists of a hierarchical attention mechanism that learns to focus on the most relevant regions of the visual scene based on the user's gaze information. We'll implement this framework as a pre-processing step for the input videos in the Egocentric-555 dataset and evaluate its performance on both gaze-dependent and gaze-agnostic tasks.
CONTROLS: Compare the proposed gaze-aware tokenization with traditional visual tokenization methods and a baseline model without gaze input.
COST: 1830
PREDICTION: We expect to see improved performance on gaze-dependent tasks and comparable performance on gaze-agnostic tasks with our gaze-aware visual tokenization framework. However, it might introduce some additional computational overhead, which could impact the overall efficiency of the pipeline.

We then propose a new evaluation metric that specifically assesses the performance of MLLMs on understanding user intent from egocentric video with gaze information. PREDICTION: The proposed metric will provide a more accurate assessment of MLLM performance on understanding user intent from egocentric video with gaze information. textes.jumeau:
ACTION: REVISE 3
TITLE: Refinement of Hierarchical Modality-Gating Architecture
PROPOSAL: Refine the Hierarchical Modality-Gating (HMG) Architecture by incorporating a modality-specific embedding layer directly after the modality demixing PCA/ICA step in Proposal 2. These modality-specific embeddings can serve as gate control parameters that adjust the weighting of each modality's contribution to the shared transformer:
1. Train the modality-specific embeddings to adapt the gate weights based on the outputs of the demixing step.
2. Integrate the modality-specific embeddings into the HMG mechanism.
3. Evaluate the influence of HMG with and without gate adaptation.
4. Implement a feature attribution technique, Global Average Importance (GAI), to visualize and analyze the contribution of modality-specific embeddings to the final output of the model.
CONTROLS: Same baseline and control procedures as in prop 2. The refined HMG architecture will be evaluated on COCO dataset, for visual reasoning (VQAP) benchmark.
COST: 1400
PREDICTION: The refined HMG architecture can improve the performance of the modality-shared AR transformer, especially in the early stages of training, by dynamically controlling the contribution of each modality. However, the improvement may plateau or degrade as the model overfits to the modality-specific embeddings.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Adaptive Modality-Weighting for Improved Training Stability
PROPOSAL: To improve the training stability of the modality-shared AR transformer, we propose an adaptive modality-weighting (AMW) mechanism that adjusts the modality weights based on the gradient interference metrics computed in Proposal 1:
1. Compute the gradient interference metrics at each layer and update the modality weights accordingly.
2. Implement a simple gradient-based step-size adaptation (SGA) to avoid oscillations in the modality weights update.
3. Incorporate a clipping mechanism to prevent the modality weights from exploding or vanishing.
CONTROLS: Baseline DDPM with fixed modality weights and refined HMG architecture with fixed gate weights. Compare the validation performance and training stability of each architecture on the COCO dataset.
COST: 1200
PREDICTION: The adaptive modality-weighting mechanism can help prevent gradient interference and improve the training stability of the modality-shared AR transformer, especially in the early stages of training. However, the improved performance may come at the cost of increased computational overhead and sensitivity to hyperparameters.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Investigating the Impact of Modality Alignment on Gradient Interference

TITLE: Investigating Gradient Interference in Modality-Shared AR Transformers
PROPOSAL: Conduct a comprehensive analysis to quantify the disagreement between text and vision gradients in a modality-shared AR transformer on the COCO Captions (COCO-CAP) dataset, a popular benchmark for visual question answering and image captioning. Specifically, we will:
1. Train a modality-shared AR transformer on the COCO-CAP dataset and collect predictions at each layer.
2. Compute the gradient ∇E between the transformers' predictions and a modality-specific loss function (e.g., cross-entropy for text, per-pixel loss for images).
3. Investigate how the gradient interference between modalities evolves along the depth of the network.
4. Compare our findings to the theoretical bounds of gradient interference in standard transformers (e.g., guarantees on gradient similarity/divergence).
CONTROLS: A modified version of the DDPM model (DDPM-Aorgeti) will serve as a baseline for ablation experiments, and CLEVR, a synthetic dataset for visual reasoning will serve as a control for comparison with state-of-the-art (SOTA) results.
COST: 1500
PREDICTION: We expect to identify significant gradient interference between modalities in the first few layers, which will worsen as the network becomes progressively deeper. However, the precise form and asymptotics of this interference are uncertain and may relate to the challenging problem of distinguishing monotonic successions in discrete image sequences versus typical shift-invariant textures.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Measuring Layer-Wise Modality Conflicts in Autoregressive UMMs
PROPOSAL: We propose a set of layer-wise conflict metrics to quantify the disagreement between text and vision gradients in a modality-shared AR transformer. Specifically, for each layer $l$ and modality $m \in \{text, vision\}$, we will compute the gradient similarity $G_l(m)$ between the $l$-th layer's gradients for the text and vision tasks. We will use the pearson correlation coefficient as the similarity metric and evaluate $G_l(m)$ at every layer to get a profile of conflicts along the network depth. This will help us understand how modality conflicts evolve as representations become increasingly abstract and semantic.
CONTROLS: We will compare our metrics to a baseline using mutual information as a conflict metric, which is commonly used in multi-task learning but lacks layer-wise resolution.
COST: 3600
PREDICTION: We expect a clear pattern of modality conflicts to emerge along the network depth, with higher conflicts observed at intermediate layers where representations become increasingly abstract and semantic. However, accurately modeling these conflicts may require many more experiments and is not inherently certain, as conflict patterns can be unforeseen.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Investigating Inter-Modal Conflict Patterns in AR UMMs
PROPOSAL: We propose a set of experiments to systematically investigate the inter-modal conflict patterns observed in the modality-shared AR UMMs. Specifically, we will control for different image textural properties, such as visual complexity and abstraction, to see how they influence modality conflicts. We will use popular image-text datasets such as COCO Captions and ImageNet Captions.
CONTROLS: We will ablate different parts of the transformer architecture, such as its depth and width, to investigate how architectural choices influence modality conflicts.
COST: 5400
PREDICTION: Our experiments might reveal that inter-modal conflicts are affected by the visual complexity of images, with more abstract images inducing higher conflicts. However, modality conflicts can also arise from other factors, such as text's semantic difficulty or language expertise, and results may not always yield only to just variation in in-textural complexity.

TITLE: Revise Modality-Aware Training of AR UMMs through Layered Gradient Projection
PROPOSAL: To reduce the risk of overfitting or mode collapse issues, we propose an adaptation of our method that incorporates spectral regularization on the projection matrices. This regularization technique, derived from the idea of graph-based spectral clustering, aims to ensure that the projected gradients are as globally orthogonal as possible, thereby reducing the explosive growth of the projection matrices' eigenvalues. Additionally, we will implement a mechanism for automatic mixing of the modality-agnostic and modality-aware projections, allowing the model to adapt to the task at hand.

COST: 7200
PREDICTION: The incorporation of spectral regularization should help mitigate overfitting and mode collapse issues, allowing the model to generalize better to novel tasks and datasets, but may also reduce the model's ability to adapt to specific task needs.

ACTION: ADD 
TITLE: Evaluating Reasoning Errors in Audiovisual Emotion Recognition
PROPOSAL: 
We'll develop a novel evaluation benchmark, dubbed "AVER", that generates synthetic 2D and 3D video clips with audio tracks to simulate human interactions in various social scenarios. To ensure diversity, we'll compose these clips from a collection of separately labeled facial expressions, body language, and speech transcripts. We'll use this AVER benchmark to assess five existing MLLMs' ability to identify and explain audiovisual cues relevant to emotions. Specifically, we'll compute the frequency and accuracy of tieing emotions to unintended cues, such as those unrelated to the emotional expression in the input.
CONTROLS: 
Our baseline includes the original performance metrics of the five MLLMs on standard emotion recognition tasks (e.g. FER+). We will also remove audio or visual components from the input and assess how this affects the models' ability to tie emotions to unintended cues.
COST: 171000 
PREDICTION: We expect to find AVER is more effective than current benchmarks in highlighting reasoning errors in audiovisual emotion recognition and that the frequency and accuracy of tying emotions to unintended cues will be significantly higher than in standard emotion recognition tasks. However, this might fail if the models' hallucinations are simply random, without being influenced by text priors.

ACTION: ADD 
TITLE: Identifying Perception Errors
PROPOSAL: 
We'll develop a method to automatically detect perception errors in MLLMs' generated emotion descriptions. By comparing the output of these models with human annotated transcripts of the same videos, we'll use similarity metrics (e.g., BLEU, ROUGE) and relevance scores (e.g., ROUGE-L) to identify cases where models invent or omit cues. Our approach will also involve using natural language processing tools to detect cue-emotion associations not supported by the input.
CONTROLS: 
We'll compare our method to existing benchmarks for detecting hallucinations and evaluate ablations where the complexity of the language model backbone is reduced.
COST: 248000 
PREDICTION: We expect our method to significantly outperform current benchmarks in detecting perception errors. However, this might fail if human annotations are inconsistent, leading to reduced performance in cue-emotion association detection tasks.

ACTION: REVISE 2
TITLE: Identifying Perception Errors
PROPOSAL: 
We'll develop a more robust method to automatically detect perception errors in MLLMs' generated emotion descriptions. Our revised approach will incorporate multimodal fusion techniques to jointly analyze the audio and visual components of the input videos. This will enable us to better capture the context in which emotions are expressed, and detect cases where models invent or omit cues. Specifically, we'll use a spatial attention-based mechanism to weight the input video frames and audio spectrograms according to their relevance to the predicted emotion, and use a temporal self-attention mechanism to model the sequential relationships between the input cues and the predicted emotion.
CONTROLS: 
We'll maintain our original baseline controls, but also evaluate ablations where we remove the spatial attention mechanism or the temporal self-attention mechanism from our revised approach.
COST: 330000 
PREDICTION: We expect our revised approach to significantly outperform the original method in detecting perception errors, especially in cases where the input cues are complex or multimodal. However, this might fail if the MLLM's hallucinations are highly context-dependent, making it difficult to capture the relationships between input cues and predicted emotions.

ACTION: ADD 
TITLE: Regularization Techniques for Reducing Reasoning Errors
PROPOSAL: 
We'll investigate the impact of regularization techniques on the ability of MLLMs to reduce reasoning errors in audiovisual emotion recognition. Specifically, we'll explore the effect of adding L1 and L2 regularization terms to the model's loss function, as well as the use of weight decay. Our goal is to determine whether these techniques can encourage the model to focus on relevant cues and reduce the frequency of tieing emotions to unintended cues.
CONTROLS: 
We'll compare our findings to the original performance metrics of the five MLLMs on standard emotion recognition tasks, as well as evaluate ablations where we remove specific regularization techniques from the model.
COST: 341000 
PREDICTION: We expect to find that regularization techniques can significantly reduce the frequency of tieing emotions to unintended cues, but may introduce new challenges such as decreased model accuracy or overfitting.

TITLE: Instruction Tuning for Emotion-Specific Cue Extraction
PROPOSAL: 
We'll develop an instruction tuning approach specifically designed to emphasize the extraction of relevant audiovisual cues for emotion recognition. Our method will involve fine-tuning a pre-trained MLLM on a subset of the AVER benchmark that focuses on scenarios where emotions are expressed through specific, easily recognizable cues (e.g. loud speech for anger). Through this approach, we aim to reduce the severity of tieing emotions to unintended cues and increase the model's reliance on relevant audiovisual information.
CONTROLS: 
We'll compare our method to standard instruction tuning approaches and evaluate ablations where the model is fine-tuned on different subsets of the AVER benchmark.
COST: 400000 
PREDICTION: We expect to find that instruction tuning can significantly improve the model's ability to extract relevant audiovisual cues, but may require careful selection of the instruction dataset to avoid overfitting to specific cue-emotion associations.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Emotion Grounding Adversarial Training for Multimodal Large Language Models
PROPOSAL: We'll propose a new training approach for MLLMs, called Emotion Grounding Adversarial Training (EGAT), which leverages a discriminator to identify when the model's emotion predictions are not grounded in the input audiovisual cues. During training, we'll provide the model with weakly labeled datasets where emotions are only provided at the clip-level, and the discriminator will try to predict when the model's predictions are inconsistent with the actual audiovisual cues.
CONTROLS: Baseline: MLLMs trained on the same weakly labeled datasets without EGAT.
COST: 23400
PREDICTION: This proposal is expected to reduce hallucination rates in MLLMs by encouraging them to rely more heavily on the audiovisual input, but it may also lead to over-regularization and under-preparation of the model for out-of-distribution examples.

TITLE: Quantifying Emotion Hallucinations using Weakly-Supervised Contrastive Learning
PROPOSAL: We'll develop a novel approach to detect emotion hallucinations in MLLMs using weakly-supervised contrastive learning. Specifically, we'll create two separate datasets: one with true audiovisual cues and one with artificially crafted hallucinations. We'll then fine-tune the model on a set of weakly-supervised objectives that force the model to distinguish between these two datasets.
CONTROLS: Baseline: MLLMs without contrastive learning or hallucination detection.
COST: 37000
PREDICTION: This proposal is expected to detect hallucinations more accurately and provide insights into the types of hallucinations that occur in MLLMs, but may also require significant computational resources to fine-tune the model on the designated objectives.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Intrinsic Process Reward for Agentic Search via Reward Normalization and Turn-Level Credit Assignment
PROPOSAL: Implement a turn-level intrinsic process reward function that computes the normalized difference in intermediate reasoning and tool outputs between each rollout in a group, while penalizing rollouts that incur errors or inconsistency with prior turns, to encourage informative and productive turns. The reward for each turn is calculated as the average of normalized KL divergence between the current and previous turn's reasoning distributions, plus a penalty term for consistency and accuracy.
CONTROLS: Compare against Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) alone with outcome rewards, and also with GRPO-plus-standard process rewards which use external oracle knowledge to judge intermediate steps.
COST: 1200
PREDICTION: This approach should help mitigate advantage collapse, improve fine-grained credit assignment, and reduce sparsity of rewards, leading to better sample efficiency and more accurate agentic search agents, with potential to work especially well in multi-hop question answering scenarios. 

Note: There may be a potential for high variability in reward estimates if the turn-level reasoning distributions are highly dynamic.

textes.jumeau:
ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Agentic Search with Hierarchical Reward Decomposition for Multi-Turn Credit Assignment
PROPOSAL: Extend the previous proposal by applying hierarchical reward decomposition to break down the reward function into multiple levels, each corresponding to different turn types and reward signals. The top level uses the intrinsic process reward, while lower levels assign reward to individual turns based on their contribution to solving the query, with a critic network tuning the reward weights through gradient descent. This method should further enhance the ability to distinguish productive from unproductive turns and allocate credit accordingly.
CONTROLS: Compare against one baseline of intrinsic process reward alone (proposed in turn 1), another baseline where rewards are binned by turn number (i.e., rewarding only turns that produce a known gold evidence or ask an informed follow-up question), and against GRPO alone with outcome rewards for a basis comparison.
COST: 2400
PREDICTION: This approach should significantly improve fine-grained credit assignment and overall performance, especially in complex multi-hop question answering scenarios, with the critic network learning to adaptively prioritize relevant turns and allocate credit.

ACTION: REVISE 2
TITLE: Agentic Search with Hierarchical Reward Decomposition for Multi-Turn Credit Assignment
PROPOSAL: For the lower levels of hierarchical reward decomposition, assign reward based on turn-level reasoning quality, in addition to turn contribution. Inject contrarian rewards at each turn if the current candidate answer is contradicted by the next turn's information, or if the candidate answer produces inconsistencies with prior turns, with a learnable weight parameter to modulate the impacts of these rewards. This design aims to identify and penalize unwanted intermediate states.
CONTROLS: Experiment with learning the weight parameter for contrarian rewards through cross-validation on a validation set, while also comparing with separate baselines that remove or adjust the weight modulation, or rely solely on turn contribution for off-diagonal terms in reward matrices.
COST: 3600
PREDICTION: By integrating turn-level reasoning quality and focusing on unwanted intermediate states, this extension may remove additional "poison pill" value patterns from turn-level optimization and provide more explicit, targeted guidance to reduce errors in intermediate turns.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Agentic Search with Temperature-Controlled Exploration and Informed Sampling
PROPOSAL: Incorporate a temperature-controlled exploration mechanism into the policy optimization process. TITLE: Multi-Agent Interaction Framework for Agentic Search
PROPOSAL: Model the agentic search process as a distributed problem among multiple agents, with each agent responsible for evaluating one or more turns in the sequence. Introduce communication mechanisms among the agents to share intermediate reasoning and allow for the formation of consensus. ACTION: REVISE 3
TITLE: Multi-Agent Interaction Framework for Agentic Search
PROPOSAL: Implement a distributed decision-making protocol within the multi-agent framework, where each agent evaluates and refines its own turn proposals based on a joint Bayesian inference mechanism. The agents exchange credible evidence and updated belief states, accounting for the probabilistic nature of intermediate information and facilitating a rational inference process. This enables the framework to elegantly manage uncertainty, credit assignments, and cooperation among agents.
CONTROLS: Compare against one baseline that omits joint Bayesian inference and exchange of belief states, and another baseline that relies on centralized inference for turn-level decisions.
COST: 21600
PREDICTION: The incorporation of joint Bayesian inference and probabilistic crediting will improve the multi-agent framework's resistance to uncertainty and credit misattribution, and foster a more cooperative and rational search process among agents.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Analyzing and Mitigating Evaluation Mass Collapse in Agentic Search
PROPOSAL: Investigate the Evaluation Mass Collapse (EMC) issue in agentic search, where multiple plausible answers and solutions dominate the outcome distribution. Develop strategies to mitigate EMC by injecting noise, prioritizing diverse or novel solution candidates, and exploring the potential of (instance-wise) regularization to encourage incremental and modular contribution of intermediate turns.
CONTROLS: Explore the effects of balancing EMC mitigation techniques with baseline optimization practices and will assess the suitability of the proposed solutions across different performance metrics and problem types.
COST: 72000
PREDICTION: Addressing EMC in agentic search through joint information adaption, prioritization, and regularization will naturally yield improved policy optimization, decision-making resilience, and agent robustness.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Multi-Turn Intrinsic Rewards from Local Contrastive Learning
PROPOSAL: We investigate a new approach to assign a dense, informative reward signal to every interaction turn of a multi-turn search agent. Motivated by the principle of local contrastive learning, we define a reward as the similarity, measured by a temporal embedding discriminative model (e.g. SimCSE), between a pair of embeddings corresponding to consecutive turns. We term the similarity as the local progress made by the agent in each turn, which accords with the desired property of distinguishing productive from unproductive intermediate turns. 
CONTROLS: (1) Baseline: Using Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) with outcome rewards; (2) Ablation: Baseline but with no temporal embedding discriminative model (similarity is assumed to be 1); (3) Baseline + external oracle rewarding
COST: 500
PREDICTION: We expect this approach to outperform the baseline in terms of sample efficiency and accurately identifying productive turns. A potential shortcoming is that it might be hard to distinguish between turns that are obviously similar (e.g., retrieving the same fact) and turns that are actually 'productive' due to some reason that isn't represented in the embedding.

textes.jumeau:
ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Turn-Wise Reward Maximization via Sequence-Level Value Functions
PROPOSAL: To deal with the challenges posed by sparse outcome rewards, we explore using sequence-level value functions to derive a dense reward signal that can inform every turn. More specifically, we aim to learn a sequence-level value function that predicts the final answer's correctness based on the entire sequence of turns. This prediction, in turn, is used to evaluate and reward each intermediate turn, enabling the decoder to optimize its action choices at the turn level rather than wait for the outcome reward. 
CONTROLS: (1) Baseline: Using Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) with outcome rewards; (2) Ablation: Baseline but without the sequence-level value function (use outcome rewards only); (3) Baseline with turn-wise outcome rewards
COST: 834
PREDICTION: This approach is expected to alleviate advantage collapse and permit more sample-efficient learning. However, value-function estimation can be computationally costly, and overly loose approximations or overly constrained search may cause suboptimal agent performance.

ACTION: REVISE 2
TITLE: Revision of Turn-Wise Reward Maximization via Sequence-Level Value Functions
PROPOSAL: To mitigate the computational cost associated with sequence-level value functions, we propose learning an augmented attention-based sequence encoder within the Decoder (consider T5 style architecture). This encoder computes attention weights at each sequence position and learns to progressively focus on relevant turns to determine the answer correctness. We feed the encoded sequence representation directly into a reward module, which provides a dense, intermediate reward that encourages the decoder to optimize turn-wise performance. 
CONTROLS: (1) Baseline: Using Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) with outcome rewards; (2) Ablation: Baseline but use pre-built sequence encoder (e.g, T5 base); (3) Ablation of Reward Module
COST: 936
PREDICTION: By leveraging the augmented attention mechanism, we expect to reduce computational costs without sacrificing policy quality and encouraging the agent to identify useful intermediate steps. However, localized sequence focus might require strengthening of orthogonal capabilities like knowledge graph navigation and full-text interpretation if these lack substantial emphasis within training.

This history-aware approach aims to capture more subtle changes and fosters the decoder to visit relevant past turns and serialize more relevant information in its search space.

TITLE: History-Aware Local Progress Measure for Multi-Turn Search Agents
PROPOSAL: We extend the local contrastive learning approach (proposal 1) by incorporating explicit information from the sequence history. Specifically, we capture attention weights from previous turns and factor them into the embeddings to measure similarity. This history-aware approach aims to capture more subtle changes and fosters the decoder to visit relevant past turns and serialize more relevant information in its search space. 
CONTROLS: (1) Baseline-1: Using Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) with outcome rewards; (2) Baseline-2: History-Aware Local Contrastive Learning (ablate previous relevant information); (3) Baseline-1 with Additional Exploration onto intermediate results
COST: 11400
PREDICTION: This extension is expected to improve the tracking of endeavor through handful threads of evidence with softly-intersecting surfaces. By retaining aspect from histories in mind during said preference propositions, it is expected to swiftly summarize informative queries in the information needed, but recognition capabilities may be divorced from learning connection to intermediate facts very tangentially explicit in history.

ACTION: REVISE 3
TITLE: Revision of History-Aware Local Progress Measure for Multi-Turn Search Agents
PROPOSAL: To make the model more robust and inline with informative and operational framework, we propose replacing the convolutional block used for fusion of attention weights from previous turns with a self-attention layer. This enables the model to dynamically learn which turns are more relevant and automatically aggregate them to create a more informed local progress measure. 
CONTROLS: (1) Baseline: Baseline (using previous model); (2) Ablation: Base line but using convolutional approach (no self-attention); (3) Baseline-2 with Exploration onto distant precursor turn observation.
COST: 1400
PREDICTION: By utilizing self-attention layer to weight importance and learn relevance mask, we expect to see improved model robustness by bridging dependencies in encoded assertion chains.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Interpretable Local Progress Measure via Inductive Learner
PROPOSAL: Our goal is to learn an interpretable internal representation for local progress that captures meaningful concepts such as query relevance, reasoning chaining, and search histories. We leverage an inductive learner, specifically a modular bayesian network, to infer boolean state progress variables from the sequence of turns. This representation is employed to provide an interpretable, turn-level reward, revealing and inducing meaningful intermediate cognition in deployed agents. 
CONTROLS: (1) Baseline: Revision of History-Aware Local Progress Measure for Multi-Turn Search Agents; (2) Ablation: Baseline but w/o modular bayesian network; (3) Baseline - expected with rule-based minimization
COST: 1600
PREDICTION: This approach is expected to explore localized inductive cause effect analysis yielding quality to incrementally accumulating repeated self-prediction stating current state representatively to optimize response paradigm across coherence train.

ACTION: REVISE 1
TITLE: Revision of Multi-Turn Intrinsic Rewards from Local Contrastive Learning
PROPOSAL: To improve the robustness and scalabilty of the local contrastive learning approach, we replace the SimCSE encoder with a more recent and robust variant of the SimCSE model, such as the SimCSEv2, which has been shown to outperform the original model on various text similarity tasks. Additionally, we incorporate ensemble learning techniques to combine multiple instantiations of the SimCSEv2 model, resulting in a more robust and accurate local progress measure. 
CONTROLS: (1) Baseline: Baseline (using previous model); (2) Ablation: SimCSE model but without ensemble learning; (3) Baseline-4 with margin-based objectives formulation for improved contrastive learning.
COST: 2000
PREDICTION: By leveraging the advanced variant of SimCSE and ensemble learning, we expect to see significant improvements in the model's ability to accurately capture local progress, which in turn should lead to better navigation of complex knowledge graphs and more informed decision-making in multi-turn search scenarios.

PROPOSAL: To further improve the performance of the multi-turn search agents, we propose to leverage weakly-supervised learning and fine-tuning techniques, such as pre-training on large-scale text datasets and fine-tuning on a small-scale, task-specific dataset. ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Multi-Turn Intrinsic Rewards from Local Contrastive Learning
PROPOSAL: We investigate a new approach to assign a dense, informative reward signal to every interaction turn of a multi-turn search agent. Motivated by the principle of local contrastive learning, we define a reward as the similarity, measured by a temporal embedding discriminative model (e.g. SimCSE), between a pair of embeddings corresponding to consecutive turns. We term the similarity as the local progress made by the agent in each turn, which accords with the desired property of distinguishing productive from unproductive intermediate turns. 
CONTROLS: (1) Baseline: Using Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) with outcome rewards; (2) Ablation: Baseline but with no temporal embedding discriminative model (similarity is assumed to be 1); (3) Baseline + external oracle rewarding
COST: 1500
PREDICTION: We expect this approach to outperform the baseline in terms of sample efficiency and accurately identifying productive turns. A potential shortcoming is that it might be hard to distinguish between turns that are obviously similar (e.g., retrieving the same fact) and turns that are actually 'productive' due to some reason that isn't represented in the embedding.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Turn-Wise Reward Maximization via Sequence-Level Value Functions
PROPOSAL: To deal with the challenges posed by sparse outcome rewards, we explore using sequence-level value functions to derive a dense reward signal that can inform every turn. More specifically, we aim to learn a sequence-level value function that predicts the final answer's correctness based on the entire sequence of turns. This prediction, in turn, is used to evaluate and reward each intermediate turn, enabling the decoder to optimize its action choices at the turn level rather than wait for the outcome reward. 
CONTROLS: (1) Baseline: Using Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) with outcome rewards; (2) Ablation: Baseline but without the sequence-level value function (use outcome rewards only); (3) Baseline with turn-wise outcome rewards
COST: 2500
PREDICTION: This approach is expected to alleviate advantage collapse and permit more sample-efficient learning. However, value-function estimation can be computationally costly, and overly loose approximations or overly constrained search may cause suboptimal agent performance.

ACTION: REVISE
TITLE: Revision of Turn-Wise Reward Maximization via Sequence-Level Value Functions
PROPOSAL: To mitigate the computational cost associated with sequence-level value functions, we propose learning an augmented attention-based sequence encoder within the Decoder (consider T5 style architecture). This encoder computes attention weights at each sequence position and learns to progressively focus on relevant turns to determine the answer correctness. We feed the encoded sequence representation directly into a reward module, which provides a dense, intermediate reward that encourages the decoder to optimize turn-wise performance. 
CONTROLS: (1) Baseline: Using Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) with outcome rewards; (2) Ablation: Baseline but use pre-built sequence encoder (e.g, T5 base); (3) Ablation of Reward Module
COST: 2800
PREDICTION: By leveraging the augmented attention mechanism, we expect to reduce computational costs without sacrificing policy quality and encouraging the agent to identify useful intermediate steps. However, localized sequence focus might require strengthening of orthogonal capabilities like knowledge graph navigation and full-text interpretation if these lack substantial emphasis within training.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Agentic Search Reward From Partially Correct Rollouts
PROPOSAL: In this experiment, we will explore a simple yet effective method for providing dense rewards to search agents. Instead of relying on a single correct rollout per group, we will normalize rewards within each group based on the number of rollouts with correct or most similar answers to the ground truth. This approach will encourage the agent to mimic the reasoning steps of partially correct rollouts, guiding it toward productive intermediate turns and fine-grained credit assignments.
CONTROLS: We will compare the proposed method to standard outcome-based rewards and a baseline that reports rewards solely from correct rollouts.
COST: 33.6
PREDICTION: We expect to see significant improvements in sample efficiency and learning signals due to finer-grained credit assignments, while issues with bias and reward hacking might occur if partially correct rollouts are overly weighted, pointing to the need for reward modeling or regularization techniques.

textes.jumeau:
ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Learning Implicit Rewards from Success Stories
PROPOSAL: We propose an approach that extracts implicit process rewards by analyzing successful previous rollouts in a group. We represent each rollout as a sequence of turn embeddings and use a high-level representation learning model to extract key steps in successful stories. The model outputs an importance score for each turn and an aggregating function is used to produce a trainable weighting of these scores. The implicit reward for any given rollout is the weighted sum of its turn scores.
CONTROLS: We will compare our approach to standard outcome-based rewards and process rewards methods with expensive Monte Carlo estimation or external oracle knowledge.
COST: 324.528
PREDICTION: We expect this method to leverage the success stories, avoiding the challenge of costly and biased ore-complete process observations, potentially facilitating better sample efficiency for task learning.

textes.jumeau:
ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Distilled Process Rewards via Sequence Matching
PROPOSAL: We propose a novel method to generate distilled process rewards by leveraging sequence matching between the rollout and the ground-truth answer. Specifically, we segment the rollout and the ground-truth answer into sub-sequences and compute a similarity score between these sub-sequences. This score is then used as a bonus reward to guide the policy toward productive turns. To make this approach computationally efficient, we employ a lightweight sequence matching model and pre-compute sub-sequence similarities.
CONTROLS: We will compare this approach to outcome-based rewards, process rewards methods with expensive Monte Carlo estimation or external oracle knowledge, and other proposed methods.
COST: 140
PREDICTION: We expect this approach to provide a good balance between computational efficiency and reward signal quality, leading to improved sample efficiency and learning stability in agentic search tasks.

textes.jumeau:
ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Turn-Level Evaluation Metrics for Agentic Search
PROPOSAL: We investigate the design of turn-level evaluation metrics specifically tailored for agentic search tasks. These metrics capture the progress and efficacy of the agent's search process, providing a fine-grained understanding of whether the agent is moving toward or away from the final answer. To evaluate the quality of these metrics, we propose a set of controlled experiments on real-world datasets and compare the metrics' ability to predict policy performance.
CONTROLS: We will evaluate the proposed metrics against established metrics for agentic search, such as return-based metrics or casework metrics, and assess their impact on policy optimization and reward design.
COST: 93.6
PREDICTION: We expect that by using turn-level evaluation metrics, we can better understand the agency's progress and evaluate the effectiveness of the reward signals proposed in other experiments, particularly with regard to fine-grained feedback on performative turns.

textes.jumeau:
ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Agent-Agnostic Agentic Search Evaluation Suite (AASES)
PROPOSAL: We propose a comprehensive evaluation suite, AASES, designed to assess the performance of agents in agentic search tasks. AASES incorporates a set of standardized benchmarks, including new datasets, metrics, and evaluation protocols, tailored to agentic search. This suite aims to provide a common ground for evaluating and comparing different agent architectures, reward designs, and optimization strategies, aiming to accelerate progress in the field.
CONTROLS: We will evaluate AASES through a series of controlled experiments, comparing its effectiveness to existing evaluation frameworks.
COST: 320
PREDICTION: We expect AASES to provide a more robust and agent-agnostic evaluation of agentic search agents, leading to more accurate comparisons and a better understanding of the strengths and weaknesses of different approaches, while identifying potential areas of improvement in agent design and reward modeling.

ACTION: REVISE
TITLE: Agentic Search Reward From Partially Correct Rollouts (Revised)
PROPOSAL: We extend the approach in Proposal 1 by aggregating information from multiple groups of rollouts to further mitigate issues with partially correct rollouts. The reward will be the average of 'normalized rewards' from each group, where normalized rewards are calculated based on the number of rollouts with correct or most similar answers to the ground truth within the group. This method promotes the agent to learn from diverse sets of rollouts and would decrease the impact of single incorrectly designed partially correct rollouts.
CONTROLS: This revised proposal will be compared to the original partially correct rollout-based rewards, outcome-based rewards, and the baseline reporting rewards solely from correct rollouts, while also exploring the impact of the number of groups used for aggregation on performance.
COST: 220
PREDICTION: We expect to see improved policy stability and sample efficiency in various environments, possibly, peaking at smaller warm-up period or at fewer group aggregation steps, however, increased computational cost and inferior offline performance compared to simple outcome rewards are possible.

ACTION: REVISE
TITLE: Agentic Search Reward From Partially Correct Rollouts (Revised Optimized)
PROPOSAL: We retain the core idea from Proposal 1 but optimize the normalization process. Rollouts will be ranked based on their similarity to the ground truth, with higher-ranked rollouts contributing more to the normalized reward. The reward will be calculated as a weighted sum of outcomes from top-ranked rollouts within each group, where weights are inversely proportional to the rank. This refinement aims to mitigate over-reliance on partially correct rollouts and encourage the agent to mimic expert reasoning steps.
CONTROLS: This optimized proposal will be compared to the original partially correct rollout-based rewards, outcome-based rewards, and the baseline reporting rewards solely from correct rollouts.
COST: 320
PREDICTION: We expect to see improved policy performance, especially on reasoning-intensive tasks, while handling the risk of 'lock-in' to suboptimal reasoning due to overemphasizing correct rollouts.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Distilled Process Rewards via Sequence Matching
PROPOSAL: We propose a novel method to generate distilled process rewards by leveraging sequence matching between the rollout and the ground-truth answer. Specifically, we segment the rollout and the ground-truth answer into sub-sequences and compute a similarity score between these sub-sequences. This score is then used as a bonus reward to guide the policy toward productive turns. To make this approach computationally efficient, we employ a lightweight sequence matching model and pre-compute sub-sequence similarities.
CONTROLS: We will compare this approach to outcome-based rewards, process rewards methods with expensive Monte Carlo estimation or external oracle knowledge, and other proposed methods.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Turn-Level Evaluation Metrics for Agentic Search
PROPOSAL: We investigate the design of turn-level evaluation metrics specifically tailored for agentic search tasks. These metrics capture the progress and efficacy of the agent's search process, providing a fine-grained understanding of whether the agent is moving toward or away from the final answer. To evaluate the quality of these metrics, we propose a set of controlled experiments on real-world datasets and compare the metrics' ability to predict policy performance.
CONTROLS: We will evaluate the proposed metrics against established metrics for agentic search, such as return-based metrics or casework metrics, and assess their impact on policy optimization and reward design.
COST: 280

PROPOSAL: We propose a comprehensive evaluation suite, AASES, designed to assess the performance of agents in agentic search tasks. AASES incorporates a set of standardized benchmarks, including new datasets, metrics, and evaluation protocols, tailored to agentic search. ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Regularized Relative Policy Optimization
PROPOSAL: We introduce a modified version of GRPO, Regularized Relative Policy Optimization (RRPO), which adds a regularization term that balances two terms: one encourages exploration and rewards distinct outcomes within each group, and another discourages empty rollouts by preferring groups with diverse turns. The exploration-promoting term can be achieved by normalizing the relative advantages by the number of unique answers in the group, and the diverse rollout-promoting term can be added using a KL divergence or a cross entropy penalty on the per-group rollout distributions.
CONTROLS: We compare RRPO against the original GRPO, as well as two additional variants: one where we only apply the exploration term, and another where only the diverse rollout term is added.
COST: 8340
PREDICTION: We expect RRPO to mitigate advantage collapse and significantly outperform GRPO, particularly on difficult queries, while potentially struggling with scenarios where rollouts are highly homogeneous due to hard or tractable queries.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Recursive Autonomy Reward (RAR)
PROPOSAL: We propose an intrinsic process reward, Recursive Autonomy Reward (RAR), that recursively credits turns that are essential to reaching the final answer by evaluating whether a sub-trajectory would still reach the same answer if it were truncated after each turn. The reward is computed as the average probability of reaching the final answer in all sub-trajectories truncated at each turn. This design ensures credit is given to necessary turns and de-emphasizes intermediate steps that are redundant or unproductive.
CONTROLS: We compare RAR against the baseline outcome reward, and against an oracle variant of RAR that uses precomputed evidence from external knowledge graphs.
COST: 10000
PREDICTION: We expect RAR to outperform the baseline outcome reward by more accurately attributing credit to productive turns, but may struggle with highly varied or redundant trajectories, where unnecessary sub-trajectories could disproportionately influence the reward.

TITLE: Regularized Relative Policy Optimization with Entropy Regularization
PROPOSAL: We revise the Regularized Relative Policy Optimization (RRPO) by adding an entropy regularization term to the exploration-promoting loss function. This modification encourages the policy to distribute its probability mass across a wider range of outcomes, reducing the likelihood of advantage collapse and promoting more diverse rollouts. The entropy regularization term can be added as a Lagrange multiplier or in an adversarial manner using a learned entropy critic.
CONTROLS: We compare the revised RRPO against the original RRPO, against the modified RRPO without entropy regularization, and against an oracle variant that uses a precomputed entropy map.
COST: 10680
PREDICTION: We expect the revised RRPO to further improve upon the original RRPO by effectively promoting more exploration and mitigating advantage collapse, especially in scenarios with a large number of possible outcomes and limited rollout budgets.

TITLE: Hindsight Credit Assignment (HCA) for Agentic Search Agents
PROPOSAL: We introduce Hindsight Credit Assignment (HCA), a post-hoc evaluation technique that re-runs the search trajectory and selectively assigns credit to turns that were crucial for the final answer. This approach provides a clear attribution of credit to individual turns, helping to identify areas for improvement in the search agent.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Query-Embedding Pre-Training for Sparse Perception Models
PROPOSAL: We will develop a query-embedding pre-training approach for sparse perception models, leveraging the richness of unlabeled driving data. This approach will utilize a self-supervised contrastive loss function that encourages the embedded queries to form dense manifolds in the latent space, capturing fine-grained 3D geometric relationships across multi-view images. During pre-training, the embedded queries will be used as soft anchors to augment approximate nearest neighbor (ANN) search-based pseudo-labeling for detached multi-view images. The embedding space will be parametrized by a shared multi-resolution encoder that captures long-range dependencies. To demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach, we will pre-train sparse object detectors on the KITTI-360 dataset and fine-tune them on the KITTI-Train dataset for 3D object detection and segmentation tasks.
CONTROLS: Baseline 1: Beetle++ without pre-training; Baseline 2: contrastive learning for object detection in the BEV space. We will also ablate our approach by removing the shared encoder, contrastive loss, and soft anchors to measure their individual contributions.
COST: 1800
PREDICTION: Our approach will demonstrate competitive performance with state-of-the-art methods in 3D object detection and segmentation benchmarks, leveraging the unsupervised power of unlabeled driving data. However, the density of the embedded queries might be too high for large-scale SPMs, potentially failing in terms of computational efficiency and memorization of rare objects in large scenes.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Transfer Learning for Heterogeneous Sparse Perception Models
PROPOSAL: We will investigate a transfer learning framework for sparse perception models that adapts their query spaces to different downstream tasks. Our approach will employ a two-stage transfer learning strategy. First, we will pre-train a large-scale sparse query encoder on a diverse set of tasks (e.g., object detection, semantic segmentation, and depth estimation) using a self-supervised learning objective that encourages the encoder to learn a task-agnostic representation of the query space. Second, we will fine-tune the pre-trained encoder on specific downstream tasks, allowing the query space to adapt to the task-specific requirements. To evaluate our transfer learning framework, we will adapt the pre-trained encoder to bilateral datasets (KITTI-Train and Waymo 2.0), cross-modal tasks (e.g., 3D bounding box detection and semantic segmentation), and modal-specific tasks (e.g., Depth completion and stereo matching) in autonomous driving.
CONTROLS: We will compare our approach with four baselines: (1) fine-tuning a frozen pre-trained model, (2) learning a task-specific query encoder from scratch, and (3, 4) joint training of query encoder and task-specific head from scratch, using vanilla and noisy query set respectively.
COST: 4200
PREDICTION: Our transfer learning framework will demonstrate the effectiveness of task-agnostic query space representations in preserving the generality of sparse perception models, significantly reducing the need for extensive fine-tuning and hyperparameter tuning across tasks and environments. However, the performance gap may be apparent when the pre-trained model is far from the downstream task, potentially failing to achieve state-of-the-art performance on extremely task-specific benchmarks within the domain.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Soft Anchor Clustering for Efficient Query Space Initialization
PROPOSAL: We will develop a soft anchor clustering framework to efficiently initialize the query space for sparse perception models during pre-training. Our approach will combine k-means clustering with a novel soft anchor loss function to adaptively select informative anchors from the pre-trained query embedding space, reducing the number of hard queries required for efficient adaptation. By soft anchoring, we enable incorporation of global geometric relationships between multiple queries, fostering the scalability to high-dimensional feature spaces often encountered in sparse perception models. To further improve efficiency, we will exploit pruning techniques on the selected k-means clusters. Our approach will be evaluated on the KITTI-360 dataset, comparing against a baseline that uses random query initialization and a state-of-the-art clustering approach. We will also measure its impact in terms of computational efficiency, memory requirements, and the accuracy of object detection and segmentation tasks.
CONTROLS: We will compare our approach against the following baselines: (1) Random Query Initialization, (2) K-Means++ clustering, and (3) Clustering-based pruning.
COST: 3150
PREDICTION: Our soft anchor clustering framework will accelerate the training process while yielding similar accuracy to the baseline methods and leveraging state-of-the-art clustering techniques. However, if we choose an improper number of clusters or a suboptimal anchor threshold, the method's adaptability to varying scene configurations may suffer, potentially failing to produce robust object detection and segmentation results in complex scenarios.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Self-Supervised Contrastive Learning with Spatial-Temporal Graphs for Sparse Perception Models
PROPOSAL: We will introduce a self-supervised contrastive learning framework for sparse perception models, leveraging spatial-temporal graphs to capture complex scene dynamics. Our approach will incorporate a novel pre-training objective that minimizes the dissimilarity between corresponding scene parts in adjacent frames, further contextualizing the query embeddings with a comprehensive graph-based encoding. The addition of a spatial-temporal graph over the queries will allow for the exploration of object motions and interactions with the environment, allowing sparse perception models to improve task-based perceptions in real-world driving scenarios. To verify the effectiveness of this approach, we will conduct experiments on the KITTI-360 dataset using the proposed self-supervised pre-training method, followed by fine-tuning on a variety of 3D object detection and segmentation benchmarks.
CONTROLS: Baseline 1: a standard self-supervised pre-training method without spatial-temporal graphs, and Baseline 2: a non-self-supervised pre-training method using a separate set of clean ground-truth images.
COST: 5100
PREDICTION: Our self-supervised framework will improve the depth and richness of query representations in sparse perception models, leading to significant performance boosts in real-world driving perception tasks. However, relying heavily on a graph-based structure may demand high computational resources and learning time, which may hinder scalability to higher complexity rule sets for sparse perception variables in certain drive configurations.

TITLE: Multitask Feature Learning and Query Augmentation for Robust Sparse Perception Models
PROPOSAL: We will develop a multitask feature learning and query augmentation framework for robust sparse perception models, capitalizing on the collective effectiveness of visual representations in a composite evaluation metric. This will be achieved through the reformulation of feature learning objectives that capture both geometric and semantic aspects of sparse perception tasks. To improve the query-enhanced learning process and enhance robustness of the multimodal query representation, we will design and evaluate a contrasting query resolution technique. This technique involves merging acongruent geometric perception queries to produce queries that adhere to practical assessment principles, filters and noise artifacts often encountered in autonomous driving environments. Static resolution, spatiotemporal context, and task-based approximation convergence will guide pretraining for factoring solutions to each problem, then utilizing only matching higher-level visual modules to aid deeper neural networks.
CONTROLS: Baseline 1: Using vanilla Sparse 3D object detectors, Baseline 2: Inspired instance-based SPSS Triple-waine-free single-stage One-click algorithms
COST: 5400
PREDICTION: Our framework will demonstrate the effectiveness of task-robust and query-enhanced learning in significantly improving sparse perception models' accuracy and efficiency in handling different perception tasks. However, adding extra tasks such as sensor-correct sentiment analysis and higher-order geometric validation might make models complex and resource-hungry for deployment in all scenarios, resulting in slight to moderate pitfalls when insufficient resources are available for fine-tuning models.

TITLE: Adversarial Training for Robust Sparse Perception Models
PROPOSAL: We will develop an adversarial training framework to enhance the robustness of sparse perception models to adversarial attacks. Our framework will utilize a novel two-player game setup, where the generator aims to produce adversarial examples that fool the sparse perception model, while the discriminator aims to defend against these attacks. We will also explore different types of adversarial attacks, such as white-box and black-box attacks, to evaluate the robustness of our framework. To evaluate the effectiveness of our approach, we will conduct experiments on a range of benchmark datasets and tasks.
CONTROLS: Baseline 1: Sparse perception model without adversarial training, Baseline 2: State-of-the-art adversarial training method for dense models.
COST: 9360
PREDICTION: Our adversarial training framework will significantly improve the robustness of sparse perception models to adversarial attacks, making them more suitable for real-world applications. However, the effectiveness of our approach may be limited if the generator and discriminator are not designed carefully, potentially failing to capture the complexities of sparse perception tasks and resulting in suboptimal performance.

PROPOSAL: Investigate a few-shot transfer learning approach to adapt pre-learned scene representations across different SPM models and tasks. PROPOSAL: Investigate a variant of the Self-Supervised Contrastive (SSC) pre-training strategy for sparse perception models, tailored to learn a common 3D latent space by contrasting the output features of different image encoders across a batch of self-supervised driving scene samples. Specifically, encoding pairs of images taken from a set of overlapping views will be stacked together and fed to a shared, learned decoder to produce jointly-represented 3D object features, allowing each encoder to learn distinguishable and complementary properties of the scene, and enabling the transfer of the acquired knowledge to a diverse range of query-based downstream models.
CONTROLS: Compare the pre-trained models to randomly initialized models and to models pre-trained using other self-supervised methods, such as Masked Autoencoders (MAE) and Non-local Contrast (NCL). ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Contrastive Learning with 3D Scene Reconstruction for Sparse Perception Models
PROPOSAL: Investigate a contrastive learning approach for sparse perception models that utilizes 3D scene reconstruction to learn a shared representation of the scene across different views. Specifically, pre-train a sparse perception model to reconstruct 3D scenes in a self-supervised manner using lightweight 3D rendering techniques, such as 3D Gaussian Splatting. ACTION: ADD 
 TITLE: Investigating Sparse Graph-based Contrastive Learning for Pre-training Sparse Perception Models
 PROPOSAL: We propose a novel pre-training approach based on sparse graph-contrastive learning, where SPMs are adaptively pre-trained by predicting the sparse query relationships learned from multi-view driving data. The approach involves aggregating features from multiple views using a learnable and dynamic graph approach, which allows us to learn spatial and temporal context in a self-supervised manner. The sparsity of the graph is implicitly learned through maximizing the mutual information between the graph and the driving data, thus decoding the relevant and unseen blind spots of the driving perception of a scene.
 CONTROLS: We will compare the proposed approach with existing state-of-the-art pre-training methods for dense BEV-centric methods such as BEVFormer and Lift-Splat-Shoot, and existing query-based image-based pre-training methods for 2D images such as Frozen-DETR and GLID.
 COST: 10 GPU-hours
 PREDICTION: We believe this approach can effectively learn fine-grained 3D scene representations and improve the performance of downstream sparse object detection and semantic occupancy prediction tasks for autonomous driving. However, one potential challenge is preventing the over sedeation of the model to trivial solutions that overlook inherent object occlusions.

 TITLE: Unsupervised Registration of Multi-View Frames for SPM Pre-training using 3D Heatmap Regression
 PROPOSAL: We propose a new unsupervised pre-training method that leverages the spatial-temporal relationship of multi-view frames to learn a dense and informative representation of scene geometry for SPMs. The approach involves a 3D heatmap regression task that constrains the spatial distribution of 3D points in a scene, which encourages the model to explicitly represent structural information and temporal dependencies between frames. This provides informative features for SPM queries to improve their effectiveness in learning 3D scene structures.
 CONTROLS: To evaluate this approach, we will compare the results of SPMs pre-trained using this method against those pre-trained using our previous sparse graph-based contrastive learning approach, as well as current state-of-the-art pre-training methods for SPMs.
 COST: 27.045 GPU-hours
 PREDICTION: We anticipate that this approach can provide more effective features for SPM queries, leading to improved performance in downstream tasks such as object detection and semantic segmentation. One potential concern is the scaling up of the pre-training process to larger datasets and versions of the model that are more complex, given the increased computational requirements.
