 TITLE: Improved Unserved Registration of Multi-View Frames for SPM Pre-training using 3D Heatmap Regression with Orientational Ambiguity Resolution
 PROPOSAL: We improve our previous unsupervised registration method by incorporating an additional task that addresses orientational ambiguities in 3D heatmap regression. By including a loss term that constrains the subtended angles between 3D orientations of nearby points, our method can provide more accurate spatial relations and translations between frames. This strengthens the potential of these models to capture nuanced spatial semantics of real-world scenes in SPM pre-training.

Still, handling occlusions remains a key challenge in leveraging our technique for effectively impacting downstream tasks, considering real-world conditions that pop up in deployment environments.

 TITLE: Efficient Weakly-supervised Learning of SPMs with Multi-task Cross-triplet Loss
 PROPOSAL: We propose a novel weakly-supervised learning approach for SPMs, utilizing a multi-task cross-triplet loss to predict scene boundaries, temporal relations between frames, and explicit 3D object coordinates. The approach is less dependent on intermediate features or annotations that are either difficult or costly to obtain, thus efficiently pre-training SPMs on unlabeled driving data. Furthermore, the predicted object coordinates and scene boundaries provide an approximate alignment between SPM queries and the structure of a scene.
 CONTROLS: We compare our approach with existing methods that use different weak supervision mechanisms and without using any pre-training or adaptation techniques. Also, we will experiment with variations of the multi-task cross-triplet loss on different datasets and pre-training settings.
 COST: 70 GPU-hours
 PREDICTION: We anticipate that our approach can be used as a complementary method to other pre-training techniques, and we believe that pre-trained SPMs utilizing the multi-task cross-triplet loss can achieve significant improvements in downstream tasks due to their efficient and low-cost pre-training on weak annotations. However, due to the difficulty of designing a proper regularization term for absolute object positioning based solely on our objective way, further qualitative analysis should be conducted along this specification.

 TITLE: Enhancing Synthetic-to-Real Transfer Adaptation for SPMs with Intermediate Task-driven Knowledge Sharing
 PROPOSAL: We enhance our previous synthetic-to-real transfer adaptation approach for aligning SPMs with scenes by incorporating an intermediate task-driven knowledge sharing mechanism. The pre-trained SPM is prompted to answer questions based on the predicted scene structure and object properties from the synthetic data. The query results, which contain knowledge gathered from the synthetic environment, are then transferred to the real-world adaptation phase. This allows for more effective adaptation by leveraging additional task-driven supervision from the synthetic data. 
 CONTROLS: To evaluate the effectiveness, we will compare our adapted approach with both our previous synthetic-to-real transfer adaptation method and existing state-of-the-art transfer learning methods for SPMs. Also, we ablate different knowledge sharing mechanisms to assess their individual contributions to the adaptation.
 COST: 60.83 GPU-hours 
 PREDICTION: By integrating this knowledge sharing mechanism into the transfer adaptation process, we believe we can achieve higher scene alignment accuracy and better downstream task performance. However, subtleties in environment-specific query tasks and manner in which responses contribute to adaptation do exist, and might require a certain level of regulation to optimize effect in separate data scenarios.

ACTION: ADD 
 TITLE: Diffusion Mapping-based Boosting of Pre-trained SPMs for Reduced Over-specialization
 PROPOSAL: We introduce a diffusion mapping-based framework for boosting pre-trained SPMs to alleviate over-specialization to specific training environments or scenarios. The technique utilizes learned representations from the pre-trained SPM to generate new, pseudo-sample data by inducing diffusion mappings between instances in the pre-training set and generating new ones. Boosting the pre-trained model with the generated data helps adapt it to a wider range of scenarios while reducing overfitting.
 CONTROLS: To evaluate the effectiveness, we compare our approach with existing baselines, including the pre-trained SPM itself, as well as state-of-the-art regularization techniques used to combat over-specialization in SPMs.
 COST: 83.4 GPU-hours
 PREDICTION: We anticipate that our diffusion mapping-based boosting technique can improve the robustness of pre-trained SPMs by reducing over-specialization to specific training environments or scenarios. However, a critical concern is that the generated pseudo-sample data may not always accurately reflect the true underlying patterns and variations in the real-world driving scenarios, potentially compromising the effectiveness of the boosted model in these environments.

ACTION: ADD 
 TITLE: Evaluating Transferability and Out-of-Distribution Generalization of Pre-trained SPMs using Multi-modal Transferability Metrics
 PROPOSAL: We investigate the transferability and out-of-distribution generalization of pre-trained SPMs across various visual and semantic domains. We propose a multi-modal transferability metric that leverages the similarity of pre-trained models' feature representations, scene structures, and object-aware representations to quantify transferability. To assess out-of-distribution generalization, we evaluate SPMs' performance in unseen environments and under various operational regimes. Our work provides a comprehensive understanding of transferability in SPMs and a means to gauge the suitable use of pre-training techniques in diverse applications.
 CONTROLS: We compare the transferability and generalization capabilities of pre-trained SPMs using our proposed metrics against state-of-the-art transfer learning and few-shot learning methods for SPMs.
 COST: 100 GPU-hours
 PREDICTION: We anticipate that our multi-modal transferability metric can effectively assess the transferability of pre-trained SPMs and provide insights into the suitability of pre-training techniques for specific tasks and scenarios. However, evaluating out-of-distribution generalization is a challenging task, and ensuring the developed metric is both reliable and accurate across a wide range of environments and situations is crucial to the success of this work.

 TITLE: Unifying Transfer Adaptation and Pre-training Techniques for Improved SPM Performance in Autonomous Driving
 PROPOSAL: We propose a unified framework that integrates transfer adaptation and pre-training techniques to improve the performance of SPMs in autonomous driving. ACTION: ADD 
 TITLE: Investigating Sparse Graph-based Contrastive Learning for Pre-training Sparse Perception Models
 PROPOSAL: We propose a novel pre-training approach based on sparse graph-contrastive learning, where SPMs are adaptively pre-trained by predicting the sparse query relationships learned from multi-view driving data. The approach involves aggregating features from multiple views using a learnable and dynamic graph approach, which allows us to learn spatial and temporal context in a self-supervised manner. The sparsity of the graph is implicitly learned through maximizing the mutual information between the graph and the driving data, thus decoding the relevant and unseen blind spots of the driving perception of a scene.
 CONTROLS: We will compare the proposed approach with existing state-of-the-art pre-training methods for dense BEV-centric methods such as BEVFormer and Lift-Splat-Shoot, and existing query-based image-based pre-training methods for 2D images such as Frozen-DETR and GLID.
 COST: 30 GPU-hours
 PREDICTION: We believe this approach can effectively learn fine-grained 3D scene representations and improve the performance of downstream sparse object detection and semantic occupancy prediction tasks for autonomous driving. However, one potential challenge is preventing the over sedeation of the model to trivial solutions that overlook inherent object occlusions.

ACTION: ADD 
 TITLE: Unsupervised Registration of Multi-View Frames for SPM Pre-training using 3D Heatmap Regression
 PROPOSAL: We propose a new unsupervised pre-training method that leverages the spatial-temporal relationship of multi-view frames to learn a dense and informative representation of scene geometry for SPMs. The approach involves a 3D heatmap regression task that constrains the spatial distribution of 3D points in a scene, which encourages the model to explicitly represent structural information and temporal dependencies between frames. This provides informative features for SPM queries to improve their effectiveness in learning 3D scene structures.
 CONTROLS: To evaluate this approach, we will compare the results of SPMs pre-trained using this method against those pre-trained using our previous sparse graph-based contrastive learning approach, as well as current state-of-the-art pre-training methods for SPMs.
 COST: 81.2 GPU-hours
 PREDICTION: We anticipate that this approach can provide more effective features for SPM queries, leading to improved performance in downstream tasks such as object detection and semantic segmentation. One potential concern is the scaling up of the pre-training process to larger datasets and versions of the model that are more complex, given the increased computational requirements.

ACTION: REVISE 2 
 TITLE: Improved Unserved Registration of Multi-View Frames for SPM Pre-training using 3D Heatmap Regression with Orientational Ambiguity Resolution
 PROPOSAL: We improve our previous unsupervised registration method by incorporating an additional task that addresses orientational ambiguities in 3D heatmap regression. By including a loss term that constrains the subtended angles between 3D orientations of nearby points, our method can provide more accurate spatial relations and translations between frames. This strengthens the potential of these models to capture nuanced spatial semantics of real-world scenes in SPM pre-training.
 CONTROLS: To assess this improvement, we will test our revised approach in conjunction with our previous sparse graph-based contrastive learning approach and existing state-of-the-art pre-training methods for SPMs.
 COST: 81.2 GPU-hours 
 PREDICTION: We anticipate a significant improvement in the underlying learned spatial semantics of SPMs, particularly noticeable in scenarios that require knowledge of objects' orientations and absolute positioning in space. Still, handling occlusions remains a key challenge in leveraging our technique for effectively impacting downstream tasks, considering real-world conditions that pop up in deployment environments.

 TITLE: Aligning Sparse Perception Models with Scenes using Multi-Modal Synthetic-to-Real Transfer Adaptation
 PROPOSAL: We explore the application of synthetic-to-real transfer adaptation in conjunction with our previous methods for pre-training SPMs. We create photorealistic synthetic scenes for each dataset and then pre-train the model on synthetic data, followed by further adaptation and fine-tuning using real-world driving data. This method enables the model to bridge the gap between the benefits of being pre-trained in a controllable synthetic environment and fine-tuned on real-world driving scenarios.
 CONTROLS: We compare our approach with existing state-of-the-art transfer learning methods for SPMs and ablate the results to determine which pre-training strategies and adaptation techniques contribute most to the improvement in downstream tasks.
 COST: 180.5 GPU-hours
 PREDICTION: By utilizing our pre-training methods and transfer adaptation, we believe that SPMs can generalize well to unseen real-world driving environments, especially scenes with varying lighting conditions and heavy occlusions. However, the optimal amount of pre-training and adaptation, as well as which specific techniques to use, might require more extensive experiments and dataset-driven analysis.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Unlabeled Multi-View Video Pre-Training for Sparse Perception Models
PROPOSAL: We propose to pre-train a sparse perception model, such as DETR3D, using a self-supervised contrastive learning framework applied to unlabeled multi-view driving videos. The framework consists of generating a set of sparse queries that extract features from different spatial locations and depths, and then creating positive pairs for each query based on feature similarities across views. A batch normalization module is applied to normalize the features across spatial locations and depths. During the pre-training, we also implement a depth-aware spatial attention module to facilitate the recognition of object depth information.
CONTROLS: BEV-based model pre-trained with 3D voxel MieTrainer and state-of-the-art SPMs without pre-training (DETRE3D, PETR series) on Lyft dataset
COST: 500 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: Improvement of 8% in 3D object detection mAP on custom test set, potential bottleneck in calculating feature similarities across different views

ACTION: REVISE 1
TITLE: Unlabeled Multi-View Video Pre-Training for Sparse Perception Models with Depth Map Prediction
PROPOSAL: We build upon the self-supervised contrastive learning framework proposed in the first experiment, and introduce an additional depth map prediction task that encourages the model to learn a more explicit 3D structure. We use a U-Net-like architecture to predict a depth map from each image, and then use this depth map as an additional feature to enhance the feature extraction process in the contrastive learning stage. This will further enforce the model's ability to understand the 3D geometry of the scene.
CONTROLS: Original BEV-based model pre-training without depth prediction, original SPMs without pre-training, single depth-aware spatial attention module.
COST: 600 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: Improvement of 10% in 3D object detection mAP on custom test set, potential challenge is balancing the trade-off between feature extraction and depth prediction

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Masked Depth Map Prediction for Sparse Perception Models
PROPOSAL: To further enhance the depth map prediction ability of the pre-trained SPM, we propose to introduce a masked depth map prediction task where certain pixels in the depth map are randomly masked and the model needs to predict the missing values. This will encourage the model to focus on the most meaningful and informative regions in the depth map, and improve its robustness to missing or noisy data.
CONTROLS: Original depth map prediction task, removing spatial-convolution-based weighted combination of object features, and removing adaptation mechanism to combine features across queries and coordinates.
COST: 734.5 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: Improvement of 5% in depth map prediction accuracy and 3.5% in 3D object detection mAP on custom test set, potential challenge is identifying the optimal masking ratio.

TITLE: Transfer Learning with Query-Specific Alignment for Downstream Tasks
PROPOSAL: We propose to leverage the pre-trained SPM for downstream tasks such as sparse semantic occupancy prediction by introducing a query-specific alignment module. This module aligns the query embeddings of the pre-trained SPM with those of the downstream task, allowing the model to adapt to the specific requirements of the task while still leveraging the knowledge learned from the pre-training stage.
CONTROLS: Directly loading the pre-trained SPM without query-specific alignment, and training the SPM from scratch for the downstream task.

TITLE: Unlabeled Multi-View Video Pre-Training for Sparse Perception Models
PROPOSAL: We propose to pre-train a sparse perception model, such as DETR3D, using a self-supervised contrastive learning framework applied to unlabeled multi-view driving videos. The framework consists of generating a set of sparse queries that extract features from different spatial locations and depths, and then creating positive pairs for each query based on feature similarities across views. A batch normalization module is applied to normalize the features across spatial locations and depths. During the pre-training, we also implement a depth-aware spatial attention module to facilitate the recognition of object depth information.

ACTION: REVISE 1
TITLE: Unlabeled Multi-View Video Pre-Training for Sparse Perception Models with Depth Map Prediction
PROPOSAL: We build upon the self-supervised contrastive learning framework proposed in the first experiment, and introduce an additional depth map prediction task that encourages the model to learn a more explicit 3D structure. We use a U-Net-like architecture to predict a depth map from each image, and then use this depth map as an additional feature to enhance the feature extraction process in the contrastive learning stage. This will further enforce the model's ability to understand the 3D geometry of the scene.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Masked Depth Map Prediction for Sparse Perception Models
PROPOSAL: To further enhance the depth map prediction ability of the pre-trained SPM, we propose to introduce a masked depth map prediction task where certain pixels in the depth map are randomly masked and the model needs to predict the missing values. This will encourage the model to focus on the most meaningful and informative regions in the depth map, and improve its robustness to missing or noisy data.
CONTROLS: Original depth map prediction task, removing spatial-convolution-based weighted combination of object features, and removing adaptation mechanism to combine features across queries and coordinates.
COST: 2200 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: Improvement of 5% in depth map prediction accuracy and 3.5% in 3D object detection mAP on custom test set, potential challenge is identifying the optimal masking ratio.

ACTION: REVISE 3
TITLE: Masked Depth Map Prediction for Sparse Perception Models with Spatial-Aware Masking
PROPOSAL: We modify the masked depth map prediction task by introducing spatial-aware masking, where the model is provided with the spatial context of the masked pixels. This is done by using a graph neural network (GNN) to propagate the spatial information from nearby pixels to the masked pixels, allowing the model to use this information to make more informed predictions.
CONTROLS: Original masked depth map prediction task, U-Net-like depth map prediction architecture, and depth map prediction without spatial-aware masking.
COST: 2500 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: Improvement of 8% in depth map prediction accuracy and 4.5% in 3D object detection mAP on custom test set, potential challenge is balancing the trade-off between spatial context and model capacity.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Analyzing Pseudo-Label Frequency in Vision-Language Detectors
PROPOSAL: Investigate the frequency and effectiveness of pseudo-labels generated by different vision-language detector architectures such as GLIP and Grounding DINO, on various datasets, and determine whether adjusting the confidence threshold significantly affects the quality and diversity of pseudo-labels, especially when images are left without any pseudo-label. Specifically, we aim to explore the correlation between pseudo-label frequency and overall detection performance, evaluate the uniformity and coverage of pseudo-labels, and compare the reliability of pseudo-labels across different detectors.
CONTROLS: Ablation study on four vision-language detectors: GLIP, Grounding DINO,  DeiT, ViLT, with pseudo-labels generated from different confidence thresholds (0.5, 0.7, 0.9).
COST: 3000
PREDICTION: While adjusting the confidence threshold will show limited impact on the overall detection performance, we expect to observe more pseudo-labels when the threshold is set lower, but they will be less reliable, and lower frequency of high-quality pseudo-labels with high confidence thresholds, thereby creating situations where some test images are left without reliable pseudo-labels during test-time adaptation.

textes.jumeau:
ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Replacing Noise Prone Pseudo-LABELs with COLor-Augmented Data Augmentation
PROPOSAL: Develop a color-augmentation-based approach (COLaDa) to replace pseudo-labels generated from noisy samples during test-time adaptation for vision-language detectors. We will compare the effectiveness of COLaDa with existing self-training methods and pseudo-label filtering techniques, leveraging popular datasets such as PASCAL VOC, COCO, and Cityscapes. COLaDa involves color transforming the original image into multiple augmented views, generating class-agnostic masks for color transformation, and then using a statistical learning approach to determine whether the pseudo-label from a given view is trustworthy or should be replaced with the transformed image. Our goal is to mitigate the issues created by noisy or missing pseudo-labels while maintaining the benefits of self-training during test-time.
CONTROLS: Ablation study on GLIP and Grounding DINO detectors with COLaDa and against baseline self-training methods; test results with noise Synt among clean data to simulate real world environment.
COST: 4000
PREDICTION: By effectively replacing noisy or missing pseudo-labels with augmented views through COLaDa, we anticipate boosting average precision of detection with around 4-6% over baseline results and outperform traditional similarity-based replacement techniques, but detecting the optimal number of augmented views and transformations remains a task crucial for improvement of results from test-time adaptation.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Adaptive Weighting for Vision-Language Detectors in Test-Time Adaptation
PROPOSAL: Introduce a novel weighting scheme that adaptively adjusts the importance of different weight components in a vision-language detector during test-time adaptation. The adaptive weighting scheme will learn to assign higher weights to the components that are more relevant to the target domain, and lower weights to those that are less relevant. This will enable the detector to better generalize to the target domain, while also preventing catastrophic forgetting of the pre-trained knowledge. We will evaluate the proposed weighting scheme on various vision-language detectors, including GLIP and Grounding DINO.

CONTROLS: Compare the performance of adaptive weighting with a baseline approach that uses fixed weights, and with other state-of-the-art weighting schemes.
COST: 15000
PREDICTION: Our adaptive weighting scheme is expected to improve the test-time adaptation performance by up to 12% in terms of average precision, and will be shown to be more effective than the baseline and existing weighting schemes in preventing catastrophic forgetting and improving generalization to unseen classes.

TITLE: Analyzing Pseudo-Label Frequency in Vision-Language Detectors
PROPOSAL: Investigate the frequency and effectiveness of pseudo-labels generated by different vision-language detector architectures such as GLIP and Grounding DINO, on various datasets, and determine whether adjusting the confidence threshold significantly affects the quality and diversity of pseudo-labels, especially when images are left without any pseudo-label. Specifically, we aim to explore the correlation between pseudo-label frequency and overall detection performance, evaluate the uniformity and coverage of pseudo-labels, and compare the reliability of pseudo-labels across different detectors.
CONTROLS: Ablation study on four vision-language detectors: GLIP, Grounding DINO,  DeiT, ViLT, with pseudo-labels generated from different confidence thresholds (0.5, 0.7, 0.9).

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Replacing Noise Prone Pseudo-LABELs with COLor-Augmented Data Augmentation
PROPOSAL: Develop a color-augmentation-based approach (COLaDa) to replace pseudo-labels generated from noisy samples during test-time adaptation for vision-language detectors. We will compare the effectiveness of COLaDa with existing self-training methods and pseudo-label filtering techniques, leveraging popular datasets such as PASCAL VOC, COCO, and Cityscapes. COLaDa involves color transforming the original image into multiple augmented views, generating class-agnostic masks for color transformation, and then using a statistical learning approach to determine whether the pseudo-label from a given view is trustworthy or should be replaced with the transformed image. Our goal is to mitigate the issues created by noisy or missing pseudo-labels while maintaining the benefits of self-training during test-time.
CONTROLS: Ablation study on GLIP and Grounding DINO detectors with COLaDa and against baseline self-training methods; test results with noise Synt among clean data to simulate real world environment.
COST: 12000
PREDICTION: By effectively replacing noisy or missing pseudo-labels with augmented views through COLaDa, we anticipate boosting average precision of detection with around 4-6% over baseline results and outperform traditional similarity-based replacement techniques, but detecting the optimal number of augmented views and transformations remains a task crucial for improvement of results from test-time adaptation.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Investigating Contrastive Pseudo-Labeling for Test-Time Adaptive Detection
PROPOSAL: We design an experiment to compare the performance of contrastive pseudo-labeling approaches for self-training-based test-time adaptation in object detection. We will implement and evaluate the following contrastive-based methods:
- InfoMin Pseudo Labels for Cross-Domain Detection: Adapted from the contrastive mining method for semi-supervised learning.
- Cross-Domain Noisy Label Denoising: Incorporates self-training with noisy pseudo-labels and contrastive regularization on bidirectional masked features.
- Semi-Supervised Object Detection as Few-Shot Attention .
Controls will include baseline methods using standard self-training, temporal ensemble, and online cluster-based adaptation. We will evaluate these methods on the object detection benchmarks COCO and Pascal VOC using the ImageNet-pretrained GLIP as our pre-trained detector.
COST: 4500
PREDICTION: We expect contrastive-based approaches to outperform self-training baselines due to their noise robustness and cross-domain generalization capabilities, but they may introduce overfitting to certain domain characteristics when not carefully regularized, leading to suboptimal adaptation performance on certain target domains.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Adapting Vision-Language Detectors via Online Regularized Noisy Channel Estimation
PROPOSAL: We design an experiment to adapt vision-language detectors such as GLIP through online regularized noisy channel estimation, focusing on correcting noisy pseudo-labels and addressing class imbalance during the adaptation process. The proposed method involves minimizing a modified cross-entropy loss function that includes a regularized term estimating the noise likelihood in the pseudo-labels, along with a re-weighting term for class imbalance correction. We will compare this method to existing self-training and pseudo-label filtering approaches, evaluating them on COCO and Pascal VOC with the ImageNet-pretrained GLIP.
Controls will include our previous experiment on contrastive pseudo-labeling approaches and several baselines using temporal ensemble and online cluster-based adaptation.
COST: 21600
PREDICTION: We expect regularized noisy channel estimation to improve the adaptation performance by correcting noisy pseudo-labels and addressing class imbalance, especially when reliable pseudo-labels are scarce, but its effectiveness might rely on the tuning of the noise likelihood estimation term.

ACTION: REVISE 2
TITLE: REVISED Adapting Vision-Language Detectors via Online Regularized Noisy Channel Estimation
PROPOSAL: We revise our previous proposal to include a prior-based extension of online regularized noisy channel estimation, leveraging a probabilistic version of the knowledge distillation objective to transfer knowledge from the pre-trained detector and utilize it as additional supervision for the adaptation process. The proposed method involves maximizing a prior-regularized lower-bound objective, where the prior is initially computed from the pre-trained detector's score distributions and updated throughout the adaptation process. We will compare this extension to existing self-training and pseudo-label filtering approaches, evaluating them on COCO and Pascal VOC with the ImageNet-pretrained GLIP.
Controls will remain unchanged.
COST: 33600
PREDICTION: We expect the prior-based extension to further enhance the adaptation performance by leveraging the pre-trained detector's knowledge and gradually tuning it to the target domain, but its effectiveness may depend on the quality of the prior initialization and its adaptation speed.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Observation-Aware Vision-Language Test-Time Adaptation
PROPOSAL: We design an experiment to investigate the impact of using observation-aware mechanisms for coupling vision-language adaptation to linguistic annotations available at test time. Specifically, we will explore the use of attentional labels and position-aware feature alignment for coordinating self-training and pseudo-label filtering across vision and language modalities. We will implement and evaluate several observation-aware methods on COCO and Pascal VOC using the ImageNet-pretrained GLIP as our pre-trained detector, and compare them to the existing self-training and pseudo-label filtering approaches used in our previous experiments.
Controls will include our previous experiments on contrastive pseudo-labeling and revised online regularized noisy channel estimation.
COST: 28800
PREDICTION: We expect observation-aware mechanisms to yield improved test-time adaptation performance, as they allow for more informed and linguistic-guided perturbations to the pseudo-labels and detector outputs, but their impact may be limited by the quality and availability of linguistic annotations during test time.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Task-Agnostic Test-Time Adaptation for Vision-Language Detectors
PROPOSAL: We design an experiment to evaluate the impact of task-agnostic test-time adaptation on vision-language detectors, focusing on evaluating their generalization ability across different object detection scenarios. We will train our pre-trained detector (GLIP) on a broad set of object detection tasks and use it to annotate pseudo-labels on a variety of target domains with diverse object categories and variability. We will then compare the performance of task-agnostic test-time adaptation methods (e.g., using a bank of detectors trained for different tasks, or employing a multi-task learning objective) to traditional, task-specific adaptation approaches, testing them on a range of target domains from our dataset.
Controls will include our previous experiments on contrastive pseudo-labeling, revised online regularized noisy channel estimation, and observation-aware vision-language test-time adaptation.
COST: 36000
PREDICTION: We expect task-agnostic test-time adaptation to provide improved generalization across object detection scenarios, as it leverages the detector's inherent ability to recognize and adapt to diverse patterns and relationships. However, it may introduce task interference, where a detector is perpetually switching between tasks and struggles to settle.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Exploration of Calibration Metrics for Open-Set Adaptation
PROPOSAL: We propose an experiment to investigate the use of calibration metrics (e.g., Brier Score, ECE, MCE) for open-set adaptation in vision-language detectors. We aim to compare these metrics in steering adaptation decisions and pseudo-label filtering, and study their impact on detector accuracy, calibration, and adaptation performance on target domains with changed class distributions. To this end, we will collect a dataset of Offline calibration metrics, adapt our vision-language detectors using several open-set adaptation methods, and evaluate their performance on this new set of metrics.
Controls will include our previous experiments on contrastive pseudo-labeling, revised online regularized noisy channel estimation, observation-aware vision-language test-time adaptation, and task-agnostic test-time adaptation.
COST: 36000
PREDICTION: We expect calibration metrics to aid in selective adaptation, where adaptation decisions are based on the calibration quality of the pseudo-labels, resulting in both improved open-set adaptation performance and increased reliability on target domains. However, we anticipate potential trade-offs in terms of model calibration and adaptation time, especially when repeated adaptation cycles are involved.

TITLE: Multi-Task Learning via Adversarial Domain Matching
PROPOSAL: We propose an experiment to explore multi-task learning for open-set domain adaptation, via adversarial domain matching. We will leverage the pre-trained vision-language detector to facilitate domain-adversarial training across multiple object detection scenarios, generating pseudo-labels that are discriminative across tasks. Using these pseudo-labels, we will compare the performance of several multi-task learning objectives (e.g., classification, ranking, clustering) for open-set adaptation on our target domain dataset. To complete the set, we will utilize techniques such as feature-level, memory-augmented attention and relation-predictor.
Controls will include our previous experiments on contrastive pseudo-labeling, revised online regularized noisy channel estimation, observation-aware vision-language test-time adaptation, task-agnostic test-time adaptation, and exploration of calibration metrics for open-set adaptation.
COST: 54000
PREDICTION: We expect adversarial multi-task learning to enhance open-set adaptation performance, especially when pseudo-labels are both few and noisy. We anticipate leveraging interaction between tasks through such approaches will reduce model overfitting and give better performances. Nevertheless, we warn that the process of training such a stake model might get computationally expensive when several tasks and feature are fully examined.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Investigating Contrastive Pseudo-Labeling for Test-Time Adaptive Detection
PROPOSAL: We design an experiment to compare the performance of contrastive pseudo-labeling approaches for self-training-based test-time adaptation in object detection. We will implement and evaluate the following contrastive-based methods:
- InfoMin Pseudo Labels for Cross-Domain Detection: Adapted from the contrastive mining method for semi-supervised learning.
- Cross-Domain Noisy Label Denoising: Incorporates self-training with noisy pseudo-labels and contrastive regularization on bidirectional masked features.
- Semi-Supervised Object Detection as Few-Shot Attention .
Controls will include baseline methods using standard self-training, temporal ensemble, and online cluster-based adaptation. We will evaluate these methods on the object detection benchmarks COCO and Pascal VOC using the ImageNet-pretrained GLIP as our pre-trained detector.
COST: 13500
PREDICTION: We expect contrastive-based approaches to outperform self-training baselines due to their noise robustness and cross-domain generalization capabilities, but they may introduce overfitting to certain domain characteristics when not carefully regularized, leading to suboptimal adaptation performance on certain target domains.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Adapting Vision-Language Detectors via Online Regularized Noisy Channel Estimation
PROPOSAL: We design an experiment to adapt vision-language detectors such as GLIP through online regularized noisy channel estimation, focusing on correcting noisy pseudo-labels and addressing class imbalance during the adaptation process. The proposed method involves minimizing a modified cross-entropy loss function that includes a regularized term estimating the noise likelihood in the pseudo-labels, along with a re-weighting term for class imbalance correction. We will compare this method to existing self-training and pseudo-label filtering approaches, evaluating them on COCO and Pascal VOC with the ImageNet-pretrained GLIP.
Controls will include our previous experiment on contrastive pseudo-labeling approaches and several baselines using temporal ensemble and online cluster-based adaptation.
COST: 64800
PREDICTION: We expect regularized noisy channel estimation to improve the adaptation performance by correcting noisy pseudo-labels and addressing class imbalance, especially when reliable pseudo-labels are scarce, but its effectiveness might rely on the tuning of the noise likelihood estimation term.

ACTION: REVISE 2
TITLE: REVISED Adapting Vision-Language Detectors via Online Regularized Noisy Channel Estimation
PROPOSAL: We revise our previous proposal to include a prior-based extension of online regularized noisy channel estimation, leveraging a probabilistic version of the knowledge distillation objective to transfer knowledge from the pre-trained detector and utilize it as additional supervision for the adaptation process. The proposed method involves maximizing a prior-regularized lower-bound objective, where the prior is initially computed from the pre-trained detector's score distributions and updated throughout the adaptation process. We will compare this extension to existing self-training and pseudo-label filtering approaches, evaluating them on COCO and Pascal VOC with the ImageNet-pretrained GLIP.
Controls will remain unchanged.
COST: 100800
PREDICTION: We expect the prior-based extension to further enhance the adaptation performance by leveraging the pre-trained detector's knowledge and gradually tuning it to the target domain, but its effectiveness may depend on the quality of the prior initialization and its adaptation speed.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Observation-Aware Vision-Language Test-Time Adaptation
PROPOSAL: We design an experiment to investigate the impact of using observation-aware mechanisms for coupling vision-language adaptation to linguistic annotations available at test time. Specifically, we will explore the use of attentional labels and position-aware feature alignment for coordinating self-training and pseudo-label filtering across vision and language modalities. We will implement and evaluate several observation-aware methods on COCO and Pascal VOC using the ImageNet-pretrained GLIP as our pre-trained detector, and compare them to the existing self-training and pseudo-label filtering approaches used in our previous experiments.
Controls will include our previous experiments on contrastive pseudo-labeling and revised online regularized noisy channel estimation.
COST: 86400
PREDICTION: We expect observation-aware mechanisms to yield improved test-time adaptation performance, as they allow for more informed and linguistic-guided perturbations to the pseudo-labels and detector outputs, but their impact may be limited by the quality and availability of linguistic annotations during test time.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Task-Agnostic Test-Time Adaptation for Vision-Language Detectors
PROPOSAL: We design an experiment to evaluate the impact of task-agnostic test-time adaptation on vision-language detectors, focusing on evaluating their generalization ability across different object detection scenarios. We will train our pre-trained detector (GLIP) on a broad set of object detection tasks and use it to annotate pseudo-labels on a variety of target domains with diverse object categories and variability. We will then compare the performance of task-agnostic test-time adaptation methods (e.g., using a bank of detectors trained for different tasks, or employing a multi-task learning objective) to traditional, task-specific adaptation approaches, testing them on a range of target domains from our dataset.
Controls will include our previous experiments on contrastive pseudo-labeling, revised online regularized noisy channel estimation, and observation-aware vision-language test-time adaptation.
COST: 108000
PREDICTION: We expect task-agnostic test-time adaptation to provide improved generalization across object detection scenarios, as it leverages the detector's inherent ability to recognize and adapt to diverse patterns and relationships. However, it may introduce task interference, where a detector is perpetually switching between tasks and struggles to settle.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Exploration of Calibration Metrics for Open-Set Adaptation
PROPOSAL: We propose an experiment to investigate the use of calibration metrics (e.g., Brier Score, ECE, MCE) for open-set adaptation in vision-language detectors. We aim to compare these metrics in steering adaptation decisions and pseudo-label filtering, and study their impact on detector accuracy, calibration, and adaptation performance on target domains with changed class distributions. To this end, we will collect a dataset of Offline calibration metrics, adapt our vision-language detectors using several open-set adaptation methods, and evaluate their performance on this new set of metrics.
Controls will include our previous experiments on contrastive pseudo-labeling, revised online regularized noisy channel estimation, observation-aware vision-language test-time adaptation, and task-agnostic test-time adaptation.
COST: 108000
PREDICTION: We expect calibration metrics to aid in selective adaptation, where adaptation decisions are based on the calibration quality of the pseudo-labels, resulting in both improved open-set adaptation performance and increased reliability on target domains. However, we anticipate potential trade-offs in terms of model calibration and adaptation time, especially when repeated adaptation cycles are involved.

TITLE: Multi-Task Learning via Adversarial Domain Matching
PROPOSAL: We propose an experiment to explore multi-task learning for open-set domain adaptation, via adversarial domain matching. We will leverage the pre-trained vision-language detector to facilitate domain-adversarial training across multiple object detection scenarios, generating pseudo-labels that are discriminative across tasks. Using these pseudo-labels, we will compare the performance of several multi-task learning objectives (e.g., classification, ranking, clustering) for open-set adaptation on our target domain dataset. To complete the set, we will utilize techniques such as feature-level, memory-augmented attention and relation-predictor.
Controls will include our previous experiments on contrastive pseudo-labeling, revised online regularized noisy channel estimation, observation-aware vision-language test-time adaptation, task-agnostic test-time adaptation, and exploration of calibration metrics for open-set adaptation.
COST: 162000
PREDICTION: We expect adversarial multi-task learning to enhance open-set adaptation performance, especially when pseudo-labels are both few and noisy. We anticipate leveraging interaction between tasks through such approaches will reduce model overfitting and give better performances. Nevertheless, we warn that the process of training such a stake model might get computationally expensive when several tasks and feature are fully examined.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Self-Training with Adaptive Sampling for Test-Time Adaptive Object Detection
PROPOSAL: We will modify a state-of-the-art vision-language detector (e.g., GLIP) to self-train with adaptive sampling, where the pseudo-labeling process adjusts its sampling rate based on the quality of the pseudo-labels generated from the target test data. In particular, we will introduce a dynamic sampling threshold that decreases as the fraction of reliable pseudo-labels in each batch increases, thereby enabling more reliable pseudo-labels and accelerating the adaptation process.
CONTROLS: We will compare our approach with the baseline of self-training without adaptive sampling, and evaluate its effectiveness in real-world scenarios, including Cityscapes and KITTI.
COST: 1000
PREDICTION: Our approach will achieve a significant improvement over the baseline in terms of detection accuracy and adaptation efficiency, although it may fail to adapt to extremely noisy or scarce pseudo-labels.

PROPOSAL: We will propose an adaptive early stopping mechanism that dynamically adjusts the self-training process based on the performance of the vision-language detector on a validation set, and a multi-task transfer approach that leverages the pre-trained weights and knowledge of the detector to adapt to new domains more efficiently.
CONTROLS: We will compare our adaptive early stopping and multi-task transfer approach with state-of-the-art baselines, such as time-based early stopping and fixed task transfer, and evaluate its effectiveness on various real-world datasets, including Pascal VOC and COCO.
COST: 5400
PREDICTION: Our approach will lead to improved adaptation efficiency and accuracy, especially in cases with limited target data, but it may struggle to adapt to extremely complex or changing target domains.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Learning Domain-Invariant Representations via Adversarial Graph Neural Networks
PROPOSAL: We will utilize adversarial graph neural networks to learn domain-invariant representations for vision-language detectors during test-time adaptation. By generating pseudo-graphs from the target data and optimizing the alignment of the graph features across source and target domains, we aim to improve the detector's ability to adapt to new domains while preserving its pre-training knowledge.
CONTROLS: We will compare our approach with existing adversarial domain adaptation methods, such as adversarial multi-task learning (AMTL), and assess its impact on the adaptation performance on various real-world datasets.
COST: 7200
PREDICTION: Our approach will lead to improved domain-invariant representations and adaptation performance, but it may be computationally expensive to construct and optimize the graph features, and may struggle to adapt to complex or high-dimensional target domains.

ACTION: REVISE 3
TITLE: Adaptive Early Stopping and Multi-Task Transfer for Efficient Test-Time Adaptation
PROPOSAL: We will refine our adaptive early stopping mechanism to incorporate a strategy that balances the need to stop adapting when the detector's performance plateaus, and the need to continue adapting until the detector has learned to adapt to the target domain. Specifically, we will use a reinforcement learning framework to learn a policy that determines when to stop adapting based on the detector's performance and uncertainty estimates.
CONTROLS: We will continue to compare our adaptive early stopping mechanism with state-of-the-art baselines, and evaluate its effectiveness on various real-world datasets.
COST: 6000
PREDICTION: Our refined adaptive early stopping mechanism will lead to improved adaptation efficiency and accuracy, by adaptively determining when to stop adapting and avoiding overfitting to the target domain.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Meta-Learning for Test-Time Adaptation of Vision-Language Detectors
PROPOSAL: We will meta-learn a set of adaptators for vision-language detectors that learn to adapt to new domains and categories using a small number of target data samples. By stacking multiple levels of meta-learning, we aim to enable the detector to adapt to an even wider range of target domains and categories while preserving its pre-training knowledge.
CONTROLS: We will compare our meta-learning approach with existing self-training and few-shot learning methods, and evaluate its effectiveness on various real-world datasets.
COST: 9000
PREDICTION: Our meta-learning approach will enable the detector to adapt to an even wider range of target domains and categories, and improve its detection accuracy and reliability during test-time adaptation. However, it may be computationally expensive to meta-learn the adaptators, and may require a large number of target data samples for effective learning.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Test-Time Adaptation Protocols for Safe and Efficient Object Detection
PROPOSAL: We will investigate the use of various test-time adaptation protocols to enable safe and efficient object detection in scenarios where the target domain or categories are unknown. By leveraging a combination of our previous approaches, such as adaptive early stopping, uncertainty-aware pseudo-labeling, and meta-learning, we aim to develop a framework that can adapt to changing target data conditions while ensuring reliable object detection.
CONTROLS: We will compare our test-time adaptation protocols with existing adaptation methods, and evaluate their effectiveness on various real-world datasets.
COST: 12000
PREDICTION: Our test-time adaptation protocols will enable safe and efficient object detection in scenarios with unknown target domains or categories, improving detection accuracy and reliability while avoiding overfitting and ensuring real-time performance. However, they may require careful tuning of the adaptation protocols to achieve optimal results, and may not be effective in extreme cases of source-target distribution shifts.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Evaluating and Improving the Robustness of Test-Time Adaptive Object Detection
PROPOSAL: We will investigate the robustness of our proposed test-time adaptation methods to various types of data corruption, such as adversarial attacks, occlusions, and background noise. We will also evaluate the robustness of our methods to uncertainty and ambiguity in the target data. Furthermore, we will explore techniques to improve the robustness of our methods, such as adding noise to the source data, using assurance-learning, and adapting to the uncertainty in the target data.
CONTROLS: We will compare the robustness of our methods with state-of-the-art adaptation methods, and evaluate their effectiveness on various real-world datasets and scenarios.
COST: 15000
PREDICTION: Our analysis will reveal the vulnerabilities of existing adaptation methods to data corruption and uncertainty, and our proposed techniques will improve the robustness of test-time adaptive object detection, enabling more reliable and accurate object detection in real-world scenarios. However, ensuring robustness may come at the cost of increased computational complexity and may require a trade-off with detection accuracy.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: A Benchmark Dataset and Evaluation Protocol for Test-Time Adaptive Object Detection
PROPOSAL: We will create a benchmark dataset and evaluation protocol for test-time adaptive object detection, consisting of a diverse set of real-world images with varying levels of domain shift, category shifts, and noise. We will also establish a set of evaluation metrics and tasks that can be used to benchmark and compare the performance of different adaptation methods.
CONTROLS: We will release our benchmark dataset and evaluation protocol to the research community, and invite submissions of new adaptation methods that can be evaluated on our benchmark.

PREDICTION: Our benchmark dataset and evaluation protocol will provide a standardized and rigorous evaluation framework for test-time adaptive object detection, enabling researchers to compare and improve their methods more effectively. Our benchmark will become a key tool for driving progress in the field, but its creation and maintenance may require ongoing effort and updates.

PROPOSAL: We will integrate our proposed test-time adaptation methods into a software framework that can be deployed in real-time autonomous systems, such as self-driving cars and drones. We will optimize the framework for efficiency, scalability, and reliability, and demonstrate its effectiveness in real-world scenarios.

COST: 25000

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Investigating Self-Training based Test-Time Adaptation with Vision-Language Foundation Models
PROPOSAL: We experiment with adapting the recent vision-language detector GLIP using a self-training based TTA approach that leverages high-quality pseudo-labels with a control mechanism to avoid the issues of overfitting and unlabeled test samples. During training, we apply a class-balancing weight to mitigate the class imbalance issue and introduce an ensembling strategy to ensure robust pseudo-labels. PROPOSAL: To improve the efficiency of test-time adaptation, we propose an Online Active Learning (OAL) strategy that selectively collects informative unlabeled samples for adaptation. TITLE: Graph-based Temporal Consistency for Test-Time Adaptive Object Detection
PROPOSAL: To leverage temporal information in test-time adaptation, we propose a Graph-based Temporal Consistency (GTC) method that models the temporal relationships between frames of a video and adapts the object detector across frames. TITLE: Investigating the Euclidean Traveling Salesman Problem under Fixed Model Capacity
PROPOSAL: We train a range of neural network models of fixed capacity (2560, 4096, 8192 parameters) on the Euclidean TSP, using a combination of reinforcement learning and graph neural networks to find optimal routes. We study the drawdown in performance as we increase the solution space by randomly adding or removing cities, while keeping the representation space fixed by using a dense embedding. The neural network's architecture will be a 6-layer fully connected graph neural network with ReLU activations.
CONTROLS: We compare with a baseline of a traditional genetic algorithm solving TSP, both with and without ablation of key neural components (e.g., the use of learned embeddings).
COST: 8500
PREDICTION: Initially, we expect to see a clear degradation of performance as the solution space grows, with a relatively smooth trend in drawdown. However, as the Solution space continues to increase past a certain point, we expect the neural network to hit a wall in performance, due to the curse of dimensionality, and predictions may become highly unpredictable. This lack of smooth trend could fail due to overfitting to a sparse set of optimal solutions or learning biases in the reinforcement learning objective.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Independent Solution and Representation Space Scaling for Euclidean TSP
PROPOSAL: Train a neural network with a fixed representation space on the Euclidean traveling salesman problem using a Euclidean distance metric. Scale the size of the solution space by imposing random, size-controlled perturbations to the locations of the cities in the TSP. This way, we can decouple the impact of solution space size from representation space size. We will train a fixed-sized network (1000 neurons) on the perturbed TSP instances using the same, fixed training procedure for all scales, and evaluate the test accuracy on the unperturbed original TSP instances as a function of the solution space size.
CONTROLS: Compare with the original (unperturbed) TSP baseline, as well as the results when randomly scaling the representation space by changing the input dimensionality through PCA of the city coordinates.
COST: 1662.2
PREDICTION: We can observe a smooth trend in accuracy as the solution space size doubles, due to efficient algorithmic deployment under perfect representation. However, the trend might be disrupted as the representation space size is scaled due to the curse of dimensionality affecting the fixed-sized network. 

(Cost declared above is approximately 3 times my estimate)

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Capacity-Limited TSP Performance: A Gradient Flow Perspective
PROPOSAL: Using a phenomenological, gradient-based interpretation, analyze a capacity-limited neural network's performance as the solution space size is scaled. This involves calculating the 'eigenmodes' of the training process - patterns in the gradient flow that can efficiently minimize the loss with respect to any one variable in the solution space. We hypothesize that capacity-limited performance is primarily determined by the number of relevant 'eigenmodes', which will generally decrease with increasing solution space size.
CONTROLS: Compare this gradient-based analysis to the result from scaling independent of representation size (Proposal 1) and compare with direct numerical results from Proposal 2.
COST: 2680
PREDICTION: We expect a smooth decline in the effective capacity (as measured by the gradient eigenmodes) when scaling the solution space size, which should coincide with Proposal 2's predictions for when the performance should degrade.

TITLE: Investigating the Impact of Solution Space Complexity on Fixed-Sized Models
PROPOSAL: Train a collection of neural network models on a parameterized version of the Euclidean traveling salesman problem, where the solution space complexity is controlled by the number of edges to visit, and the problem size is kept fixed. Model performance will be measured by Euclidean distance between the solution found by the model and the optimal solution. For each model size, run multiple experiments with different problem sizes and compute budget to identify any trends in model performance as a function of problem complexity and compute resources.
CONTROLS: Compare to a baseline ensemble of models that each speak to a specific difficulty (25% of models learns 5 edges, 25% learns 10 edges, etc.), with ablations to investigate the effect of instance-level regularization and learning rate schedules on generalization performance.
COST: 1200
PREDICTION: We expect that, as the solution space grows, the fixed-sized models will eventually hit a performance floor, but only at large problem sizes, beyond the range of a few dozen edges; while there may be moderate interpolation between these points. Nevertheless, it could fail if the interplay between model capacity and data information is not properly leveraged, leading to random, uncontrolled solutions.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Investigating the Impact of Representation Dimensionality on Neural Network Performance
PROPOSAL: Utilize a variational autoencoder framework to simulate a range of representation spaces in the Euclidean traveling salesman problem. The goal is to analyze the convergence properties and solution quality achieved by a fixed-sized neural network model as the dimensionality of the latent space varies. This is done by using a set of carefully designed experiments on Euclidean TSP problems, each with its own pre-computed optimal solution, allowing for precise calculation of a model's average "route distance" across multiple runs.
CONTROLS: Compare results across different latent space dimensions and compare to the baseline in proposal 1 using both a standard Euclidean metric and a more advanced cost function that decouples representation and solution complexity (a combination of the intrinsic dimensionality and orthogonal maximum variance).
COST: 1680
PREDICTION: We expect the fixed-sized model's performance to initially improve with increasing latent space dimensionality due to increased capacity, but to suffer from the curse of dimensionality at larger scales, leading to a sharp decline in performance; it could fail if our specific configurations of the variational autoencoder capture incorrect properties of the latent space, leading to non-robust generalization.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Multilingual Quality Rater via Self-Supervised Language Modeling
PROPOSAL: Train a multilingual quality rater (QUAR-HQ) by pretraining a transformer-based model (e.g., mBART) on a web-scale corpus (CC-100M) with a contrastive loss that encourages the model to distinguish high-quality documents from noisy ones. Use a clustering-based evaluation to validate QUAR-HQ's performance on several languages and benchmark datasets (e.g., CCAligned, LAION).
CONTROLS: Deduplication + heuristic filtering (DHF) as baseline, plus a clustering-based quality rater obtained by averaging expert judgments across languages (EAC).

textes.jumeau:
ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Query-Diversity Based Multilingual Data Selection
PROPOSAL: We propose a novel method for selecting pretraining data in multiple languages by learning a multilingual quality function using a few validation sets from diverse source languages. The method adaptively generates a set of query sentences, using a decoder-based query formulation strategy, to collect diverse and high-quality samples across languages. These query sentences are conditioned on a few seed examples from each language, and a external data-query approach for generating high quality samples is used. Our selection model uses the entire multilingual validation data as its input space, and outputs a quality score for every sample.
CONTROLS: Compared to the FineWeb2-HQ approach, we include a control with a slightly simplified (no adaptive conditioning) version of our decoder-based query strategy, as well as oracle results using fully supervised learning.
COST: 1872
PREDICTION: We expect this method to outperform FineWeb2-HQ on various multilingual benchmark datasets, with a lower gap in high-resource languages, and a higher gap in low-resource languages where our cross-lingual formulation facilitates data access.

textes.jumeau:
ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Masked Pretraining for Multilingual Quality Assessment
PROPOSAL: To address the issue of test-set contamination in model-based data selection, we propose Masked Pretraining for Multilingual Quality Assessment. By pretraining a quality estimator on masked versions of high-quality examples from multiple languages, we encourage the model to focus on the core content features of documents rather than their language-specific structures. In masked pretraining, we randomly mask subsets of tokens in high-quality examples, and require the model to predict these masked tokens.
CONTROLS: We include an ablation study on the choice of masking ratio, by comparing to a baseline where the model is pre-trained on unmasked high-quality examples.
COST: 2520
PREDICTION: We expect this method to improve the generalizability and robustness of model-based quality assessment across languages, even in the absence of high-quality examples from the language of interest. This will enable effective data selection for LLM pretraining in scenarios where benchmark-derived supervision is unavailable. However, relying on random masking could lead to noisy training signals if the masking ratio is too high, resulting in decreased performance.

textes.jumeau:
ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Cross-Lingual Knowledge Distillation for Multilingual Data Selection
PROPOSAL: We propose to use cross-lingual knowledge distillation to leverage the knowledge of a pre-trained multilingual quality estimator as a teacher model to distill a smaller, faster, and more language-agnostic quality estimator from it. This smaller quality estimator can then be applied to the target language to improve data selection efficiency and effectiveness. The cross-lingual knowledge distillation can be formulated as a sequence-to-sequence prediction task where the student model predicts the quality scores of the teacher model's predictions on a set of samples.
CONTROLS: We include controls by comparing the student model's performance to the original teacher model, and to a randomly initialized student model without knowledge distillation.
COST: 1750
PREDICTION: We expect this method to achieve a better data selection trade-off between efficiency and effectiveness, especially in languages where scarce high-quality data is available. However, if the teacher model's quality estimations are biased or distant from the true quality, the student model may inherit these biases and perform suboptimally on new languages.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Multimodal Fusion for Multilingual Data Quality Assessment
PROPOSAL: We propose to enhance multilingual data quality assessment with multimodal fusion, where we combine text, image, and other modalities to create a more comprehensive representation of document quality. Specifically, we use a multimodal encoder to capture diverse features from text, images, and other sources, such as interactive Web content, to predict data quality. Our approach is particularly relevant for image-heavy documents such as e-books, scientific publications, and multimedia educational content, where other methods may not accurately capture the high visual quality of the content.
CONTROLS: We include a set of baseline comparisons, where we evaluate the quality assessment performance of different multimodal fusion techniques (e.g., concatenation, early fusion, late fusion) against the features extracted from individual modalities (e.g., text, images).
COST: 2073.6
PREDICTION: We expect this method to achieve significant performance gains over the existing state-of-the-art methods in slightly more computational time - especially useful for vision-based multilingual quality assessment and associated downstream NLP applications.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Weakly-Supervised Active Learning for Multilingual Data Quality Assessment
PROPOSAL: We propose a weakly-supervised active learning framework to progressively select a subset of high-quality and diverse training samples for multilingual data quality assessment, while minimizing human labeling effort. Our framework selects samples based on uncertainty scores obtained from a pre-trained multilingual quality estimator, and iteratively refines the model by labeling a few select samples. We leverage the rich text and multimodal data available on the web to create weak supervision signals, allowing us to efficiently collect and utilize feedback.
CONTROLS: We compare our active learning approach to random sampling and an iterative noisy-oracle framework where an oracle model selects the next batch of samples to label, and evaluate the performance on a diverse set of regional datasets for varying ranges of supervision.
COST: 2640
PREDICTION: We expect this weakly-supervised active learning framework to greatly reduce the manual effort required for data quality assessment, while achieving state-of-the-art performance on a variety of multilingual datasets with only 1-5% of the available data labeled; still vulnerable to surge of noise samples if small batch sizes are used.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Scalable Framework for Multilingual Pretraining Corpus Curation via Efficient Distributed Processing
PROPOSAL: To efficiently process web-scale multilingual data, we develop a scalable framework for multilingual pretraining corpus curation. Our framework leverages a combination of cloud-based distributed computing and a microservice-based architecture to parallelize data selection and processing tasks. We implement a flexible data pipeline that integrates various data selection methods, allowing for seamless exploration of different strategies and optimizable configurations for specific use cases. Our framework significantly reduces the computational overhead associated with large-scale corpus curation, enabling researchers to rapidly iterate and refine their approaches.
CONTROLS: We evaluate the performance and efficiency of our framework using various datasets and compare it to a centralized computing approach.
COST: 3360
PREDICTION: We expect our scalable framework to greatly accelerate the development of high-quality multilingual pretraining corpora, facilitating more frequent experimentation and refinement of data selection methods. Although distributed computing may introduce some added technical complexity, it will ultimately enable researchers to effectively tackle the challenges associated with large-scale multilingual corpus curation.

ACTION: REVISE
TITLE: Revision of Query-Diversity Based Multilingual Data Selection
PROPOSAL: In the original query-diversity based multilingual data selection proposal, we adaptively generated query sentences to collect diverse and high-quality samples across languages. However, we recognize that this approach has high computational cost due to the need to generate and evaluate multiple query sentences. To improve efficiency, we propose to simplify the decoder-based query formulation strategy by using a pre-trained multilingual language model to generate a fixed set of input encoding representations for each language, rather than adaptively conditioning on seed examples from each language. This revised approach still allows the model to capture language-specific features while being more computationally efficient.
CONTROLS: We retain the original ablations, and include additional controls comparing to a naive random sampling approach without the use of query diversity.
COST: 4080
PREDICTION: We expect this revised method to achieve better trade-off between efficiency and effectiveness, and improve data selection results in languages with limited available data. While this revised approach may benefit from pre-training on larger or more diverse datasets, it may not generalize well to languages with very different input distributions or structures, in which case traditional adapted condition may yield better performance.

Note: While the actual cost reduction for the revised method is 1520 (7560 - 6040), the new cost is still 3 times higher than the actual estimate.

TITLE: Language-Agnostic Quality Assessment via Referring Expression Generation

PREDICTION: Experiments on several multilingual datasets should demonstrate the effectiveness of LARQ in identifying high-quality documents across languages, with low bias towards any specific language. PROPOSAL: We propose a hierarchical and incremental learning framework for scalable multilingual data selection, where we first train a general-purpose data selector on a small-scale multilingual dataset and then incrementally adapt it to new languages and larger datasets. PREDICTION: Experiments on a set of multilingual benchmarks should demonstrate the effectiveness of HILM in solving the multilingual data selection task efficiently and accurately, with improved adaptability to new languages and datasets. TITLE: Active Learning for Efficient Multilingual Data Quality Assessment
PROPOSAL: We propose an active learning approach to improve the efficiency of multilingual data quality assessment, where we select a subset of most informative instances from a large unlabeled dataset and label them, which in turn enables the quality selector to improve its accuracy and adaptability across languages. Our approach, dubbed ALEM (Active Learning for Efficient Multilingual) combines a mutual information-based strategy to select the most relevant instances.
CONTROLS: We will compare the performance of ALEM with state-of-the-art active learning methods and experimentally investigate the effect of label quality, dataset size and computational cost on its performance.
COST: 900,000
PREDICTION: Experiments on a set of multilingual benchmarks should demonstrate the effectiveness of ALEM in improving the efficiency of quality assessment, leading to better adaptation and generalization performance across languages. However, ALEM might fail to select the most informative instances when the underlying patterns are not well-represented or extremely subtle, such as for high-stakes or complex domains.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Evaluating Model-Based Data Quality Selectors with Human Evaluation
PROPOSAL: We propose a novel approach to evaluate the performance of model-based data quality selectors using human evaluation, where we assess the quality of selected documents using a crowdsourcing platform. Our approach, dubbed EMDQS (Evaluating Model-Based Data Quality Selectors), combines a multi-task learning framework to improve the inter-rater reliability and reduce the annotation cost.
CONTROLS: We will compare the performance of EMDQS with existing evaluation methods and experimentally investigate the effect of labeling strategies, annotation protocols and crowdsourcing scenarios on its performance.
COST: 1,100,000
PREDICTION: Experiments on a set of human-labeled benchmarks should demonstrate the effectiveness of EMDQS in improving the accuracy and reliability of model-based quality selectors, leveraging human evaluation to evaluate the impact of different annotation protocols and strategies. However, EMDQS might fail to capture model-specific biases or complex relationships between documents and tasks that are difficult for annotators to evaluate.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Investigating the Impact of Pretraining on Multilingual Data Quality Selectors
PROPOSAL: We design a series of experiments to investigate the impact of different pretraining strategies and objectives on the performance of multilingual data quality selectors, drawing insights from recent studies on the role of pretraining in improving model robustness and adaptability.
CONTROLS: We will compare the performance of quality selectors with varying pretraining objectives, text sizes, and initialization strategies, and analyze the effects of pretraining on the quality selector's ability to handle out-of-distribution data and adapt to new languages.
COST: 1,500,000
PREDICTION: Experiments should provide valuable insights into the relationship between pretraining and quality selector performance, highlighting the importance of pretraining in improving model robustness and adaptability. However, the investigation might reveal that the benefits of pretraining are most pronounced in certain language families or domains, limiting its generalizability.

TITLE: REVISED Learning a Unified Cross-lingual Data Quality Signal
PROPOSAL: We will incorporate a decoder-based autoencoder structure into the multilingual sentence embedding model to leverage task-specific information from an auxiliary classification task into the data quality signal. COST: 1400
PREDICTION: The combined model should be able to improve the data quality signal in terms of quality-dependent prediction capability, by leveraging contextual features from the auxiliary classification task.

 ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Investigating Ensemble Methods for Data Quality Signal
PROPOSAL: We will investigate whether combining the quality signals from different languages or models can improve overall data quality. CONTROLS: Compare to the baseline model, and to the ensemble methods applied to language specific quality signals.
COST: 9000
PREDICTION: We expect the ensemble methods to provide a trade-off between improvement in predictive performance and increased model complexity.

textes.jumeau:
ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Evaluating Grid-Based 3D Representations Using Real-World Benchmarks
PROPOSAL: Conduct a comprehensive evaluation of existing grid-based 3D representations using a range of real-world benchmarks, including the challenging real-world datasets ModelNet40 and ShapeNetV2. Compare the efficacy of different grid resolutions, occupancy field representations (e.g., voxels vs. Sign Distance Fields), and training objectives (e.g., Chamfer distance vs. L1 loss). Investigate how well these representations can recover the geometric structure and view-dependent appearance of real-world objects, and identify potential areas for improvement.
CONTROLS: Compare 3D-MPA (a variant of the 3D-Primitive-based method with reduced data requirements), Occupancy Chance Field (for occupancy), and MeshCNN (for standard Lobes-based methods), with regular training and fixed occupancy for all experiments.
COST: 100 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: Grid-based representations demonstrate competitive performance, particularly with high-resolution grids and occupancy field representations; however, struggles to handle complex and nuanced view-dependent effects, revealing a need for novel representations.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Architecture and Training Strategy for Joint 3D Geometry and Appearance Representation
PROPOSAL: Design a novel neural network architecture that combines the strengths of geometric and appearance feature extractors, using a novel encoder-decoder framework with a 3D convolutional encoder and a view-dependent spatial transformer decoder. Train the model on a large dataset of 3D objects with view-dependent appearance captured using a multi-camera setup, and evaluate its ability to recover both geometric structure and view-dependent appearance. Investigate the impact of different training objectives (e.g., Chamfer distance, L1 loss, photometric consistency loss) and architectures (e.g., encoder-only, decoder-only, both).
CONTROLS: Compare the proposed architecture with View-Driven Sparse Voxel Feature (ViDIn) network (a state-of-the-art method that uses a multi-stage approach, and achives several state-of-the-art results).
COST: 240 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: The novel architecture demonstrates significantly improved performance in recovering both geometric structure and view-dependent appearance, and exhibits adaptability to diverse object shapes and material properties. However, requires careful tuning of hyperparameters to achieve optimal results.

textes.jumeau:
ACTION: ADD
TITLE: View-Dependent 3D Model Generation from a Single Image
PROPOSAL: Develop a method that can generate 3D models from a single image, which includes the recovered 3D geometry and appearance, under a specific viewpoint. To achieve this, use the model trained in Proposal 2 and add a novel refinement network to generate888 a latent code that, when decoded using the original model, produces a 3D model that matches the input image in both geometry and appearance. Use a coarse-to-fine strategy to optimize the refinement network and a novel loss function that combines photometric and geometric consistency.
CONTROLS: Compare with current state-of-the-art single-image 3D model generation methods, such as Pix2Vox++ (using a UNet-based network for view-predicting) and PiFu (using a multi-stage framework for 3D surface fitting).
COST: 336 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: The method demonstrates the ability to generate high-quality 3D models that are consistent with the input image in both geometry and appearance, and showcases the feasibility of view-dependent 3D model generation from a single image. However, the refinement network may require extensive hyperparameter tuning to balance photometric and geometric consistency, and the method may struggle with complex scenes and occlusions.

ACTION: REVISE 3
TITLE: Revised: View-Dependent 3D Model Generation from a Single Image
PROPOSAL: Incorporate structured residuals into the attention-based refinement network from the revised Proposal 4, such that the refinement process repeatedly refines the 3D model by iteratively predicting residuals between the input image and the current 3D model, as well as residuals between the current 3D model and the ground truth 3D model. This approach aims to improve the precision and accuracy of the generated 3D model. Additionally, evaluate the proposed method on IAM3D dataset by using the ground truth 3D models of objects under different views as target outputs for the refinement process.
CONTROLS: Compare the revised approach with current state-of-the-art methods using IAM3D dataset.
COST: 400 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: The structured residual refinement network demonstrates improved precision and accuracy in view-dependent 3D model generation from a single image, and showcases the potential of IAM3D as a challenging benchmark for this task, where the results can achieve a synthesis accuracy of 0.85+ on the entire IAM3D dataset while struggling to generalize outside of IAM3D and obviously real world environments.
