ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Investigating the Role of Multi-Task Learning in Joint 3D Geometry and Appearance Representation
PROPOSAL: Incorporate multi-task learning into the architecture from Proposal 2 to simultaneously learn 3D geometry and appearance representation, as well as related tasks such as 3D surface normal estimation, material classification, and view-point estimation. Use a shared neural network to facilitate the transfer of knowledge between tasks and improve the overall performance. Evaluate the proposed method on the tasks of 3D geometry and appearance representation, and compare its performance with the state-of-the-art methods in those tasks.
CONTROLS: Compare the multi-task learning approach with the baseline architectures that learned geometry and appearance representation without multi-task learning.
COST: 500 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: The proposed multi-task learning approach demonstrates improved performance in joint 3D geometry and appearance representation, as well as the related tasks, by leveraging the shared knowledge and features learned across tasks, and achieving a F1 score of 0.95+ on ShapeNet and 0.83+ on IAM3D in joint rendering.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Analyzing the Impact of Radiance Fields on Joint 3D Geometry and Appearance Representation
PROPOSAL: Investigate the effect of radiance fields on joint 3D geometry and appearance representation, by incorporating a rendering module into the architecture from Proposal 2 that uses a pre-trained neural radiance field to generate images from the learned 3D geometry and appearance representation. Evaluate the proposed method on the tasks of joint 3D geometry and appearance representation, and compare its performance with the state-of-the-art methods in those tasks.
CONTROLS: Compare the radiance field-based rendering approach with the baseline architectures that used standard rendering methods (e.g., surface normal estimation and material classification).
COST: 600 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: The proposed radiance field-based rendering approach demonstrates improved performance in joint 3D geometry and appearance representation, by leveraging theinciple of visual coherence of real-world data and whose effective bounds are decided by some learning data structures containing enough geometric and appearance information, and achieving a F1 score of 0.97+ on ShapeNet and 0.90+ on IAM3D, while making the critical drawback to general quality appear as the computational cost slowly increasing.

TITLE: Evaluating the Robustness of Joint 3D Geometry and Appearance Representation Models to Real-World Variability
PROPOSAL: Evaluate the robustness of the joint 3D geometry and appearance representation models from Proposal 2 on real-world datasets with variability such as textures, lighting conditions, and occlusions. Compare the performance of the robustness of different models, including the ones proposed in this set of proposals.
CONTROLS: Compare the robustness of models from Proposals 2, 4, and 5 with state-of-the-art models for 3D object recognition and segmentation (e.g., PointNet, PointRCNN).
COST: 670.1 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: The robust models proposed in this set of proposals demonstrate improved robustness to real-world variability, as evidenced by their competitive performance on the benchmark datasets, but their robustness comes at the expense of some detectable compromise in lower performance and may be biased to the set of variability scenarios tested.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Neural 3D Scene Reconstruction from Multi-View Images
PROPOSAL: Extend the joint 3D geometry and appearance representation models from Proposal 2 to reconstruct 3D scenes from multi-view images. Use a neural network to integrate the predicted 3D models from each view and produce a final 3D scene representation. Evaluate the proposed method on the tasks of 3D scene reconstruction and benchmark datasets like the DTU dataset and the Bosch Sensortec Model and Scene repository.
CONTROLS: Compare the proposed method with state-of-the-art models for 3D scene reconstruction (e.g., multi-view stereo, lidar-based methods).

However, requires careful tuning of hyperparameters to achieve optimal results, and may struggle with scenes with highly varying lighting conditions.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Direct Geometry-Appearance Inscription Learning for 3D Object Reconstruction
PROPOSAL: Implement a novel deep neural network architecture, DubIns, that directly inscribes a 3D latent representation to capture an object's geometry and its view-dependent appearance simultaneously. Specifically, DubIns combines a geometry-aware feature extractor with an appearance-aware feature extractor, both of which are learned within a shared Latent Space. The geometry-aware extractor uses a structurally-aware 3D CNN (e.g., FCGF) to process point clouds or meshes, while the appearance-aware extractor employs a vision Transformers (e.g., ViT) to model view-dependent effects. The shared Latent Space then leverages an auxiliary consistency loss to ensure that the learned geometry and appearance representations are coherent and consistent with each other. This co-learning scheme enables joint optimization for both geometry and appearance.
CONTROLS: Train and test DubIns against a mix of geometry-only baselines (e.g., DVR, Nest), and appearance-focused models (e.g., SIREN4Plus model with differentiable renderer). EvaluateDubIns on commonly-used real-world benchmarks for 3D reconstruction (e.g., ShapeNet45, ModelNet40).
COST: 1200
PREDICTION: DubIns should significantly outperform existing geometry-only and appearance-focused models in terms of both quantitative metrics (e.g., mIoU, Chamfer Dist) and qualitative visualizations of the reconstructed objects. The joint attention mechanism in DubIns might lead to improved generalization across different viewpoints, object patterns, and complex real-world scenes. When geometry and appearance are less coherent (e.g., objects with weird geometry), DubIns might perform poorly.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Joint 3D Geometry and Appearance with Implicit Lightweight Neural Representations
PROPOSAL: We propose to extend the power of implicit neural representations (INRs) to represent both 3D geometry and view-dependent appearance by combining INRs for the surface of the shape, integrating neural oscillating ternary convolutional layers that jointly predict view-dependent lighting, materials, and normal maps, and predict UV coordinates of a latent texture atlas to capture surface details and transparencies directly, allowing us to generate high-quality images from arbitrary viewpoints using an invertible image-to-3D translation network.
CONTROLS: We ablate this new neural architecture by comparing it against an existing geometry-only INR, while also evaluating on a simplified version of the model without neural oscillating ternary convolution (cutting off the direct modeling of the appearance).
COST: 147.42
PREDICTION: by leveraging the implicit power of neural representations to unite 3D rendering and learning, we expect to reach better image synthesis results compared to the compared INR baselines, while leveraging real-time learnability meanwhile to handle changing tasks and scene complexity, and minimizing the traded-off with resolution since even high sampled inter-stage and coarse initial network levels manage the appearance faithfully. It may struggle with view-dependent occlusion and generalization of environmental lighting to novel viewpoints.

TITLE: Neural Rendering for Real-Time 3D Reconstruction and View-Dependent Appearance
PROPOSAL: We propose a neural rendering-based approach for real-time 3D reconstruction and view-dependent appearance. Our method uses a neural network to render a 2D image from a 3D scene, and then uses stereo matching to estimate the depth map. We represent the scene as a neural radiance field, which is an occupancy field that encodes the reflectance and appearance of the scene. Our network takes a set of RGB images as input and outputs a neural radiance field, which can be used to render new views of the scene.
CONTROLS: We compare our results with existing state-of-the-art methods for 3D reconstruction and view-dependent appearance, and also evaluate the robustness of our method to various levels of occlusion and lighting conditions.

PREDICTION: The neural rendering-based approach should provide accurate 3D reconstruction and view-dependent appearance, and also enable real-time rendering. However, we may face issues with reconstructing scenes with complex occlusions or non-Lambertian materials, where the neural network may struggle to capture the appearance and reflectance of the scene.

TITLE: Investigating Structural Regularization for Joint Geometry-Appearance 3D Representations
PROPOSAL: Compare the performance of a standard generative 3D model like SPSL [1] trained with and without structural regularization. We propose adding spatial and appearance-oriented regularizers to encourage structural consistency in the latent space, investigating how this impacts results in both 3D reconstruction and image-to-3D generation. We will use a combination of rendered synthetic ShapeNet [2] data and real-world images from the Pascal3D+ [3] dataset to train and evaluate the models.
CONTROLS: We will train a standard SPSL model without regularization, using standard evaluation procedures for 3D reconstruction (e.g., Chamfer distance, precision of surface normal estimation) and image-to-3D generation (evaluation of generated object appearance fidelity, viewpoint consistency).
COST: 1500 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: According to previous research, incorporating spatial regularization can help 3D models better capture object geometry. However, we predict that appearance-oriented regularization will have a more significant impact on the quality and coherence of view-dependent effects in generated objects, including accurate representation of shading and reflections. Potential challenges include optimizing the regularizer strength and initialising latent spaces properly.

References:

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Evaluating the Impact of View-Dependent Supervision on 3D Geometry-Appearance Learning
PROPOSAL: Investigate the effect of incorporating view-dependent supervision signals, such as pixel-wise rendering losses or spatial.temporal coherence on the shape and appearance of reconstructed objects. We will add multiple rendering views to the dataset and supervise the model simultaneously using a combination of viewpoint-agnostic 3D reconstruction loss (e.g., Chamfer distance) and viewpoint-dependent rendering losses (e.g., photometric error, structure similarity).
CONTROLS: This study will be a direct extension of proposal 1, with structural regularization active to encourage coherent geometry and appearance in the latent space. Three controlled versions will be evaluated: (1) baseline SPSL with no regularization and far-from view-dependent supervision, (2) SPSL with structural regularization and view-dependent supervision, and (3) an additional simple baseline using a task-conditioned model (like pi-GAN) specifically trained on each viewpoint, optimizing a direct photometric loss.
COST: 2800 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: We expect that incorporating view-dependent supervision will improve the coherence and quality of view-dependent effects in reconstructed objects, but may push the geometry-only performance slightly worse by overfitting to specific views. Failure points include finding the optimal weight for combining viewpoint-dependent and viewpoint-agnostic losses, particularly for scenes with very small datasets.

ACTION: REVISE 3
TITLE: REVISED: Using Viewpoint-Consistent Image Abstraction for Single-Image-to-3D Generation
PROPOSAL: Investigate whether using an abstraction of images from the given viewpoint can help reduce the discrepancy between 3D reconstruction results from different observations. We will apply a standard image analysis process such as edge-preserving smoothing to convert input images into a set of viewpoint-consistent image features that capture object structures in a way which gets read by the model during reconstruction. This study is a direct response to the limitations of current models in generating 3D objects consistent with a input image viewpoint. We will conduct experiments on T-LESS [4] and ShapeNet datasets.
CONTROLS: This baseline study will build on previous 3D generation experiments from the first two proposals and evaluate three variations: (1) image featurization alone, (2) featurization of viewpoint-aware outlier rejection to aid edge detection and rejection functionality in terms of robustness and less view inconsistent results, and (3) a more extensive dataset of images with accurate camera poses providing reliable and contrast instance viewpoint dependencies.
COST: 3600 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: This approach aims to provide a complementary information source that can alleviate viewpoint inconsistency, but may come at the cost of reducing spatial detail and suppressing subtle view-dependent appearance features. Successful implementation will necessitate fine-tuning the edge-preserving process, selecting the right viewpoint-aware outlier rejection method and thoroughly evaluate the permutation of relevant metrics across experiments.

[4] Hodan et al., "T-LESS: A Large Dataset and Validation of 3D Object Recognition and Pose Estimation Algorithms in Cluttered Scenes", 3DV 2017

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Investigating Implicit Neural Representations for Joint Geometry-Appearance Modeling
PROPOSAL: Explore the application of implicit neural representations, such as occupancy fields [5], for joint geometry-appearance modeling. We will compare the performance of an occupancy field model with the existing model and analyze its ability to capture view-dependent effects. Specifically, we will evaluate the model's capacity to generate realistic appearances under different lighting conditions and viewpoints using a synthetic dataset generated through tools like ShapeNet Render [6].
CONTROLS: We will compare our occupancy field model to the current model (SPSL) and also investigate the performance of a model that combines occupancy fields with the structural regularization introduced in proposal 1. Additionally, we will analyze the learnt latent embedding using latent space visualization techniques to gain insights into how view-dependent effects are captured in the model.
COST: 5400 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: Implicit neural representations have shown great promise in various computer vision tasks, such as image generation and surface reconstruction. We expect that occupancy fields will capture view-dependent effects more effectively than the current model, but predict that the combination of occupancy fields with structural regularization will provide the best results. However, this may come at the cost of increased computational complexity and memory requirements, which could be limitations in certain hardware or deployment settings.

References:

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Axiomatic Analysis of View-Dependent Effects in 3D Geometry-Appearance Models
PROPOSAL: Develop a theoretical framework to analyze and understand the view-dependent effects in 3D geometry-appearance models. We will derive axioms that represent the essential properties of view-dependent effects, such as translational and rotational invariance, and analyze how these axioms are satisfied in the models proposed in previous studies. Additionally, we will investigate the implications of these axioms on the model's performance and generalize the analysis to other 3D vision tasks.
CONTROLS: We will compare the performance of the models that satisfy the axioms with those that do not, using metrics such as rendering accuracy and viewpoint consistency.
COST: 9000 GPU-hours (fully simulation-based and would largely in theory assume the above objectives.)
PREDICTION: By developing a theoretical framework, we expect to identify key factors that contribute to view-dependent effects and provide a deeper understanding of how these effects are captured in the models. This analysis will help guide the design of future models that better capture view-dependent effects, and may reveal open questions or challenges in the field that warrant further investigation.

TITLE: Transfer Learning for 3D Geometry-Appearance Models across Different Domains and Tasks
PROPOSAL: Investigate the transfer learning capabilities of 3D geometry-appearance models across different domains and tasks. We will train models on a diverse set of tasks, such as object reconstruction, shape prediction, and text-to-3D generation, and evaluate their performance on novel tasks and domains. Additionally, we will analyze the similarity between task and domain embeddings to understand the underlying relationships between tasks and domains.
CONTROLS: We will compare the performance of models trained from scratch with those that use pre-trained weights, and evaluate the robustness of the models across different datasets and domains.
COST: 12000 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: By exploring transfer learning capabilities, we expect to identify key factors that affect transferability, such as task similarity, domain similarity, and model architecture. This analysis will help guide the development of more effective 3D geometry-appearance models that can adapt to new tasks and domains, and may reveal opportunities for cross-domain knowledge sharing and meta-learning.

TITLE: HyBridge: A Hybrid Approach to Joint Geometry-Appearance Learning
PROPOSAL: Combine the strengths of multiple approaches to develop a hybrid model, HyBridge, which leverages structural regularization, implicit neural representations, and transfer learning to achieve state-of-the-art performance in joint geometry-appearance modeling. HyBridge will consist of a shared geometry representation learned through structural regularization, an appearance model using implicit neural representations, and a transferable task-conditioned module for learning across different tasks and domains.
CONTROLS: We will compare the performance of HyBridge with individual models, including those proposed in previous studies, and evaluate its ability to adapt to new tasks and domains.

However, the development of HyBridge will require careful design and integration of its components, as well as thorough evaluation of its performance across different scenarios.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Theoretical Expressiveness of Unidirectional One-Step Generators
PROPOSAL: We prove that a one-step generator that maps a latent variable to a sequence of tokens in a teacher-student framework, as described in the problem statement, cannot exactly replicate the output distribution of the teacher AR model under the assumption that the codebook sizes are finite and the teacher-student framework involves permutation-invariant operations. This is because a unidirectional one-step generator, by definition, cannot capture the correlations between tokens that arise from the feedback loop of the teacher AR model. We will use the framework of information theory to show that the joint entropy of the output token sequence produced by the teacher AR model is strictly greater than the conditional entropy of the same sequence conditioned on the latent variable, which implies that the one-step generator cannot match the teacher's output distribution exactly.
CONTROLS: Information-theoretic lower bound for AR models as teacher, random and permutation-invariant mappings as students
COST: 500
PREDICTION: The lower bound will hold, but establishing it precisely might be less straightforward due to the teacher-student framework.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Minimum Computational Complexity of Solving the One-Step Generator Learning Problem
PROPOSAL: We prove that learning a one-step generator that matches the output distribution of a teacher AR model is NP-hard. Specifically, we show that the problem of finding a one-step generator that minimizes the Kullback-Leibler divergence (KL divergence) between its output distribution and the teacher AR model's output distribution is NP-hard. This hardness result implies that there will not be a polynomial-time learning algorithm for one-step generators, and we will provide evidence from previous work on related token-by-token generation problems.
CONTROLS: Reduction from a known NP-hard problem (e.g., 3-SAT), teacher AR model as a black box, and a variety of output distributions
COST: 1000
PREDICTION: The hardness result will be established, but it remains to be seen how the proposed methods can mitigate the challenge and leverage the teacher AR model efficiently.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Discrete bilevel optimization framework for one-step generators
PROPOSAL: We introduce a discrete bilevel optimization framework to learn the mapping from a latent variable to a sequence of tokens in a single forward pass. This framework involves minimizing the KL divergence between the teacher AR model's output distribution and the one-step generator's output distribution, and imposing regularization on the generator's representation to ensure realizability. We propose to use tractable approximations to optimize the expectation over the teacher's output distribution, and we will design an efficient solvers for the subproblems in the bilevel framework using techniques for discrete optimization.
CONTROLS: Bilevel optimization framework with separable subproblems, tractable approximations to optimize expectations, and algorithms for discrete optimization
COST: 1400
PREDICTION: The framework will provide a tractable approach to learn one-step generators, but optimizing the discrete bilevel objectives might be computationally expensive due to their non-convexity.

TITLE: One-Step Generator via Parameter-Space Distillation
PROPOSAL: Train a one-step generator using parameter-space distillation: optimize the parameters of the generator to minimize the Kullback-Leibler (KL) divergence between the output distribution of the generator and the teacher AR model, on the condition that the generator maps a latent variable to a complete token sequence in a single forward pass. The KL divergence will be approximated using a Monte Carlo estimate, where the generator is run multiple times with different latent inputs and the output token sequences are averaged.
CONTROLS: Compare the one-step generator to the DD1 and speculative decoding baselines. Vary the number of Monte Carlo samples used to estimate the KL divergence and analyze the trade-off between accuracy and computational cost.
COST: 1500
PREDICTION: This approach should be competitive with DD1, but slower due to the computational cost of the KL divergence estimate. It may outperform speculative decoding if the generator can learn a better mapping from latent to token sequence.

TITLE: Learning a Mapping from Latent to Sequence through Inverse Autoregression
PROPOSAL: We introduce a novel approach, Inverse Autoregression (IAR), to train a one-step generator. Instead of relying on flow matching or predefined noise-to-data mappings, IAR uses the teacher AR model to compute the inverse autoregression, i.e., the mapping from a sequence of tokens to their corresponding?(:inputs to the model) standalone tokens. The IAR model is then trained to learn this mapping, conditioned on the prior distribution, to generate the entire sequence from a single latent variable.
CONTROLS: We compare IAR against Distilled Decoding 1 (DD1), the state-of-the-art one-step AR generation model, and ablate the inverse autoregression component to understand its contribution.
COST: 268
PREDICTION: IAR should outperform DD1 in terms of sample quality and diversity, potentially narrowing the gap to the original AR model. IAR might fail to match the teacher's diversity if the inverse autoregression mapping does not capture the teacher's input correlations well, or if it struggles to generate coherent sequences from latent variables.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Evaluating the Quality of One-Step AR Generation via Multiscale Reconstruction
PROPOSAL: We investigate the quality of one-step AR generation through multiscale reconstruction. Given a generated sequence, we encode it into a lower-dimensional embedding and measure the similarity to the embedding of the ground-truth sequence at the same scale. This framework evaluates the generator's ability to capture global and local features of the input distribution. ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Learning a Mapping from Latent to Sequence through Inverse Autoregression
PROPOSAL: We introduce a novel approach, Inverse Autoregression (IAR), to train a one-step generator. Instead of relying on flow matching or predefined noise-to-data mappings, IAR uses the teacher AR model to compute the inverse autoregression, i.e., the mapping from a sequence of tokens to their corresponding?(:inputs to the model) standalone tokens. The IAR model is then trained to learn this mapping, conditioned on the prior distribution, to generate the entire sequence from a single latent variable.
CONTROLS: We compare IAR against Distilled Decoding 1 (DD1), the state-of-the-art one-step AR generation model, and ablate the inverse autoregression component to understand its contribution.
COST: 800
PREDICTION: IAR should outperform DD1 in terms of sample quality and diversity, potentially narrowing the gap to the original AR model. IAR might fail to match the teacher's diversity if the inverse autoregression mapping does not capture the teacher's input correlations well, or if it struggles to generate coherent sequences from latent variables.

textes.jumeau:
ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Structured Routing with Expert Activations
PROPOSAL: We train a MoE model but also track expert activation patterns at each training step and act on this data: at the end of each 'expert activation monitoring' period, we weight update the (already tuned) routing matrices by a fraction of the past-activation-weighted cross-entropy (CAWC) loss.
CONTROLS: We compare to uniform (load-balancing) routing, sparse routing with CAWC loss-only updates, as well as expert activation monitoring without CLAWC loss updates.
COST: 40 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: We expect improved specialization, partly due to activation-event dependent cross-entropy minimization that is sensitive to each pattern of routing over training time. It is difficult to predict how much actual, optimized specialization improvement will occur. There is a non-vanishing risk that the activation records simply capture irrelevant statistical contingent behavior.

TITLE:  Structured Routing with Expert Activations

ACTION: REVISE 4
TITLE: Analyzing Local Relevance and Global Interactions in Expert Activations
PROPOSAL: We introduce graph attention networks (GATs) to compute a localized relevance score for each expert, which is used to modulate the supervisory signal. Additionally, to tackle global patterns that evaded the local view, we incorporate graph convolutional networks (GCNs) to model the interaction between experts. Our final objective function combines graph attention and convolution losses with a supervised cross-entropy loss.
CONTROLS: We compare to uniform (load-balancing) routing, sparse routing with CAWC loss-only updates, as well as expert activation monitoring without CAWC loss updates.
COST: 180 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: By incorporating graph attention and convolution mechanisms, we expect to capture both local relevance and global interactions among experts, leading to enhanced expert specialization and more effective routing. However, this added complexity may lead to over-fitting if not properly regularized.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Taskonomy-based Expert Pruning and Knowledge Transfer
PROPOSAL: We leverage the taskonomy of language modeling and task-specific representations to prune experts that are redundant or irrelevant to specific tasks. We achieve this by computing a knowledge graph of task-semantic relationships and identifying experts that specialize in redundant or overlapping tasks. We then prune these experts and use knowledge transfer mechanisms to adjust the weights of remaining experts to compensate for the loss.
CONTROLS: We compare to uniform (load-balancing) routing, sparse routing with CAWC loss-only updates, as well as expert activation monitoring without CAWC loss updates.
COST: 240 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: By removing experts that specialize in redundant tasks, we expect to reduce model capacity and improve generalization to unseen tasks, while also promoting more efficient routing and better knowledge transfer between experts. However, this may require careful pruning and regularization to prevent over-fitting or catastrophic forgetting.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Temporal Expert Dynamics
PROPOSAL: We study the evolution of expert dynamics over time and propose a temporal routing mechanism to dynamically adjust expert activation weights based on their performance, usage, and adaptation. This mechanism allows experts to specialize over time and adapt to changing task requirements. By integrating this approach with our existing proposals, we expect to further enhance expert specialization and routing efficiency.
CONTROLS: We compare to uniform (load-balancing) routing, sparse routing with CAWC loss-only updates, as well as expert activation monitoring without CAWC loss updates.
COST: 360 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: Temporal expert dynamics should allow experts to continuously adapt and specialize, leading to improved routing efficiency and more accurate language modeling performance. However, this may also introduce time-varying instability in the model, particularly if not properly regularized.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Ensemble-Based Routing with Mixture-of-Experts and Catastrophic Forgetting Mitigation
PROPOSAL: We propose an ensemble-based routing approach that combines the predictions of multiple MoE models with different routing mechanisms, such as Structured Routing and Taskonomy-based Expert Pruning. To mitigate catastrophic forgetting, we use a knowledge distillation technique to regularize the ensemble model and promote consistent routing decisions across experts. By exploiting the strengths of each routing mechanism, we expect to achieve improved expert specialization and adaptability.
CONTROLS: We compare to uniform (load-balancing) routing, sparse routing with CAWC loss-only updates, as well as expert activation monitoring without CAWC loss updates.
COST: 480 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: The ensemble-based routing approach should effectively leverage the strengths of multiple routing mechanisms, reducing catastrophic forgetting and achieving more accurate language modeling performance. However, this may require careful tuning of the ensemble architecture and knowledge distillation parameters to avoid over-complexity and performance degradation.

TITLE: A Theoretical Framework for Analyzing Expert Specialization and Routing Efficiency
PROPOSAL: We derive a stochastic process model to describe the evolution of expert specialization and routing efficiency in MoE models. Our framework provides a mathematical foundation for understanding the interplay between expert dynamics, routing mechanisms, and model performance. By analyzing the stationary distribution of the stochastic process, we establish sufficient conditions for optimal expert specialization and routing efficiency.
CONTROLS: N/A

PREDICTION: Our theoretical framework should provide valuable insights into the underlying mechanisms of expert specialization and routing efficiency in MoE models. By establishing a solid mathematical foundation, we expect to identify key factors that contribute to optimal model performance and develop more effective routing mechanisms in the future.

textes.jumeau:
ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Guided Expert Specialization via Dynamic Routing Labels
PROPOSAL: We propose a new training objective for MoE language models that incorporates dynamic routing labels. For each token in a batch, we assign metadata that specify the intended domain or sub-task that each expert should focus on (e.g., coreference, sentiment analysis, or question answering). A set of Interactive Attention Modules (IAMs) upscales these labels to every other token in the batch, creating a coarse proxy of the routing that we wish to see. The IAMs do this by aggregating multi-head attention across a nearest neighbor preserving softmax with relative position attention between tokens. The contrastive loss between the IAM's representation of desired routing and predicted routing is minimized. Predicted routing is the latent product of the router's output and the input, through reweighting, to the applicable expert.
CONTROLS: We compare our model against MoE with the standard routing loss plus orthogonality regularization (Meena et al., 2019), and the normally deployed Mixture-of-Experts models via standard load-balancing losses (Shazeer, 2017).
COST: 17100
PREDICTION: We anticipate that including guided information from the IAM in the loss leads to noticeable degrees of expert specialization during training.

ACTION: REVISE 2
TITLE: Investigating Reward-Shaping via Dynamic Routing Rewards
PROPOSAL: We propose a novel reward-shaping strategy to leverage MoE's routing information more effectively. Inspired by reinforcement learning (RL), we invoke an auxiliary reward function that encourages the router to direct experts to attend to relevant input tokens. To avoid high variance in gradient estimates, we incorporate a normalization term into the reward, computed as the weighted average of expert activations. The weights are proportional to the inhibition term from the router's output, acting as a quality measure of each expert's contribution.
CONTROLS: We compare our model against MoE with the standard routing loss plus orthogonality regularization and the original MoE model with standard load-balancing losses.
COST: 13650
PREDICTION: Our results will show improved expert specialization with reward shaping, but it may introduce unhealthy expert competition and further sharpen resource constraints in converged model weights.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Tiered Reward-Shaping for Maximizing Routing Diversity
PROPOSAL: We extend the previous proposal by introducing a tiered reward-shaping mechanism that promotes routing diversity across experts. Each expert reward is calculated as a weighted sum of the original reward and a novelty bonus, which encourages experts to explore diverse input tokens. The novelty bonus is computed based on the entropy of the expert's activations across the input tokens.
CONTROLS: We compare our tiered model with the basic reward shaping model and the baseline MoE model without reward shaping.
COST: 124322.236
PREDICTION: Our results will show improved routing diversity and expert specialization, and that the tiered reward-shaping mechanism helps to mitigate expert competition and resource constraints.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Prompt-based Auxiliary Loss for Expert Specialization
PROPOSAL: We add an auxiliary prompt-based loss to the standard MoE training objective to guide expert specialization. For each input, we generate a customized prompt that is relevant to a specific expert, and apply a loss on the expert's output to ensure that it produces a coherent and semantically meaningful response tailored to that prompt.
CONTROLS: We compare this approach against the standard load-balancing loss and an additional architectural modification (adding an always-active shared expert) to alleviate expert homogenization.
COST: 150
PREDICTION: Our approach enables better expert specialization, with expected results showing improvement in language modeling performance by 5% on the English language benchmark and 2% on the Chinese language benchmark, while also reducing the entropy of expert usage (a proxy for homogenization) by 30%. The shared-expert modification yields smaller improvements. However, we expect some failure in mathematical reasoning tasks where evaluation conditions require nuanced understanding, but this would depend on the effectiveness of the prompt generation mechanism.

We comprehensively evaluate the MoE models trained with each of the proposed mechanisms and analyze their performance on a range of metrics, including perplexity, accuracy, F1-score, and ROUGE score.
CONTROLS: We compare the performance of MoE models trained with each of the proposed mechanisms against standard MoE models and previous state-of-the-art models on multiple tasks and domains.
COST: 25920

The proposed mechanisms are expected to achieve state-of-the-art results on multiple tasks and domains.

TITLE: Prompt-based Auxiliary Loss for Expert Specialization
PROPOSAL: We add an auxiliary prompt-based loss to the standard MoE training objective to guide expert specialization. For each input, we generate a customized prompt that is relevant to a specific expert, and apply a loss on the expert's output to ensure that it produces a coherent and semantically meaningful response tailored to that prompt.
CONTROLS: We compare this approach against the standard load-balancing loss and an additional architectural modification (adding an always-active shared expert) to alleviate expert homogenization.
COST: 450
PREDICTION: Our approach enables better expert specialization, with expected results showing improvement in language modeling performance by 5% on the English language benchmark and 2% on the Chinese language benchmark, while also reducing the entropy of expert usage (a proxy for homogenization) by 30%. The shared-expert modification yields smaller improvements. However, we expect some failure in mathematical reasoning tasks where evaluation conditions require nuanced understanding, but this would depend on the effectiveness of the prompt generation mechanism.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Adaptive Expert Routing based on Adversarial Consistency
PROPOSAL: We introduce an adaptive routing strategy that minimizes the inconsistency between the original MoE routing and an adversarially distorted version of it, trained to suppress any significant expert specialization. This consistency minimization objective complements the load-balancing loss, promoting routing diversity while discouraging homogeneous behavior among experts.
CONTROLS: We compare our adaptive routing against standard routing with the load-balancing loss alone, our prompt-based auxiliary loss from Proposal 1, and an ablation of the adversarial distortion mechanism to quantify its contribution.
COST: 765
PREDICTION: Our adaptive routing method should significantly reduce expert homogenization, exhibiting a 50% decrease in the entropy of expert usage compared to the standard routing, while showing minor gains (0.8% improvement) in language modeling performance on the English language benchmark and 1.5% on the Chinese language benchmark, due to the reduced redundancy among experts. If the adversarial distortion mechanism is too aggressive, our model might fail to generalize to novel tasks.

ACTION: REVISE
TITLE: Adaptive Expert Routing based on Adversarial Consistency
PROPOSAL: We revise our adaptive routing strategy by incorporating a secondary loss term that enforces a minimal volume constraint on the parameter space of the expert routers, preventing them from collapsing to a single highly active expert. This regularization promotes a more diverse and organized distribution of router weights, thereby challenging homogeneous expert behavior.
CONTROLS: The revised adaptive routing is compared against the previous version without the volume constraint, in addition to the standard routing, prompt-based auxiliary loss, and ablation of the adversarial distortion mechanism. We also analyze its performance on synthetic data to visualize the reduced router "crowding" effect.
COST: 1035
PREDICTION: The revised adaptive routing should improve the diversity of expert usage, showing a 30% increase in the number of effectively distinct (or "influential") experts within a small tolerance of maximum entropy, while maintaining minor improvements in language modeling performance (consistent with the 1.1% and 1.7% gains on English and Chinese benchmarks, respectively). Failure might occur in highly data-dense or complex domains, where the imposed regularization is too restrictive.

textes.jumeau:
ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Structured Routing Diversity through Expert Pair Loss
PROPOSAL: We propose introducing a novel routing objective that encourages experts to form diverse pairwise relationships rather than mere individual diversity. Specifically, for each pair of experts, the pairwise interaction is computed from the similarity and dissimilarity between their learned representations. This pairwise loss, called Expert Pair Loss (EPL), is added to the load-balancing loss and evaluated on expert activations. The goal is to have experts learn unique domain-specific patterns beyond mere load-balancing.
CONTROLS: Compare with standard MoE and the existing setups where shared experts are added or experts are merged into a single expert per sequence, both with the original batch-level load-balancing loss.
COST: 2000
PREDICTION: The EPL objective should significantly reduce expert homogenization and improve overall capacity utilization, as routed experts learn structured interactions with one another. However, finding optimal pairwise relationships might be brittle, leading to unstable performance when scaling large models or over a long training period.

textes.jumeau:
ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Task-Specific Expert Grouping with Meta-Learning
PROPOSAL: Introducing a meta-learning framework that dynamically forms expert groups based on task-specific criteria during N-shot and few-shot learning. For each adaptation task, a set of experts will be organized into groups according to the demonstrated preferences (i.e., choices of experts) observed during the previous N-shot learning task, thus enabling task-specific knowledge transfer. In order to form task-consistent expert groups, we fine-tune a separate meta-expert to learn clustered expert patterns for each of the tasks from the N-shot learning tasks.
CONTROLS: Comparison will be made with current MoE architecture and expert grouping methods such as adding global shared experts.
COST: 2680
PREDICTION: The proposed task-specific grouping strategy will empower the model to resemble task-experts and reduces the probability of slowly generalizing knowledge to previously unseen tasks. This is likely to improve performance, particularly in domain adaptation tasks where limited-domain knowledge matters, but this method could be brittle and work best for tightly related sequence tasks.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Regularized Expert Selection through Orthogonal Constraints
PROPOSAL: We introduce a regularizer that promotes the router's weight matrix to have orthogonal rows, encouraging experts with diverse and non-overlapping specialization patterns. This regularization, inspired by techniques in extreme learning machines, complements the load-balancing loss and can structure the routing diversity into more meaningful functional specialization.
CONTROLS: Comparison will be made with standard MoE and the existing setups where shared experts are added or experts are merged into a single expert per sequence, both with the standard batch-level load-balancing loss.
COST: 3000
PREDICTION: The regularizer should improve over-specialization and redundancy among experts, allowing the model to cover a broader range of tasks and topics. However, the choice of the regularization strength is challenging, and overly aggressive regularization might prevent experts from collaborating effectively, especially when tasks require overlapping knowledge.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Activated Expert Aggregation with Task-Aware Weighting
PROPOSAL: We propose a novel aggregation mechanism that activates a weighted sum of the instantiated experts after a task-specific activation function and routing step, enabling experts to collaborate and weigh the information retrieved from their routing mechanisms while collaborating through gate functions to prune the less critical information.
CONTROLS: Together with our previous methods, compare with baseline models like shared experts and frequency-based weighting.
COST: 3360
PREDICTION: The novel aggregation mechanism would have an increased computation cost due to the additional task-aware weights, but with strong synergies between activated experts, lead to more diverse and competitive activation signals.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Supervised Expert Refining with Knowledge Distillation
PROPOSAL: We propose refining the existing experts through a supervised learning process, using the routing patterns and task-specific information to guide the refinement. The goal is to adapt the expert representations to better match the task requirements, leveraging knowledge distillation to transfer the knowledge from the teacher model to the refined experts.
CONTROLS: Together with our previous methods, compare with the baseline models like shared experts and frequency-based weighting, as well as previous knowledge distillation methods for MoE.
COST: 4323.055
PREDICTION: The supervised expert refinement with knowledge distillation would have a strong synergistic effect with other methods, potentially leading to significant performance improvements, especially when the teacher model is well-tuned and the distillation process is effectively designed. However, there is a risk of overfitting to the refined experts, reducing the model's adaptability to new tasks.

ACTION: ADD 1
TITLE: Dynamic Configuration of Multi-Label Image Classifiers for Improved Training Stability and Efficiency
PROPOSAL: Implement a meta-learning-based adaptive configuration manager for multi-label image classifiers, which dynamically adjusts the data augmentation strategy, optimizer, learning-rate schedule, and loss function based on the current learning state and evolving label correlations. Utilize a neural-based recommender system to generate adaptive configurations that leverage recent policy gradient methods and reinforcement learning for taking into account the interactions among the four training components.
CONTROLS: Compare against static configuration pipelines (e.g., AutoAugment, RandAugment) and prior adaptive techniques (e.g., learned augmentation policies, adaptive optimizers).
COST: 3,030.21 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: Improved training stability and around 1.5% to 2.5% higher accuracy on benchmark multi-label image classification datasets like PASCAL VOC, CUB-200-2011, and NABirds. Training may exhibit higher sensitivity to initial learning rates and require re-scale optimization.

ACTION: ADD 2
TITLE: Analyzing the Impact of Inter-Component Interactions on Multi-Label Image Classification
PROPOSAL: Investigate the nonlinear interactions among data augmentation, optimizer, learning-rate schedule, and loss function using a systematic mapping of their joint performance landscapes on a variety of real-world multi-label image classification datasets. Utilize a combination of Monte Carlo sampling and Random Search to efficiently explore the quadratically expanded configuration space and identify configurations exhibiting synergy or antagonism among components.
CONTROLS: Compare against uniform random sampling across the configuration space to identify patterns and correlations between component interactions and performance.

PROPOSAL: Introduce a hierarchical framework for learning-stage aware data augmentation, where the high-level decision-making module (DMM) uses a policy network to determine the augmentation strategy for each learning stage, and a low-level deformation module (DLM) generates the actual augmented data based on the DMM's output. ACTION: ADD 1
TITLE: Adaptive Multi-Component Configuration Learning for Multi-Label Image Classification
PROPOSAL: We propose a novel approach, ACOMTL, based on a model-free, actor-critic reinforcement learning framework. ACOMTL learns to adaptively manipulate the data augmentation strategy, optimizer, learning-rate schedule, and loss function jointly, guided by validation performance at various stages of training.
CONTROLS: We compare ACOMTL to a baseline "static optimization" pipeline, using Fixed 224x224 image resizing for data augmentation, SGD optimizer, constant learning rate of 0.001, and Binary Cross-Entropy loss. Ablation studies will be conducted by independently modifying each component's configuration settings.
COST: 336 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: ACOMTL is expected to achieve state-of-the-art performance on the PASCAL VOC 2010 and VOC 2007 datasets, outperforming static configuration pipelines. However, its performance may drop in the presence of significantly imbalanced labels or complex class relationships.

textes.jumeau:
ACTION: ADD 2
TITLE: Inter-Component Coordination via Graph Autoencoders for Multi-Label Image Classification
PROPOSAL: We propose a novel method, ICC-GAE, that utilizes graph autoencoders to model the complex interactions among data augmentation, optimizer, learning-rate schedule, and loss function. ICC-GAE encodes each component's configuration as a node in a graph, generating latent representations that capture inter-component correlations and nonlinear relationships.
CONTROLS: ICC-GAE will be compared to a variant using independent component representations (i.e., without graph autoencoder), as well as to ACOMTL, to evaluate its effectiveness in jointly optimizing multiple components.
COST: 734.5 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: ICC-GAE is expected to improve the validation performance of ACOMTL on the aforementioned datasets, particularly when dealing with rare labels or complex label hierarchies. However, it may be computationally expensive for very large configuration spaces.

ACTION: ADD 4
TITLE: Robust Regularization for Multi-Component Configuration Learning
PROPOSAL: We propose a regularization framework, MultiTask-RO, that incorporates multiple stabilization components to mitigate the risks of overfitting, noisy exploration, and unstable optimization in multi-component configuration learning. By introducing soft constraints on component interactions and augmenting the reinforcement learning objective with regularized terms, MultiTask-RO enhances the robustness and generalizability of ACOMTL-RLH.
CONTROLS: MultiTask-RO will be compared to ACOMTL-RLH without regularization, as well as to other configurations with varying degrees of regularization.
COST: 1260 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: MultiTask-RO is expected to significantly improve the stability and generalization performance of ACOMTL-RLH, especially under noisy exploration and unstable optimization conditions. However, the impact of regularization terms may be fragile to parameter tuning choices.

textes.jumeau:
ACTION: ADD 5
TITLE: Multitask Learning with Multi-Component Configuration Sharing
PROPOSAL: We propose a new paradigm, MC-SHARE, that leverages the idea of multi-task learning by sharing the multi-component configuration settings across a family of related tasks, therefore promoting the reuse of learned knowledge and increasing overall efficiency. This multi-component configuration sharing strategy facilitates regular transfer of optimization knowledge to other tasks and helps them adapt more effectively.
CONTROLS: MC-SHARE will be evaluated in comparison to multi-task learning without configuration sharing, ACOMTL-RLH configured for single-task optimization, and predictive models specific to each task learned separately from the training set.
COST: 1534.2 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: MC-SHARE is expected to exhibit improved overall efficiency, decreased training time, and enhanced task-agnostic generalization performance compared to the other evaluated approaches, yielding state-of-the-art performance across tasks in multi-label image classification by leveraging shared knowledge from related tasks. It may not perform as well in very distinct scenarios requiring one-off modifications of configurations.

TITLE: Efficient Online Exploration of the Configuration Space via Thompson Sampling
PROPOSAL: We modify the ExtConfig-ES framework to incorporate a hierarchical exploration strategy by utilizing the representation learning capabilities of neural models, facilitating more informed decision-making based on the estimated configuration-performance probability space, in addition to adaptively learning distinct exploration probabilities for varying combinations of components.

textes.jumeau:
ACTION: ADD 6
TITLE: Meta-Learning for Multi-Component Configuration Adaptation Across Domains and Scales
PROPOSAL: We propose a novel meta-learning framework, M-CODA, that pursues few-shot adaptation of the multi-component configuration learning to unseen image classification tasks with significantly different attributes or task complexity. By learning a representation of task similarity and shared configurations across multiple tasks during meta-training phase, M-CODA enables adaptable knowledge transfer to address various multi-label classification challenges efficiently.
CONTROLS: We compare M-CODA against existing transfer learning strategies and baseline deep learning models, parameterizing ablation studies to assess the contributions of inter-component configuration learning, feature adaptation, and few-shot learning to the final performance.
COST: 2340 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: The key benefits M-CODA is expected to show include improved task-agnostic generalization performance, suitable for new, unseen image classification tasks with distinct domain-specific features, combining ExtConfig-ES's automatic exploitation of task-specific parameters and strategy adaptability with fast few-shot learning capabilities, outperforming other methods within this proposed work. Its main limitations may lie in balancing adaptation capacity and parameters-sparse picture compatibilities inherent to M-CODA meta-learning solution.

ACTION: ADD 1
TITLE: Adaptive Multi-Component Configuration Learning for Multi-Label Image Classification
PROPOSAL: We propose a novel approach, ACOMTL, based on a model-free, actor-critic reinforcement learning framework. ACOMTL learns to adaptively manipulate the data augmentation strategy, optimizer, learning-rate schedule, and loss function jointly, guided by validation performance at various stages of training.
CONTROLS: We compare ACOMTL to a baseline "static optimization" pipeline, using Fixed 224x224 image resizing for data augmentation, SGD optimizer, constant learning rate of 0.001, and Binary Cross-Entropy loss. Ablation studies will be conducted by independently modifying each component's configuration settings.
COST: 1000 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: ACOMTL is expected to achieve state-of-the-art performance on the PASCAL VOC 2010 and VOC 2007 datasets, outperforming static configuration pipelines. However, its performance may drop in the presence of significantly imbalanced labels or complex class relationships.

ACTION: ADD 2
TITLE: Inter-Component Coordination via Graph Autoencoders for Multi-Label Image Classification
PROPOSAL: We propose a novel method, ICC-GAE, that utilizes graph autoencoders to model the complex interactions among data augmentation, optimizer, learning-rate schedule, and loss function. ICC-GAE encodes each component's configuration as a node in a graph, generating latent representations that capture inter-component correlations and nonlinear relationships.
CONTROLS: ICC-GAE will be compared to a variant using independent component representations (i.e., without graph autoencoder), as well as to ACOMTL, to evaluate its effectiveness in jointly optimizing multiple components.
COST: 2200 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: ICC-GAE is expected to improve the validation performance of ACOMTL on the aforementioned datasets, particularly when dealing with rare labels or complex label hierarchies. However, it may be computationally expensive for very large configuration spaces.

CONTROLS: The baseline compared to ICC-GAE-TGS remains the same, with additional ablations exploring the impact of varying graph traversal strategies and the involvement of additional historical data points.
COST: 2500 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: ICC-GAE-TGS is expected to outperform the original ICC-GAE by 2-5% on the validation set, especially in cases where the inter-component relationships are highly dynamic. However, its performance might degrade if the historical performance data is incomplete or biased.

textes.jumeau:
ACTION: ADD
TITLE: MetaConfig: Adaptive Multi-Label Image Classification Training with Learning-to-Configure
PROPOSAL: We propose to leverage the power of model-based optimization (MBO) to dynamically adapt the training configuration of a multi-label image classifier throughout the learning process. By maintaining a probabilistic representation of the optimal configuration and iteratively refining it, we can develop a learning-to-configure (L2C) mechanism that aligns with the evolving dynamics of training, effectively addressing the limitations of static configurations.
CONTROLS: We compare against a baseline of staged scheduling, where configurations are pre-determined and fixed at predefined milestones. Ablations include exploring individual components of the L2C mechanism, such as leveraging different variants of MBO algorithms (e.g., Bayesian optimization, evolutionary strategies) or excluding certain components from adaptation.
COST: 33,600
PREDICTION: Our approach, MetaConfig, significantly outperforms staged scheduling on multiple multi-label image classification datasets, showcasing improved convergence, reduced overfitting and enhanced learning of rare labels. However, scaling this method to larger models and datasets may be a challenge, where factors such as partially-deterministic exploration strategies and inadequate modeling of complex interaction effects could limit its generalizability.

textes.jumeau:
ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Augmentation Regulation: Co-Adaptation of Augmentation and Loss Functions for Multi-Label Classification
PROPOSAL: We aim to investigate the impact of dynamically co-adapting the data augmentation and loss functions on multi-label image classification. Specifically, we evaluate learning objectives that modulate augmentation strategies (e.g., cutout, mixup) to focus on specific label-pairs or classes, complemented with adaptive weighting of loss terms to balance the contributions of different labels. Our idea is to create an adaptive framework that not only finds optimal augmentation strategies but also identifies label-key augmentation interactions.
CONTROLS: To assess the standalone impact of deformation-based and total variance loss methods, we control for these baselines in comparison with the outcome from implementing Augmentation Regulation. Further analysis includes exploring variations of automatically learnable augmentation constraints (e.g., dropout techniques applied to augmentation tactics).
COST: 78,000
PREDICTION: By designing Augmentation Regulation and subsequently optimizing the interaction between augmentation and loss functions based on the unseen data characteristics, we expect substantial improvement in classification performance, weighted time to convergence and risk of excessive needed epochs, finding branding backbone models that are proficient at parsing specifics by trading carefully designed label-related augmentations together.

TITLE: MetaConfig: Adaptive Multi-Label Image Classification Training with Learning-to-Configure
PROPOSAL: We refine the learning-to-configure mechanism in MetaConfig to incorporate a more rigorous embedding of the probabilistic neural architecture and an exploration-exploitation trade-off leveraging Thompson sampling. Additionally, we evaluate the impact of using a curriculum learning strategy to gradually increase the complexity of the optimization space.
CONTROLS: Compare against the original MetaConfig and a variant that removes the Thompson sampling component, as well as evaluate the impact of different curriculum learning strategies.
COST: 2,460,000
PREDICTION: Our revised MetaConfig demonstrates further improvements in convergence and robustness to rare labels, while also showcasing its ability to adapt to changing data distributions. However, the increased complexity of the optimization space may lead to overfitting in certain scenarios.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Learning to Adapt: Multi-Task Learning for Multi-Label Image Classification with Adaptive Training Configurations
PROPOSAL: We propose to develop a multi-task learning framework that leverages the strengths of different training configurations for multi-label image classification. By learning to adapt between different configurations, our approach can dynamically switch between optimization strategies to handle changing data distributions and improve overall performance.
CONTROLS: We compare against a state-of-the-art multi-task learning approach and a fixed configuration baseline, as well as conduct ablation studies to evaluate the impact of different adaptation mechanisms.
COST: 315,000
PREDICTION: Our approach, Learning to Adapt, demonstrates improved robustness to changing data distributions and yields competitive performance on multiple multi-label image classification benchmarks. However, the computational cost of training and adapting between configurations may be high for large-scale models.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: MetaConfig: Adaptive Multi-Label Image Classification Training with Learning-to-Configure
PROPOSAL: We propose to leverage the power of model-based optimization (MBO) to dynamically adapt the training configuration of a multi-label image classifier throughout the learning process. By maintaining a probabilistic representation of the optimal configuration and iteratively refining it, we can develop a learning-to-configure (L2C) mechanism that aligns with the evolving dynamics of training, effectively addressing the limitations of static configurations.
CONTROLS: We compare against a baseline of staged scheduling, where configurations are pre-determined and fixed at predefined milestones. Ablations include exploring individual components of the L2C mechanism, such as leveraging different variants of MBO algorithms (e.g., Bayesian optimization, evolutionary strategies) or excluding certain components from adaptation.
COST: 101,000
PREDICTION: Our approach, MetaConfig, significantly outperforms staged scheduling on multiple multi-label image classification datasets, showcasing improved convergence, reduced overfitting and enhanced learning of rare labels. However, scaling this method to larger models and datasets may be a challenge, where factors such as partially-deterministic exploration strategies and inadequate modeling of complex interaction effects could limit its generalizability.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Augmentation Regulation: Co-Adaptation of Augmentation and Loss Functions for Multi-Label Classification
PROPOSAL: We aim to investigate the impact of dynamically co-adapting the data augmentation and loss functions on multi-label image classification. Specifically, we evaluate learning objectives that modulate augmentation strategies (e.g., cutout, mixup) to focus on specific label-pairs or classes, complemented with adaptive weighting of loss terms to balance the contributions of different labels. Our idea is to create an adaptive framework that not only finds optimal augmentation strategies but also identifies label-key augmentation interactions.
CONTROLS: To assess the standalone impact of deformation-based and total variance loss methods, we control for these baselines in comparison with the outcome from implementing Augmentation Regulation. Further analysis includes exploring variations of automatically learnable augmentation constraints (e.g., dropout techniques applied to augmentation tactics).

textes.jumeau:
ACTION: ADD 1
TITLE: Gradient-Based Dynamic Optimization of Multi-Label Image Classifiers
PROPOSAL: We propose to use a gradient-based method to dynamically adjust the training configuration of a multi-label image classifier. Specifically, we will analyze the gradient of the validation loss with respect to the training configuration, and update the configuration at each step in the direction of the maximum gradient. We will use a gradient-based optimizer (AdamW) to compute the gradient, and update the learning rate using a one-cycle policy. We will also use a novel tensor to store the gradients w.r.t. each component of the configuration, and use a attention mechanism to select the most informative components to update.
CONTROLS: (1) Static configuration baseline, where the training configuration is fixed at the beginning of training; (2) Random search of configuration space; (3) Gradient-based optimization with a fixed attention mechanism.
COST: 1500
PREDICTION: We expect to see a significant improvement in validation performance (10-15% mAP) and a reduction in training time (20-30%) compared to the static configuration baseline, with the proposed method achieving state-of-the-art performance on the PASCAL VOC 2012 dataset. However, this method may fail to generalize well to datasets with very different distributions or complexities.

textes.jumeau:
ACTION: ADD 2
TITLE: Online Meta-Learning for Multi-Label Image Classification
PROPOSAL: We propose to use online meta-learning to adapt the training configuration of a multi-label image classifier to the changing training data. Specifically, we will use the Model-Agnostic Meta-Learning (MAML) algorithm to learn a set of initialization parameters for the training configuration that can be adapted to different datasets. We will also use an episodic training strategy to partition the training data into a set of episodes, and adapt the configuration at each episode boundary to the changing data distribution.
CONTROLS: (1) Static configuration baseline; (2) Offline meta-learning ( MAML with episodic training).
COST: 2100
PREDICTION: We expect to see a significant improvement in validation performance (15-20% mAP) and a reduction in training time (30-40%) compared to the static configuration baseline, with the proposed method achieving state-of-the-art performance on the PASCAL VOC 2012 and COCO 2014 datasets. However, this method may require a large number of episodes and adaptation steps to converge, which may increase the computational cost.

ACTION: REVISE 2
TITLE: Online Meta-Learning for Multi-Label Image Classification (Revised)
PROPOSAL: We revise the online meta-learning proposal to add a feedback loop from the validation set to the meta-model. Specifically, we will use a validation set to compute a validation loss, and use this loss to update the meta-model's parameters and adapt the training configuration to the changing data distribution. We will also use a regularization term to prevent overfitting to the validation set.
CONTROLS: (1) Static configuration baseline; (2) Offline meta-learning (MAML with episodic training); (3) Baseline with feedback loop from training set only.
COST: 2100
PREDICTION: We expect to see a significant improvement in validation performance (18-22% mAP) and a reduction in training time (35-45%) compared to the static configuration baseline, with the proposed method achieving state-of-the-art performance on the PASCAL VOC 2012 and COCO 2014 datasets. However, this method may require a large number of episodes and adaptation steps to converge, and may overfit to the validation set if not regularized properly.

ACTION: ADD 3
TITLE: Hierarchical Configuration Search for Multi-Label Image Classification
PROPOSAL: We propose to use a hierarchical search strategy to search for the optimal training configuration for multi-label image classification. Specifically, we will use a coarse-to-fine search strategy, where we first search for the optimal strategy at a high level (e.g. batch size, optimizer), and then refine the search at a lower level (e.g. learning rate, data augmentation). We will use a reinforcement learning algorithm to guide the search, and use a novel policy gradient method to update the policy.
CONTROLS: (1) Static configuration baseline; (2) Random search of configuration space; (3) Hierarchical search with a random policy.
COST: 2400
PREDICTION: We expect to see a significant improvement in validation performance (20-25% mAP) and a reduction in search time (50-60%) compared to the random search baseline, with the proposed method achieving state-of-the-art performance on the PASCAL VOC 2012 and COCO 2014 datasets. However, this method may require a large number of iterations and a well-designed policy to converge, and may not scale well to very large configuration spaces.

ACTION: ADD 1
TITLE: Gradient-Based Dynamic Optimization of Multi-Label Image Classifiers
PROPOSAL: We propose to use a gradient-based method to dynamically adjust the training configuration of a multi-label image classifier. Specifically, we will analyze the gradient of the validation loss with respect to the training configuration, and update the configuration at each step in the direction of the maximum gradient. We will use a gradient-based optimizer (AdamW) to compute the gradient, and update the learning rate using a one-cycle policy. We will also use a novel tensor to store the gradients w.r.t. each component of the configuration, and use a attention mechanism to select the most informative components to update.
CONTROLS: (1) Static configuration baseline, where the training configuration is fixed at the beginning of training; (2) Random search of configuration space; (3) Gradient-based optimization with a fixed attention mechanism.
COST: 4500
PREDICTION: We expect to see a significant improvement in validation performance (10-15% mAP) and a reduction in training time (20-30%) compared to the static configuration baseline, with the proposed method achieving state-of-the-art performance on the PASCAL VOC 2012 dataset. However, this method may fail to generalize well to datasets with very different distributions or complexities.

ACTION: ADD 2
TITLE: Online Meta-Learning for Multi-Label Image Classification
PROPOSAL: We propose to use online meta-learning to adapt the training configuration of a multi-label image classifier to the changing training data. Specifically, we will use the Model-Agnostic Meta-Learning (MAML) algorithm to learn a set of initialization parameters for the training configuration that can be adapted to different datasets. We will also use an episodic training strategy to partition the training data into a set of episodes, and adapt the configuration at each episode boundary to the changing data distribution.
CONTROLS: (1) Static configuration baseline; (2) Offline meta-learning ( MAML with episodic training).
COST: 6300
PREDICTION: We expect to see a significant improvement in validation performance (15-20% mAP) and a reduction in training time (30-40%) compared to the static configuration baseline, with the proposed method achieving state-of-the-art performance on the PASCAL VOC 2012 and COCO 2014 datasets. However, this method may require a large number of episodes and adaptation steps to converge, which may increase the computational cost.

Specifically, we will use a validation set to compute a validation loss, and use this loss to update the meta-model's parameters and adapt the training configuration to the changing data distribution. We will also use a regularization term to prevent overfitting to the validation set.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Adaptive Configuration via Dynamic Meta-Optimizer
PROPOSAL: We introduce a meta-optimizer that takes as input the current state of the model, the training data, and the desired performance metrics, and outputs a configuration (data augmentation strategy, optimizer, learning-rate schedule, and loss function) that is tailored to the current stage of training. This meta-optimizer is trained using multi-task learning, where it is supervised by both the performance of the model and the optimization metrics (e.g., convergence rate, stability). The goal is to develop a system that can adaptively and jointly optimize the training components.
CONTROLS: Baseline: a static configuration; Ablation: using a fixed meta-optimizer or training it only on model performance metrics.
COST: 1662.2
PREDICTION: Our meta-optimizer should be able to find better configurations than a static configuration, and adapt to the evolving training state. However, it may suffer from overfitting if the training set is small or the optimization landscape is complex, and may not be able to capture the whole configuration space.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Multi-Task Meta-Learning for Joint Optimization of Augmentation and Optimizer
PROPOSAL: We explore a multi-task meta-learning approach that trains a meta-model to jointly optimize data augmentation strategies and optimizers. The meta-model is conditioned on the task-specific data characteristics and the performance metrics, allowing it to output a pair of augmentation strategy and optimizer that are tailored to the current stage of training. We evaluate this approach on a range of multi-label image classification benchmarks and compare it to various baselines, including our adaptive configuration via dynamic meta-optimizer from Proposal 1.
CONTROLS: Baseline: using a fixed augmentation strategy and optimizer; Ablation: training the meta-model only to optimize one of augmentation or optimizer.
COST: 4000
PREDICTION: Our multi-task meta-learning approach should be able to find better configurations than the baselines, especially for tasks with complex label correlations and class imbalances. However, it may require larger training sets and more compute resources to achieve reliable performance.

TITLE: investigating non-stationarity of the optimization landscape in multi-label image classification
PROPOSAL: We conduct a theoretical analysis of the non-stationarity of the optimization landscape in multi-label image classification. Specifically, we explore the effects of class imbalances, label correlations, and data augmentations on the optimizer dynamics and the convergence behavior of different optimization algorithms. We develop a set of mathematical models to describe these effects and provide insights into the underlying dynamics of the optimization process.
CONTROLS: Baseline: using standard optimization algorithms without any modifications.
COST: 2680
PREDICTION: Our analysis should provide valuable insights into the optimization dynamics in multi-label image classification, enabling the development of more effective optimization algorithms and strategies for addressing class imbalances and label correlations.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Transfer Learning for Optimization Algorithms: Can We Transfer Knowledge Across Tasks and Domains?
PROPOSAL: We investigate the possibility of transferring knowledge across tasks and domains for optimization algorithms in multi-label image classification. We propose a framework for transfer learning that leverages a shared space of optimization dynamics across tasks and domains, and explore the potential benefits of this approach. We also investigate the challenges and limitations of transfer learning in optimization, and provide insights into the development of more effective transfer learning strategies.
CONTROLS: Baseline: training optimization algorithms from scratch for each task and domain; Ablation: transferring knowledge across tasks but not domains, or vice versa.
COST: 3360
PREDICTION: Our transfer learning framework should enable more efficient optimization and better generalization across tasks and domains, reducing the need for extensive hyperparameter tuning and domain-specific expertise. However, it may require careful selection of tasks and domains for transfer, as well as effective methods for adapting the transferred knowledge to the new task or domain.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: End-to-End System for Adaptive Optimization in Multi-Label Image Classification
PROPOSAL: We integrate all our previous proposals into an end-to-end system for adaptive optimization in multi-label image classification. The system leverages the adaptive configuration via dynamic meta-optimizer with partial model adaptation, multi-task meta-learning for joint optimization of augmentation and optimizer, learning to schedule learning rate via augmented actor-critic algorithm, loss function adaptation via hierarchical reinforcement learning, online hyperparameter tuning via Bayesian optimization with surrogate modeling, ensemble of configurators, investigating non-stationarity of the optimization landscape in multi-label image classification, and transfer learning for optimization algorithms to achieve state-of-the-art performance in multi-label image classification.
CONTROLS: Baseline: using standard optimization algorithms without any modifications.
COST: 40000
PREDICTION: Our end-to-end system should achieve a significant improvement over existing optimization algorithms for multi-label image classification, by adaptively configuring the optimization process to the specific task and dataset. However, it may require careful tuning of hyperparameters and more compute resources to achieve reliable performance, and may be challenging to generalize to other domains and tasks.
